Does the national strategy/policy include an action plan with measures to be implemented in the open data field?

For Explanation:
If yes, please briefly describe the main measures described by the action plan.
column13: Yes. National strategy of the informatization of the public administration 2021 defines these measures in area of open data:1) To transpose into legislative framework PSI Directive 2019, 2) To ensure that public bodies will be publish information primary as open data, in open formats and register them at data.gov.sk, 3) To publish HVD via API, 4) To provide methological, technical, educational support to public bodies and make available re-usable technical solutions that will help publish data, 5) To support accessibility of research data by  FAIR principle incorporated into national measures, 6) To implement methodologies, tools, standards, principles measured within ODMI, etc. https://www.mirri.gov.sk/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/Narodna-koncepcia-informatizacie-verejnej-spravy-2021.pdf (p. 56). As mentioned above, MIRRI is currently working on the Action plan of National strategy of the informatization of the public administration with detailed description of goals, milestones, measures. Additionally, working paper Strategic priortity Management of Data is in the process too - this document will update previous Strategic priority Open Data from 2017 that is still valid.

column6:
Does the national strategy/policy outline measures to support the reuse of open data by the private sector?

For Explanation:
* If yes, please briefly describe the measures.
column13: Yes, one of the main goal of the Strategic priority of open data  is to release the economic potential of open government data. It expects establishment of a strong open data industry in IT technologies, e.g. data analyses, innovative startups. https://www.mirri.gov.sk/wp-content/uploads/2018/10/SP_Otvorene_udaje_schvalena-2.pdf Measures are e.g.  focus on publishing the most requested datasets by public, ideally via API, to support re-use of open data in commercial/noncommercial solutions, to increase quality of open data, publication of open data via API, accessibility of open data in english language. Additionally, since 2020, Governmental organization and public administration has an access to financial resources within Operational Program Integrated Infrastructure that provides founding for individual IT projects that aim to accomplish strategic goals of the government in the IT segment. Multiple open calls "Data Management of public administration" aim to support accessibility of open data , ***HVD, the most requested datasets by public*** that are considered as datasets with high potential to be re-used. https://www.mirri.gov.sk/projekty/projekty-esif/operacny-program-integrovana-infrastruktura/prioritna-os-7-informacna-spolocnost/vyzvania-a-vyzvy/vyzva-c-opii-2021-7-15-dop/index.html

column6:
Are there any processes in place to assess if public sector bodies are charging for data above marginal cost? (please see directive (EU) 2019/1024 on open data and the reuse of public sector information).

For Explanation:
* If yes, please specify the process(es).
column13:
2025:
Slovak parliament adopted amendment of Freedom of Information Act which allowed public bodies to charge if extremely extensive information search is needed. This amendment was stopped by Constitutional court in March 2025.
2024:
According to Freedom of Information Act (https://www.slov-lex.sk/pravne-predpisy/SK/ZZ/2000/211/ § 21) all information shall be available free of charge, only marginal cost can be charged (such as cost of copying, cost of technical mediums or postal costs). Every public body shall have its own directive on providing information according to act and on charged fees. (f.e. Ministry of Finance - https://www.mfsr.sk/sk/verejnost/informacny-servis/poskytovanie-informacii/smernica-zabezpeceni-slobodneho-pristupu-k-informaciam-podmienkach-mf-sr/, https://www.mfsr.sk/sk/verejnost/informacny-servis/poskytovanie-informacii/sadzobnik-spravnych-poplatkov/, marginal cost are not charged if less than 6,64 EUR). If any unjustified fees are charged, these requirements can be reviewed by a court.

column13:
1) Uvostat.sk - portal that analyses open data on public procurement of the central government bodies, government companies and institution. By analysing and visualisation of data, public purchases are more transparent and understandable (the most successful companies, contractors), the "biggest" government buyers and the scope of missbehavior is limited.  https://uvostat.sk/topstatistiky Uvostat makes also various type of analyses about efficiency of public spending/ or potential biases based on the data on public procurements https://uvostat.sk/blog Project led by volunteer, programator and activist Miroslav Babič. Datasets: https://data.slovensko.sk/datasety?publisher=https%3A%2F%2Fdata.gov.sk%2Fid%2Flegal-subject%2F31797903
2) www.Zindex.sk is a tool for analysing public procurement  data. Based on data, it measures how transparently and efficient  particular contracting authority has acted. Zindex compares individual contracting authority and gives them feedback - where they thrive and where they have reserves. It analyses public procurements of contral government organizations, self-governing regions and other public administration bodies. Based on evaluation, it creates various rankings https://www.zindex.sk/category/detail/KRAJ/11/ Datasets are same as for Uvostat.sk

the 2023-2025 National Action Plan for the implementation of the Open Government Partnership aims to develop new commitments in areas such as:
● anti-corruption & beneficial owners;
● access to justice;
● digital transformation and innovation;
● fiscal transparency;
● public services;

 Anti-corruption. Awareness and education for anti-corruption mechanisms are two areas provided in the Cross-Cutting Strategy Anti-Corruption, 2015-2023 and its action plans. Specifically, measures are provided in the function of raising awareness and education of the general public on the consequences of corruption, promoting the public and increasing confidence in anti -corruption mechanisms, as well as increasing civil society involvement in these initiatives. The measures provided in the ISAC 2015-2020 and the Action Plan in force of 2020-2023 have influenced the creation of a climate of cooperation between the public and public institutions. Qualitative and efficient mechanisms for prevention and awareness of corruption have been created, there is good cooperation but more frequency is required.
The Ministry of Justice has a communication and visibility strategy, and an annual action plan with activities and initiatives with CSOs and interest groups. Annual, regular editions of the Week of Integrity since 2020, a close collaboration with business, the CSO and the Academy are good evidence but also to be replicated throughout the year. Continuing work by intensifying efforts to raise public awareness and education will create appropriate conditions for a society aware of the danger of corruption and with high confidence in public institutions, improving the public perception of corruption, not only by Local and regional and international organizations such as Transparency International.                                                                                                                                                                                                            Access to Justice: This component has found wide scope by being materialized and strongly related to the
implementation of the justice reform, the Crosscutting Justice Strategy (CSJS), the Crosscutting Strategy for Juvenile Justice (CSJJ), the Strategy for Public Legal Education(SPLE), and other measures taken by the Government in fulfillment of its mission
for an open, transparent and accountable governance/policy. With the initiation of the Justice Reform, a deep reform that is affecting in its entirety every element of the current justice system, a reformation of the legal aid system was also initiated, offering a new spirit, in sync with the requirements and legislation of the European Union and as a facilitating mechanism used to increase access to justice for groups who do not have the financial means to pay legal fees to the bodies/courts and at the same time to enable legal
counseling or protection. Free legal aid programs aim to bring the justice system closer to the needs of citizens. For this reason, this component is focused on providing effective but also accessible and affordable legal remedies for solving problems.                                          Fiscal Transparency: The public finance management reform continues to be a priority of the Albanian government not only as one of the preconditions for accession to the European Union under public administration reform (PAR), but also as part of the Open Government Partnership aims at supporting a more developed economy with better services to citizens. Satisfactory progress in the implementation of reforms to improve public financial management. Referring to the 2021 SIGMA monitoring report1, the overall trajectory for Albania in PFM is upwards, from 2.8 in 2017 to 3.3 in 2021, and is above the regional average of 3.1. Compared to the regional average, performance is similar or stronger in each indicator in the PFM domain, except for the functioning of internal audit (IA). Most pronounced is the strong performance in the domains of public procurement and the foundations for the functioning of Financial Management Control (FMC), IA and external audit.                                                                                                                                        PROMOTION OF DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION AND INNOVATION: E-Albania acts as a front-end point for government institutions to deliver their services, thusoperating as a one stop single access point to citizens on obtaining online government services,
as well as information on public services 24/7. By offering more than 1200 electronic services, the portal has improved the accessibility of information about public services, the level of public awareness about the procedures of public service delivery, and has most importantly acted as a robust catalyst in decreasing queues in public agencies’ receptions, reducing

column13:
Law no. 33/2022 "On open data and reuse of public sector information" in Article 10 "Cost of reuse" provides that:
1. Reuse of documents, as a rule, is offered free of charge.
2. Reuse of documents may be made against a fee to cover additional costs for reasons of reproduction, provision of distribution of documents, for anonymization of personal data, as well as for measures taken to protect trade secret information.
3. Exceptions to the provision of documents free of charge:
a) public sector bodies, which, according to the special legislation for their operation, provide income to cover a significant part of the costs related to the performance of their public duties;
b) libraries, including university libraries, museums and archives;
c) public enterprises.
 4. The income from providing and allowing the reuse of documents cannot be higher than the administrative cost for the collection, production, reproduction, distribution and storage of data, and, in cases where it is applicable, the anonymization of personal data and measures taken to protect trade secret information.
5. For each case where the fee is applied, the methodology, measure and use of the fee must be determined by a decision of the Council of Ministers. The public sector body that applies fees for the right of reuse makes it public on its website, as well as on the unique government open data portal.
Article 17 "Reuse of specific sets of high value data" point 4 provides:
4. By decision of the Council of Ministers, public sector bodies may be exempted from the obligation to provide high-value data free of charge for a period not longer than 2 years, in the event that their free provision will had a substantial impact on the budget of these bodies.
From the monitoring carried out so far by the Commissioner for the Right to Information, it results that only some public sector bodies have approved costs for the data they provide. This is provided for in their specific legislation, which must be adapted to the provisions of the law on open data.

column13:
At the beginning of this year, the Commissioner for the Right to Information and Protection of Personal Data organized an event on "Understanding and Implementing the Law on Open Data and the Reuse of Public Sector Information." At the end of April, AKSHI, in collaboration with World Bank partners, held a workshop on open data, where best European practices and the assessment of open data readiness in Albania were shared, with participants from academia, the public sector, and beyond.                                                                          Response to the research team: The event by the Commissioner for the Right to Information and Protection of Personal Data has been organized in 24/02/2025. https://idp.al/2025/02/24/te-dhenat-e-hapura-komisioneri-dervishi-rrisin-transparencen-dhe-mireqeverisjen-sjellin-zhvillim-dhe-inovacion/ The Office of the Commissioner for the Right to Information and Protection of Personal Data, in cooperation with the EU Good Governance Project, organized a roundtable with public institutions and state-owned enterprises to discuss the implementation of the new Law on Open Data and Reuse of Public Sector Information.
The discussion focused on the importance of managing and publishing public data through the national portal opendata.gov.al, as a tool to increase transparency and accountability. Emphasis was placed on the growing volume of public data in Albania and the legal obligation to make it open and reusable, despite past institutional reluctance due to concerns over misuse or criticism.
Open data was presented as a driver of innovation, improved governance, citizen engagement, and more efficient public services. The law redefines the role of public institutions—from holding information to providing it—and requires strong cooperation and alignment with EU standards. The centralized portal aims to simplify access and maximize the value of data for businesses, citizens, and public entities alike.                                                            The exact date of the workshop organized by AKSHI and World Bank Partners is 30/04/2025. This workshop was organized to foster dialogue and knowledge exchange on open data practices and to assess the readiness for open data use in Albania. Participants included representatives from ministries, governmental institutions, academia, businesses, startups, international organizations, and open data experts from the European Union.

During the workshop, the role of open data in enhancing institutional transparency, promoting innovation, and improving the quality of public services was discussed. The current state of data in Albania was analyzed, highlighting both good practices and challenges that require further attention.

A special focus was placed on fostering collaboration between state institutions and international partners to develop long-term strategies for publishing and utilizing open data. Successful international experiences and practices were shared, with discussions on how these can be adapted to the Albanian context.
The workshop also addressed issues related to increasing access to electronic services, improving user experience, and developing citizens' digital skills to actively engage in digital transformation and strengthen digital governance.
Key topics covered included best concepts and practices in open data, assessing Albania’s readiness, the economic and social impact of open data, as well as ensuring data interoperability and protection.

2025:
Our Open Data portal is custom-built using .NET Core 8 and follows the Clean Architecture pattern. It is not based on uData or CKAN, but instead is a fully tailored solution designed to meet national requirements. The portal supports data publication in multiple formats (JSON, XML, CSV, RDF in Turtle format) and aligns with the DCAT-AP standard. It features a custom SPARQL endpoint for RDF queries, uses SQL Server with optimized indexing and views for performance, and employs Hangfire for background tasks like harvesting and report generation. Asynchronous logging and dataset access tracking are also integrated to support analytics and reporting.

column13:
Yes, we provide tools and functionalities to assist data publishers in ensuring high-quality metadata. We have implemented a dedicated management portal, available at https://admin.opendata.gov.al, where data providers can log in using their Entra ID credentials managed by the National Agency for Information Society (NAIS).
Within this portal, the publishing module includes a simple and intuitive form that guides users through the process of entering dataset metadata. Key fields such as category, license, media type, and file type are either mandatory or controlled, helping to ensure consistency and compliance with DCAT-AP standards.
To further support metadata quality, the system performs real-time validation using the Metadata Quality Assurance (MQA) methodology. With every dataset creation or update, a quality score is calculated and displayed to the user, enabling publishers to assess and improve their metadata before publishing.

column6:
Do you set any standards on metadata quality that data providers must abide by (e.g. on the use of licence, minimum metadata describes, use of certain DCAT-AP properties, etc)

For Explanation:
* If yes, please describe the standards you have in place, i.e. what is minimum information the metadata should describe
column13:
Yes, we have set standards on metadata quality that data providers must adhere to. We have implemented the Metadata Quality Assessment (MQA) method, which ensures that datasets meet minimum quality standards. The minimum acceptable metadata quality is set to Good, which corresponds to reaching a score of at least 221 points according to our MQA evaluation.
These standards ensure that essential metadata elements — such as title, description, license, access rights, publisher, and download URL — are consistently included and correctly formatted. This ensures that metadata is complete, interoperable, and aligned with open data principles.
To support data providers, we have integrated these standards into the publishing process through our Open Data Management Portal. The publishing form enforces the required fields and provides real-time validation based on MQA scoring. Data providers receive immediate feedback on metadata quality and are guided to correct any issues before submission.
The structure of the publishing form and the required metadata fields are also documented in the user manual, which is shared with data providers to ensure they are aware of the standards and how to comply with them.

* If the portal does not follow the DCAT-AP framework, please describe how interoperability with DCAT-AP is ensured
column13:
Yes, our national portal follows the DCAT-AP framework to ensure interoperability and standardization in the description of datasets. Compliance with DCAT-AP is ensured through the implementation of rules and checks that validate the metadata for every dataset before it is published. We calculate metadata quality in real time using the MQA method (Metadata Quality Assessment), ensuring that datasets meet the required standards for completeness and consistency.
We also regularly review and update the metadata to ensure continued adherence to the DCAT-AP framework.

column6: What is the percentage of metadata on your portal that is DCAT-AP compliant, in terms of mandatory classes?
column13:
The significant improvement in DCAT-AP compliance on our portal is the result of a complete redevelopment of the national Open Data portal over the past year. In designing the new platform, we adopted best practices from leading open data portals, particularly data.europa.eu.
A key part of this redevelopment was the implementation of a new management panel that enables data providers to publish datasets through a structured, user-friendly form. This form has been designed to collect all the necessary metadata fields in line with DCAT-AP standards. Required fields for both datasets and their distributions — such as title, access rights, license, format, language, and publisher details — are either mandatory or automatically inferred by the system (e.g., media type, format, and file size based on the uploaded file).
Upon submission, the system generates DCAT-AP-compliant metadata automatically. Furthermore, we validate the metadata using the MQA (Metadata Quality Assurance) methodology to ensure consistency and conformance.
Additionally, we performed a full migration of datasets from the previous version of the portal. As part of this migration, all existing metadata was regenerated using the new system and fully aligned with the DCAT-AP standard.
These initiatives collectively explain the marked improvement in our compliance.

column6: What is the percentage of datasets whose metadata provides a reference to where the data can be downloaded, or its API accessed (“download-URL” in the DCAT-AP specification)?
column13:
Over 90% of the datasets on our portal include metadata with a valid downloadURL, as defined in the DCAT-AP specification.
In our new Open Data portal, every dataset distribution must either include an uploaded file (hosted on our portal) or provide a direct download URL pointing to an external source. In both cases, the system automatically generates or stores the appropriate downloadURL in the metadata.
Previously, in the old version of the portal, DCAT-AP was not implemented and downloadURL metadata was often missing. However, during the migration to the new platform, we regenerated all metadata to conform to DCAT-AP standards and ensured that every distribution now includes a valid downloadURL.
This approach guarantees that users can reliably access the actual data behind the metadata, whether it is hosted on our infrastructure or externally.

column6: What is the percentage of datasets whose metadata provides a reference to a web page from where the data can be accessed (“access-URL in the DCAT-AP specification)?
column13:
Over 90% of the datasets on our portal include metadata with a valid accessURL, in line with the DCAT-AP specification.
In our current platform, every dataset is accessible through a dedicated page on the portal. As part of the metadata generation process, the system automatically sets the accessURL to the specific URL of the dataset’s public page on our portal. This ensures that users can always access contextual information and available distributions related to the dataset.
During the migration from the old portal, we regenerated all metadata and systematically assigned an accessURL for each dataset based on its new location within the portal.
As a result, the vast majority of our datasets now include a consistent and valid accessURL, improving transparency, traceability, and alignment with open data best practices.

column13:
2025:
Yes, France has a national open data policy supported by a comprehensive legal and strategic framework. It includes the full transposition of the EU Open Data Directive and is built on both constitutional principles and sectoral regulations. 1. Foundational Legal Basis - Article 15 of the 1789 Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen establishes the right of citizens to hold public officials accountable, laying the constitutional foundation for access to public data. 2. Key Legislation - Law of 17 July 1978 on access to administrative documents, now codified in the Code des relations entre le public et l’administration (CRPA). - Law for a Digital Republic (2016), which introduced the principle of “open data by default” and enshrined the obligation to publish certain datasets as open data. URL: https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/jorf/id/JORFTEXT000033202746 - DINUM Decree (modified in April 2023) confirming the mission of the Interministerial Digital Directorate in coordinating and promoting data opening. URL: https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/loda/id/JORFTEXT000047478124 3. EU Directive - The Open Data Directive (Directive (EU) 2019/1024) has been fully transposed into French law. Most of its principles were already present in national legislation, including free reuse and the definition of high-value datasets. 4. Sectoral Legislation For example : - Additional laws reinforce open data in specific fields: - Mobility (Law on the Orientation of Mobilities): https://www.ecologie.gouv.fr/loi-dorientation-des-mobilites - Research (Open access to public research data): https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/codes/texte_lc/LEGITEXT000006071190/ - Environment and others also include open data requirements. 5. Strategic Frameworks These legal elements are complemented by strategic documents, such as: - DINUM Roadmap: https://www.numerique.gouv.fr/uploads/Feuille-de-route-DINUM.pdf - Data & Territories Report: https://www.transformation.gouv.fr/files/ressource/Rapport_Mission_Data_Territoires.pdf - Joint Digital and Data Roadmap of the State and territories: https://www.info.gouv.fr/france-nation-verte/a-proposfeuille-de-route-numerique-donnees These elements together form a robust, coherent national open data policy combining legal obligations with strategic guidance and sectoral adaptation.
2024:
2024:
Among the new developments in terms of policy, we can mention:

The roadmap of the DINUM, which places significant emphasis on valorizing and harnessing data as a lever for the effectiveness of public action.

https://www.numerique.gouv.fr/uploads/Feuille-de-route-DINUM.pdf
The Data and Territories report dedicated to enhancing access to public services and the deployment of digital technology in territories, which aims notably to establish governance to facilitate dialogue between the State and local authorities on data and to facilitate access to data for local authorities.

https://www.transformation.gouv.fr/files/ressource/Rapport_Mission_Data_Territoires.pdf.      The State and the territories have also co-constructed a technical and organizational strategy and developed a common action plan :  the "Digital and Data" Roadmap, created with more than 300 national and territorial public agents : https://www.info.gouv.fr/france-nation-verte/a-proposfeuille-de-route-numerique-donnees
2023:
The open data policy in France is called “Politique d’ouverture et de partage des données publiques”. The French government and the local authorities are strongly committed to opening government data and never ceases to reaffirm their desire to work toward.

Article 15 of the Declaration of the Rights of Man and the Citizen of 1789, which is part of the French constitution, states that Society has the right to hold any Public Official accountable for its administration. **This principle created very early a right to access the data and never stoped guided all the evolution in open data policy in France.**

The law of 17 July 1978 on freedom of access to administrative documents (”loi CADA”) establishes a framework on access to information, codified in the Code of relations between the public and the administration (Code des relations entre le public et l’administration).

The cornerstone of the French open data policy is the 2016’s Digital Republic Law [https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/jorf/id/JORFTEXT000033202746](https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/jorf/id/JORFTEXT000033202746), also transposed in the Code of relations between the public and the administration. **The Digital Republic Law** led to significant progress in terms of open data and national data policy including the “**Open Data by default**” principle and the Public Service Data.

**According to the french decree of october 25 2019, the Interministerial Digital directorate is in charge of the coordination and the promotion of the inventory, governance, production, circulation, use and opening of data. [https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/loda/id/JORFTEXT000039281619](https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/loda/id/JORFTEXT000039281619)**

**Recently edited by a modificative decree of April 22 2023, the french government confirmed the importance allocated to the open data policy in it’s governmental roadmap.**

[https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/loda/id/JORFTEXT000047478124](https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/loda/id/JORFTEXT000047478124?init=true&page=1&query=%222022%2F868%22&searchField=ALL&tab_selection=all)

In April 2021, Prime Minister Jean Castex, through a circular on the national data, algorithms and source code policy, reiterated the need for an ambitious open data policy, and called on the Government to make data a strategic priority: "I would like the Government to have a renewed ambition in terms of the use, openness and circulation of public data, algorithms and source codes for the benefit of users, researchers, innovators and all our fellow citizens." [https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/circulaire/id/45162](https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/circulaire/id/45162).

On top of the general framework, open data policy is also characterised by specific sectoral legislation. Here are few recent examples.

- The law on the orientation of mobility [https://www.ecologie.gouv.fr/loi-dorientation-des-mobilites](https://www.ecologie.gouv.fr/loi-dorientation-des-mobilites) with specific disposition on transport data including real-time data.
- The changes to the Research code [https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/codes/texte_lc/LEGITEXT000006071190/](https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/codes/texte_lc/LEGITEXT000006071190/) implemented by the Digital Republic Law regarding open research data

The Open Data Directive has already been transposed [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/NIM/?uri=uriserv:OJ.L_.2019.172.01.0056.01.ENG](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/NIM/?uri=uriserv:OJ.L_.2019.172.01.0056.01.ENG) and most provisions were already part of the French legal framework.

**In 2022, the french lawmaker once again get into high gear with the adoption of the “3DS” law (differentiation, decentralization, deconcentration and simplification) which stated for the acceleration of the sharing data processes between administrations, and especially between central administrations and local administrations.** [https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/jorf/id/JORFSCTA000045197502](https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/jorf/id/JORFSCTA000045197502)

**During the last Inter-ministerial Committee for Public Transformation (CITP), the Prime Minister announced that each ministry will adopt new ministerial roadmaps on data, algorithms and source code policy by the end of 2023. These new roadmaps, symbol of an invariably renewed ambition, present the ambitions and challenges of public policies related to data, algorithms and public source codes, the concrete priority actions to be launched and the governance set up to ensure their implementation.**

[https://www.gouvernement.fr/actualite/offrir-un-accompagnement-clair-et-des-solutions-rapides-au-francais](https://www.gouvernement.fr/actualite/offrir-un-accompagnement-clair-et-des-solutions-rapides-au-francais)

These strategies are often aligned with national objectives but adapted to local priorities and contexts. Coordination – Open Data France Open Data France is a national association that brings together local governments committed to open data. It provides support, tools, and coordination to develop and harmonize local open data strategies across France. URL: https://www.opendatafrance.net/ Examples : Rennes Métropole – RUDI Project (Rennes Urban Data Interface) URL: https://blog.rudi.bzh/ Description: RUDI is an ambitious local data governance initiative supported by Rennes Métropole. It aims to develop a shared data platform and ecosystem involving public, private, and civil society actors. The strategy promotes transparency, data sharing, and citizen engagement through structured governance and local partnerships. Métropole de Lyon – Open Data Approach URL: https://data.grandlyon.com/portail/fr/demarche Description: Lyon’s open data strategy focuses on transparency, innovation, and support for local services. It includes a dedicated data platform, thematic datasets (e.g. mobility, environment), and regular dialogue with users and reusers to improve accessibility and quality.
2024:
2024:
See the Data and Territories report https://www.transformation.gouv.fr/files/ressource/Rapport_Mission_Data_Territoires.pdf
2023:
Subnational governments (regions for NUTS 1, departments for NUTS 3, and communes as local administrative units) remain independent in their own strategy and are not obliged to publish their data on the national portal data.gouv.fr. Nonetheless, the principle of open data by default enshrined in the law (Code des relations entre le public et l'administration) applies to all subnational governments with at least 3500 inhabitants.

Every year, more and more local actors are adopting strategies within this framework. According to the last local open data observatory provided by the french national association “Open Data France”, the number of local authorities involved in an open data strategy increased by 18% compared to 2021. Today, there are approximately 250 local open data portals in France.

(https://www.observatoire-opendata.fr/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/Copie-de-Observatoire_Open_Data_Territoires_Edition2022.pptx-1.pdf)

For example : 

- Lyon : https://data.grandlyon.com/demarche)
- Lille : https://opendata.lillemetropole.fr/page/demarche/
- Nantes’ metropolitan data charter https://metropole.nantes.fr/charte-donnee
- DataSud : https://www.datasud.fr/presentation-du-projet-datasud/

On top of that, the data, algorithms and source codes roadmap of the Ministry of Territorial Cohesion points out the strategy of the State on how to improve data sharing between national and local actors. 

(https://www.numerique.gouv.fr/uploads/feuillederoute_mctrct.pdf)

In a different way, the french government also allocated a “Digital transformation of local authorities (ITN7)" fund, part of the France Relance plan, in order to grant various projects to help local authorities to adopt open data practices and draw their own strategies in this area. This fund contributed to the implementation of “Collec-Data”, a praised project on the occasion of “Digital and Territories day”, that has helped Breton local authorities to scale up their use of open data. The Collec-data platform now allows more than 1600 local authorities to automatically publish their data and will soon allows them to massify the publication of data and systematize the valorization.

(https://www.numerique.gouv.fr/actualites/retour-sur-la-journee-numerique-et-territoires/)

This movement is also promised to a strong acceleration thanks to the adoption of the 3DS law, previously mentioned, which is going to facilitate the coordination of data exchanges between the national and local levels. In addition, and to support this movement, the french minister of transformation and public service charged three politicians to identify the opportunities for the enhancement of data exploitation by local authorities with a strong impact-driving focus. This analysis should help local authorities in the construction of their own data policies and strategies at their own level and incentivise their initiatives in the open data field.

(https://www.transformation.gouv.fr/files/presse/cp_utilisation_donnee_collectivites_territoriales_mission.pdf)

Moreover, the national association Open Data France is also currently conducting a study on the whole french territory to identify all the local open data use cases, in close connection with many different public bodies such as the national portal data.gouv.fr.

(https://www.opendatafrance.net/2023/04/12/data-impact-identifions-ensemble-les-cas-dusages-territoriaux-de-donnees/)

column6:
Does the national strategy/policy include an action plan with measures to be implemented in the open data field?

For Explanation:
If yes, please briefly describe the main measures described by the action plan.
column13:
2025:
Yes, the national strategy includes action plans with concrete measures for the open data field. The national and ministerial roadmaps clearly identify datasets to be opened or created. These plans define priorities, timelines, and responsible actors. The datasets listed in these roadmaps are centrally referenced on: https://ouverture.data.gouv.fr A key example is the France Nation Verte roadmap, which outlines numerous datasets to be opened to support ecological planning and public policy transparency. It specifies thematic priorities (e.g. environment, energy, biodiversity), associated datasets, and the public bodies responsible for their publication. URL: https://www.info.gouv.fr/france-nation-verte/a-proposfeuille-de-route-numerique-donnees
2024:
2024:
Roadmap are still produced for each ministries. The latest are not available yet. The State and the territories have also co-constructed a technical and organizational strategy and developed a common action plan :  the "Digital and Data" Roadmap, created with more than 300 national and territorial public agents : https://www.info.gouv.fr/france-nation-verte/a-proposfeuille-de-route-numerique-donnees
2023:
In April 2021, the Prime Minister, in a circular, underlined that the national data policy must be a strategic priority for the State and its relations with local authorities and private actors. The circular mandates that:

- All ministries, as well as all regional State authorities (préfets) have to nominate a CDO in order to ensure a data opening governance at the highest hierarchical level;
- The Interministerial Director for Digital Affairs, acting as General Data Administrator, will coordinate the network of CDOs
- An "ombudsman for general interest data" will be nominated to negotiate with private actors that have data that is deemed to be of general interest;
- The Ministry of Research will set up a charter to speed up the processing of requests from researchers wishing to access data;
- Each Ministry will need to animate the ecosystems of data and source code reusers, in order to identify high value-added datasets, define possible standards and encourage sharing, with a focus on the Open Government Partnership forum as an arena for such exchanges;
- Each ministry will have to set up a roadmap for data, algorithms and source code strategy, with actions and deadlines. The roadmap will also list the skills in those fields within the personnel of the ministries.
- Open data will be referenced in the national portal data.gouv.fr

Moreover, the Government made a commitment to open more high-impact key datasets, APIs and source codes in the near future. Some of those engagements are marking out their action until 2025.** The list of such datasets and their publication schedule is available here (https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/datasets/tableau-de-suivi-des-ouvertures-de-donnees-codes-sources-et-api-publics-avril-2021/)

column6:
Does the national strategy/policy outline measures to incentivise the publication of and access to real-time or dynamic data?

For Explanation:
* If yes, please briefly describe the measures.
column13:
2025:
A key focus is on the enhancement of real-time public transport data, as described in the national “France Nation Verte” and sectoral roadmaps. The objectives include: - Achieving 100% real-time information coverage for public transport services - Publishing a comprehensive, real-time database on road conditions and parking availability - Improving the real-time availability of environmental data, such as water withdrawals and hydrological measurements
2024:
2024:
The enhancement of real-time information for public transport is one of the main actions of the previously mentioned roadmap.
Among the objectives are:

Achieving 100% real-time information for public transport
Providing a comprehensive real-time database of road and parking information


Improving the real-time availability of data on water withdrawals







2023:
The 2015 law on growth, activity and equal economic opportunities (Loi Macron) had set obligations to publish data on real time transport schedules [https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/loda/id/JORFTEXT000030978561/](https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/loda/id/JORFTEXT000030978561/). The 2019 law on the orientation of mobilities [https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/jorf/id/JORFTEXT000039666574/](https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/jorf/id/JORFTEXT000039666574/) made a step further by not only transposing into national law the European Delegated Regulation 2017/1926 of 31 May 2017 [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32017R1926](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32017R1926), but also by including dynamic data. According to this law, static and dynamic travel and traffic data, as well as historical traffic data, shall be made accessible and reusable.

The Open Data parliamentary mission led by MP Éric Bothorel also points out the key role of real-time data, especially within the transport domain.

The transport.data.gouv.fr task force deploys special efforts to promote real-time data. This includes [documentation](https://doc.transport.data.gouv.fr/producteurs/operateurs-de-transport-regulier-de-personnes/temps-reel-des-transports-en-commun) on standardisation, an [inventory of real time](https://transport.data.gouv.fr/real_time) data yet to be standardised, and [discussion with stakeholders](https://doc.transport.data.gouv.fr/documentation/liste-des-rencontres-publiques/20-09-2018-transport-regulier-temps-reel).

The data, algorithms and source codes roadmap of the Ministry of Ecological Transition clearly underlines the need for systematic access to real-time data, especially related to environmental phenomena, to improve the impact of environmental policies. [https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/datasets/r/25f0f375-df81-4cc5-8eae-c277a729923f](https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/datasets/r/25f0f375-df81-4cc5-8eae-c277a729923f)

column6:
Does the national strategy/policy outline measures to incentivise the publication of and access to citizen-generated data?

For Explanation:
* If yes, please briefly describe the measures.
column13:
2025:
The roadmap explicitly supports the national portal data.gouv.fr as an open platform accessible to all—public sector bodies, but also individuals, journalists, researchers, associations, and activists. On data.gouv.fr, anyone can publish data using the same tools and processes as official institutions. A certification badge is used to distinguish data published by verified public entities, but no technical restrictions are imposed on citizen-generated content. This openness to citizen-generated data is a core principle of data.gouv.fr and is fully embedded in France’s open data strategy.
2024:
All the measures outlined in the roadmap of the Ministry of Civil Service and Public Transformation (Ministère de la transformation et de la fonction publiques) related to the national open data portal [data.gouv.fr](http://data.gouv.fr) aim also at incentivising the publication and the access to citizen-generated data. The portal allows everyone to publish data, with a badge to identify data from official sources (i.e. public sector organisations). But the guides, the publication process, and the tools are the same, whether the data provider is a ministry or a journalist, an activist, a student.

For example, the tools that help improve the quality of data, [schema.data.gouv.fr](http://schema.data.gouv.fr) and publier.etalab.studio, are both free and open to use.

column6:
Does the national strategy/policy foster the discoverability of the aforementioned types of data from your country on data.europa.eu?

For Explanation:
* If yes, please briefly describe how.
column13:
2025:
Yes, the national strategy fosters the discoverability of French data—including citizen-generated data and data from non-public stakeholders—on the European data portal, data.europa.eu. Significant investments have been made to improve DCAT compliance, ensuring that metadata from data.gouv.fr is correctly structured and interoperable. This enables seamless harvesting and high-quality display of French datasets on data.europa.eu. As a result, not only public sector data but also citizen-generated data, including datasets from journalists, NGOs, and individuals, are discoverable at the European level, supporting transparency, reuse, and cross-border innovation.
2024:
2024:
We invested a lot in DCAT lately to make sure we can display data from data.gouv.fr on data.europa.eu in the best possible maneur. Citizen generated data and data from other stakeholders such as medias are discoverable.
2023:
The French open data policy makes it mandatory for central government and national public sector organisations to publish data on [data.gouv.fr](http://data.gouv.fr) (the obligation is stated both in the 2019 decree creating the DINUM [https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/loda/id/JORFTEXT000039281619/](https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/loda/id/JORFTEXT000039281619/) and in the 2021 Prime ministerial circular on data policy [https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/circulaire/id/45162](https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/circulaire/id/45162)). This centralisation is also done in order to foster the discoverability on data.europa.eu, as the data.gouv.fr catalogue is harvested by the European portal. To keep the discoverability standards at the highest level through the time, the data.gouv team has strategically chosen to frequently integrates the feedback of the plateform’s users. Thanks to this strategy, in 2022 the national portal benefited of several modifications enhancing the discoverability of all the data uploaded and harvested such as :

- A complete overhaul of the search engine and research experience to improve its efficiency;
- An overhaul of the previsualization system and the implementation of a data explorer tool.
- An overhaul and an update of the thematic inventory to spotlight some symbolic data.

In the roadmap of the Ministry of Civil Service and Public Transformation (Ministère de la transformation et de la fonction publiques), action A24 focuses on improving data quality and the creation of a data quality label on data.gouv.fr. This label will incentivise data producers to fill in all metadata, and as a consequence will improve discoverability both on data.gouv.fr and data.europa.eu.

column6:
Does the national strategy/policy outline measures to support the reuse of open data by the public sector?

For Explanation:
* If yes, please briefly describe the measures.
column13:
2025:
1. Encouraging reuse within the administration Open data is already widely reused by public bodies in France. The national strategy actively promotes the circulation of data between administrations, whether open or restricted. This is a central focus of strategic frameworks such as the France Nation Verte roadmap: https://www.info.gouv.fr/france-nation-verte/a-proposfeuille-de-route-numerique-donnees 2. Platform to showcase public data use cases A dedicated platform is being developed: https://simplifions.preprod.data.gouv.fr/ It aims to highlight concrete use cases of public data—open or restricted—that help improve public services, demonstrating the value of reuse for administrations. 3. Access to private data of public interest The strategy also includes work on mechanisms to allow public bodies to access data held by private entities when this serves the public interest. This concept, introduced in the 2016 Digital Republic Law, is now being revisited and operationalised. For example, mobility data from navigation services could help public authorities better design transport infrastructure. This approach aligns with broader European efforts on Business-to-Government (B2G) data sharing.
2024:
2024:
The circulation between administration is a strong focus of France Strategy including open and restricted data. It has an important place of the pre-cited roadmap : https://www.info.gouv.fr/france-nation-verte/a-proposfeuille-de-route-numerique-donnees. Also the Sharing of Private Data for Public Interest is becoming more important.

Implementing the mechanism for accessing private data of public interest

A first mention of the concept of "private data of public interest" was introduced in the Digital Republic Law. It has been little used due to a lack of specifics and constraints. However, the release of certain data held by private legal entities can sometimes serve the public interest.

For example, such data can enable more effective management of sectoral public policies, better inform citizens, or improve scientific research. This is particularly true for mobility data from navigation assistants, which are necessary for better understanding, monitoring, modeling, and forecasting mobility needs. This allows local authorities to finely improve road infrastructure or public transport lines.

European work on "Business-to-Government data sharing" allows for the consideration of an evolution in these mechanisms.
2023:
**Plan de relance**

As previously mentioned, within the framework of the Next Generation EU recovery plan (France Relance), the Government set up [a grant for public administrations that want to develop the use of data in public decision-making and performance](https://france-relance.transformation.gouv.fr/96c0-developper-lutilisation-de-la-donnee-dans-vot). Such grants will fund projects focused on data-driven government (data visualisation and decision-making support tools), opening and circulation of data, improving data quality. Project leaders are encouraged to support the opening of data and the reuse of open data within the project.

**Prime Ministerial circular on data policy**

In his april 2021 circular (https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/circulaire/id/45162), Prime Minister Jean Castex reiterated the need for public administrations to strive for open data circulation and re-use. One of the roles of the ministerial CDOs is to animate the ecosystem of re-users of their ministries’ data.

**Ministerial data roadmaps**

The aforementioned ministerial roadmaps on data, algorithms, and source codes (https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/datasets/feuilles-de-route-ministerielles-sur-la-politique-de-la-donnee-des-algorithmes-et-des-codes-sources/) focus also on how to incentivise and support (open) data re-use within the respective ministries and agencies. For example, in the roadmap of the Ministry of Ecological Transition, a full section is dedicated on how to improve data quality to encourage reuse, and on how to use data for policy-making. The roadmap of the Ministry of Culture includes training measures for senior decision-makers on data-driven management.

**Raising awareness among public officials on the issue of data exploitation**

Chiefs Data Officers and Open Data Officers have been appointed in different ministries and operators. For these two categories of public servants, workshops are organised regularly (once or twice a quarter) to raise their awareness and train them on the question of data reuse (case studies, presentations of tools etc.). For example, a "data driven policy" workshop was organised during a seminar organised for the chief data officers. The objective of this workshop was to think collaboratively on how the chief data officer of each ministry could influence the development and implementation of public policies by reusing data. Examples are also given in the chief data officer report.

**At the local level**

The central government has also been fully committed to promote greater re-use of open government data by the public sector at the local level, through a partnership with [OpenDataFrance] (https://www.opendatafrance.net/), an association whose mission is to support local authorities on opening their data. OpenDataFrance has developed a service offer adapted to each territory (awareness, training, etc.) and provides resources to help local communities implement an open data strategy. The State subsidises OpenDataFrance’s actions and Etalab closely works with the association, namely on the promotion of open data re-use at a local level. Thus, their action encourages greater re-use of open government data by the local public sector.

**Etalab Inventory**
In the fall of 2021, the Etalab team inventoried projects based on the reuse of Public Data Service (PDS) reference data. This inventory highlights the large amount of open data reuse by public persons and encourages them to continue developing more projects based on open data reuse.
The dataset categorizes usage examples by issue, sector topic, type of impact, and type of public reuser.

(https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/datasets/exemples-dexploitation-des-donnees-de-reference-du-service-public-de-la-donnee-spd/)

**The creation of Datalab**

Thanks to the solid foundation of public data in France, the Interministerial Digital Directorate has recently been provided with new resources to support the ambition of fostering the reuse of data in the public sector and encouraging the emergence of impactful projects. Within this directorate, the "datalab", an incubator for data-related projects within the DINUM, has been specially created to accelerate public sector projects based in part on the reuse of open data.

(https://www.numerique.gouv.fr/espace-presse/stanislas-guerini-guichet-10-millions-deuros-projets-exploiter-donnees-publiques/)

**The implementation of a data-dedicated funding window**

In the same way, the Interministerial Digital Directorate officially launched in January 2023 a data-dedicated funding window, amounting to 10 million of euros, to co-finance projects around data in the ministries in order to fully exploite public datas as a simplification lever.

(https://www.numerique.gouv.fr/services/guichet-financement-exploitation-valorisation-des-donnees/)

column6:
Does the national strategy/policy outline measures to support the reuse of open data by the private sector?

For Explanation:
* If yes, please briefly describe the measures.
column13:
France follows a “Government as a platform” approach in order to develop its digital services for both public and private actors. The overall (open) data policy and the subsequent strategy documents have been written by taking into account the needs of both the public and the private sector. This is why the law allows for commercial reuse of open data, and the Open Licence 2.0 adopted by the government reiterates this principle.

The ministerial roadmaps also look at how to promote data re-use by the private sector.

For example, the roadmap of the Ministry of Ecological Transition includes a section on “Sharing data through public-private cooperation”. Quoting the roadmap, “The use of data by the private sector is a vector of value for citizens or the community as a whole and improves the effectiveness of public action”. Five actions are put forward to support re-use by private actors.

The importance of open data re-use by private actors is underlined also in the final report of the Open Data Mission led by MP Éric Bothorel, with a specific focus on the national company registry (base SIRENE) and land value data (demandes de valeurs foncières, DVF).

column6:
Does the national strategy/policy mandate carrying out and maintaining a data inventory by public bodies, whether at national or local level?

For Explanation:
* If yes, please briefly specify.
column13:
2025:
Yes, the national strategy mandates that public bodies maintain a Répertoire d’informations publiques (RIP)—a register of public information they hold. This requirement is established by law and applies at both national and local levels. More information: https://www.dila.premier-ministre.gouv.fr/services/repertoire-des-informations-publiques/qu-est-ce-que-le-rip While not all of these inventories are yet published on data.gouv.fr, the long-term objective is for the platform to reference all public data held by the State, whether open or access-restricted. This is already partially implemented, particularly for many APIs that provide restricted access to protected data (e.g. personal or confidential information), allowing for discoverability even when full openness is not possible.
2024:
2024:
We plan to use data.gouv.fr as the data inventory for all public bodies (open and restricted data) starting this summer hopefully : https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/pages/roadmap/
2023:
**Legal framework**

According to the code on relations between the public and the administration (Article L312-1-1) (https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/codes/article_lc/LEGIARTI000033205512/), public actors (and private actors who carry out a public service mission) have to publish in open data the inventory of administrative documents that they produce as part of their public service missions. For example, the Ministry of the Economy has the "Répertoire des Informations Publiques des Ministères Economiques et Financiers", which consists of the official publications produced by the departments of the economic and financial ministries, including date that must be opened and data that must not. (https://www.economie.gouv.fr/cedef/repertoire-des-informations-publiques).

**Prime Ministerial circular on data policy**

In his april 2021 circular (https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/circulaire/id/45162), Prime Minister Jean Castex ordered to each Ministry to develop a data strategy roadmap. Such roadmaps will list the objectives related to steering, opening, circulation, and sharing of data. The Prime Minister also asked ministries to reference open data on the national portal data.gouv.fr. Within this framework, Ministries are drafting data inventories in order to comply with the Government objectives.

**Tech.gouv strategy on inventories :**

[Tech.gouv](https://www.numerique.gouv.fr/publications/tech-gouv-strategie-et-feuille-de-route-2019-2021/), the interministerial programme for digital transformation, has created a new mission called “Data”. One of the objectives of this mission is to create a platform for data exchange between administrations. The first step of this project is to mandate ministries to conduct an inventory of the data produced. Data circulation cannot take place without a clear knowledge of the available datasets. An interdepartmental inventory is being developed to give administrations greater visibility on the data produced at a national level. This work is carried out in collaboration with the relevant contacts of each administration.

**Etalab’s work on inventories :**

- **Producers assistance:**

Etalab collaborates with chief data officers and open data officers of each ministry to help them carry out the inventory of the data within their scope. Workshops are organized to identify the key variables of the different inventories. Several ministries, such as the Ministry of Economy, Ministry of Culture, Ministry of Agriculture, Ministry of the Army, are starting to work on their respective data inventories. Ministerial staff from the Ministry of Ecological Transition and the Ministry of the Sea directly asked Etalab to assist them with the collaboration of other stakeholders in the technical development of the inventory.

- **Inventory pages**

For some subjects we gather all relevant datasets on a single page on the national portal : an example on elections data is available here (https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/pages/donnees-des-elections/). We found that it fosters data discoverability and reuse since it is possible to give more context on the datasets and link between them.

- **The data.gouv.fr catalog**

**In April 2023, nearly 45 000 datasets are referenced on data.gouv.fr**. This figure may seem dizzying for re-users who wish to discover the public data offer of data.gouv.fr. In order to provide better visibility of the published data sets, the team has provided the [data catalog of data.gouv.fr](https://www.data.gouv.fr/en/datasets/catalogue-des-donnees-de-data-gouv-fr/) in open data since June 2019. This dataset provides information on the list of datasets, resources, reuse, organizations, tags, harvesters, and discussions published on data.gouv.fr.

- **Specific inventories**

In order to focus our efforts to make more data available in an open format, Etalab has realised some inventories for specific themes: health, labour, housing, key geo-spatial reference data, COVID-19, etc. (https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/pages/thematiques-a-la-une/). These inventories, which are available in open data, list all open and closed data sources for the specific themes, for all actors involved in the field. The aim is to help us prioritise which data should be available as open data. **These specific inventories can also be used to highlight the importance of certain data according to current events. For example, in the face of a European and global energy crisis, the national portal (http://data.gouv.fr/) has undertaken to reference the main datasets related to the "energy" theme available.**

(https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/pages/donnees-energie/)

- **Interministerial catalogation tool**

In order to help ministries and public sector organisation realise a data inventory, Etalab is currently developing a tool that will allow organisations to create an inventory, manage it, publish it in open data. (https://catalogue.data.gouv.fr/)
The source code is available on GitHub (https://github.com/etalab/catalogage-donnees).

column6:
Do these data inventories include the data collected by public bodies that cannot be published as open data (e.g. in relation to the EU Data Governance Act (EU) 2022/868)? 

For Explanation:
* If yes, please briefly specify.
column13:
As pointed out in the previous answer, public actors (and private actors who carry out a public service mission) have to publish in open data the inventory of administrative documents that they produce as part of their public service missions. This includes data that cannot be published as open data.

Ministries are working on data inventories in order to list all data within their perimeter. These inventories are based on metadata, and will include data that cannot be published as open data. Inventories themselves will be published as open data.

The interministerial catalogation tool will allow users to flag whether each dataset is available as open data (providing a link to the dataset on data.gouv.fr), whether it can be opened but is not yet available, or whether it cannot be published as open data.

The French strategy for data belonging to public bodies that cannot be published as open data is to make them available via API to authorised organisations (“droit d’en connaître”). The catalogue [api.gouv.fr](https://api.gouv.fr/) showcase both open and closed APIs. The roadmap of the API portal is totally transparent [https://api.gouv.fr/feuille-de-route](https://api.gouv.fr/feuille-de-route). In order to facilitate the management of data access authorizations, Etalab developed a tool called DataPass [https://datapass.api.gouv.fr/](https://datapass.api.gouv.fr/).

**Following the adoption of the 3DS law previously mentioned, the role assumed by the [catalogue.data.gouv.fr](http://catalogue.data.gouv.fr) platform is inevitably going to grow. Indeed, this catalog will also serve as a valuable tool in the context of exchanges between administrations, now strongly encouraged through incentives to use APIs with this new law.**

2025:
Yes, France is actively applying the Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/138 on high-value datasets, and progress is well advanced. Nearly all required high-value datasets are already available directly on the national platform, data.gouv.fr, and are being harvested by data.europa.eu in accordance with the regulation. A dedicated public dashboard tracks the implementation status, detailing dataset availability, responsible organizations, and compliance progress: https://ouverture.data.gouv.fr/donnees_de_forte_valeur.html This monitoring ensures transparency and helps coordinate efforts to fully comply with the regulation.

Yes, it is progressing well. All datasets won't be available on data.gouv.fr by the 9th of June but they are already open and available. Our main focus in now on harvesting different data plateforms. The HVD directive accelerated the process.

column6:
Is there a governance structure in place that enables the participation and/or inclusion of various open data stakeholders? 

For Explanation:
*  If yes, please briefly describe the governance structure and its operating model
column13:
The interaction between open data stakeholders and the networks is designed to be both structured and dynamic, fostering continuous engagement, feedback, and collaboration. Here’s how the process generally works:

Structured Interactions within Networks
State Network:
• General Data Administrator (GDA): The GDA plays a central role in coordinating the overall open data policy across ministries. This position is responsible for setting guidelines, monitoring compliance, and ensuring that data initiatives align with national objectives.
• Ministerial Data Administrators (MDAs): In each ministry, the MDA is responsible for implementing the open data strategy within their specific domain. They often work closely with an open data referent who focuses on the operational aspects of data publication and management. Both the General Data Administrator and the Ministerial Data Administrators are public-facing roles, serving as the primary points of contact for user inquiries.
You can view the list of these administrators here: List of Ministerial Data, Algorithms, and Source Code Administrators.
• Regular Meetings and Exchanges: The State Network maintains a regular schedule of meetings and exchanges, both formal (quarterly strategic meetings) and informal (e.g., working groups or workshops on specific topics). These interactions help ensure that the ministries are aligned in their approaches and can share best practices and challenges. However, it's important to note that exchanges between Ministerial Data Administrators in the Interministerial Data Administrators Committee (CIAD) are not public.

Territorial Network:
• Data Referents in Prefectures: These officials are responsible for ensuring that open data policies are implemented at the local level. They act as intermediaries between the central government and local authorities, helping to adapt national policies to local needs.
• National Agency for Territories: This agency provides support and resources to local authorities, helping them develop and implement their data strategies. The agency might offer training, technical assistance, and access to best practices.
• OpenDataFrance Association: This association serves as a hub for local authorities engaged in open data initiatives. It provides a platform for these authorities to collaborate, share resources, and advocate for their needs at the national level.
Community and Stakeholder Engagement
Events Organized by the National Platform or other data producers:
• Hackathons: These events bring together data producers, developers, and other stakeholders to collaboratively create solutions using open data. They serve as a practical way to explore the potential of open data, identify gaps, and foster innovation.
• Public Demonstrations and Workshops: Regularly organized public events. These events provide opportunities for direct interaction between data producers (e.g., government agencies) and data users (e.g., researchers, entrepreneurs).

Systematic Processes for Interaction
• Feedback Loops: Stakeholders are encouraged to provide feedback on the open data they use. This feedback is systematically collected through platforms like data.gouv.fr, where users can comment on datasets, request new data, or report issues.
• Consultation and Co-creation: When developing new policies or strategies, both the State and Territorial Networks may consult with stakeholders, including local authorities, private sector partners, and civil society. This process can involve surveys, public consultations, and pilot projects.

Challenges and Opportunities
While there is a structured framework for interaction, the open data ecosystem also relies heavily on the voluntary participation and collaboration of stakeholders. Continuous engagement, the willingness to share data, and the proactive identification of user needs are crucial for the system to function effectively. The systematic processes in place are designed to facilitate these interactions, but the success of the open data policy also depends on the commitment and responsiveness of all involved parties.

column13:
By law, every local authority with more than 3 500 inhabitants and more than 50 employees falls under national open data obligations.

Local and regional public bodies in France who publish open data have their own open data portal and/or a designated account on the national portal data.gouv.fr with some data already published.

Many have their own open data platform (automatically harvested by the national one). Here are some examples:

Cities : Paris (https://opendata.paris.fr/explore/?sort=modified), Rennes (https://data.rennesmetropole.fr/page/home/), Lyon (https://data.grandlyon.com/), Lille (http://opendata.regionpaca.fr/), Nantes (http://data.nantes.fr/), Bordeaux (http://opendata.bordeaux.fr/), Grenoble (http://data.metropolegrenoble.fr/) ...

Regions : Provence-Alpes-Côtes-d’Azur (http://opendata.regionpaca.fr/), Loire Atlantique (http://data.loire-atlantique.fr/), Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes (http://opendata.auvergnerhonealpes.eu/)

Department : Hérault (https://www.herault-data.fr/pages/accueil/), Morbihan (https://www.opendata56.fr/pages/home/) ...

The association OpenDataFrance manages an observatory that aims at listing all local open data initiatives [https://www.observatoire-opendata.fr](https://www.observatoire-opendata.fr/). The list of the initiatives is available here [https://airtable.com/shrKrV6KY7BlhHDx7](https://airtable.com/shrKrV6KY7BlhHDx7).

The list identifies more than 250 local and regional open data portals for more than 1060 local actors, including 850 local authorities (regions, departments, cities, metropolitan areas, groups of cities, etc.). This observatory confirms a French trend marked by a regular increase of approximately 150 local authorities per year, i.e. an increase of 18%, underlining the vitality and attractiveness of the practices of opening and circulating data at all levels and in all French territories. Moreover, it is possible to consider that all the local authorities have already been brought to collaborate within the framework of the national strategy in terms of open data, and more especially the communes (local administrative units) notably on the occasion of the publication in open data of the data relative to the elections and accessible on the national portal. In the same way, all French local authorities must contribute to the gathering of addresses from municipalities to constitute the national address database open to the public.

[https://www.observatoire-opendata.fr/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/Copie-de-Observatoire_Open_Data_Territoires_Edition2022.pptx-1.pdf](https://www.observatoire-opendata.fr/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/Copie-de-Observatoire_Open_Data_Territoires_Edition2022.pptx-1.pdf)

Does the governance model include the appointment of official roles in civil services that are dedicated to open data (e.g. open data officers)?

For Explanation:
* If yes, please describe how this task is fulfilled at public body level.
column13:
2025:
Yes, the governance model in France includes the appointment of official roles within civil services dedicated to open data and data governance more broadly. At the national level, the Administrateur général des données (AGD)—or General Data Administrator—is responsible for coordinating the overall public data policy. The AGD defines strategic priorities, ensures coherence across administrations, and oversees the network of Chief Data Officers (CDOs) in each ministry. This role is central in guiding and supervising the implementation of open data and broader data governance policies across the State. At the ministerial level, three key roles are identified: 1. Chief Data Officers (CDOs): Each ministry is encouraged to appoint a CDO, as requested in the Prime Minister’s circular of April 2021. CDOs are responsible for the ministry’s data policy, including open data, data quality, and reuse. They operate under the authority of the AGD and are supported by Etalab, which coordinates the national CDO network. → List of CDOs: https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/datasets/liste-des-administrateurs-ministeriels-des-donnees/ 2. Open Data Officers: Some ministries also appoint dedicated open data officers, although this is not mandatory. These officers focus specifically on open data publication, acting as intermediaries between Etalab and internal departments, helping prioritize datasets for publication, and ensuring coordination. 3. Data Stewards: At the operational level, certain departments appoint data stewards to assist with the technical and organizational aspects of data publication and reuse, supporting their colleagues in applying best practices. At the local level, each Préfet (regional representative of the State) to appoint a referent for data, algorithms, and source codes, tasked with supporting local services and promoting data openness. Additionally, DINUM coordinates a network of API managers in public bodies to ensure effective development and reuse of APIs, which are essential for dynamic and real-time data access. This structured governance framework ensures a strong and coordinated approach to open data across all levels of government.
2024:
2024:
There is also a role of data referent within the prefectures. This role has been reaffirmed and strengthened since the "Data and Territories" report : https://www.transformation.gouv.fr/files/ressource/Rapport_Mission_Data_Territoires.pdf
2023:
Three types of actors are appointed within ministries:

- **Chief data officers** are proactively appointed by ministries, as asked by the Prime Minister in his April 2021 circular. They are in charge of the data policy within their ministries. The CDO is under the responsibility of the "General Data Administrator", the state CDO. Etalab leads this network and supports each CDO in the implementation of its missions, including the opening and circulation of its data. The list of CDOs is available in open data (https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/datasets/liste-des-administrateurs-ministeriels-des-donnees/)
- **Open data officers:** although the role is not mandatory, since open data is a prerogative of the CDO, some ministries and inter-ministerial services choose to appoint open data officers alongside the CDOs, with the specific role of managing the open data policy within their structure. The open data officer's missions are to prioritise which datasets to open, to act as an intermediary between Etalab and the divisions of his ministry and to report needs and feedback to the CDO.
- **Data stewards :** although their role is not mandatory, data stewards are appointed by some ministerial directions to reinforce the publication of public data by some public administrations and their re-use by services of the direction.

The DINUM also coordinates a network of API managers in different public bodies.

At the local level, the Prime Minister circular of April 2021 asks every regional representative of the national government (Préfet) to nominate a referent for data, algorithms and source codes, in order to support local state services.

column13:
2025:
Yes, there is a regular and structured exchange of knowledge and experience between the national open data team and the wider network of open data officers in France. 1. The CDO Network The network of Chief Data Officers (CDOs) plays a central role in coordinating open data efforts across central government. It brings together CDOs from each ministry and serves as a forum for sharing progress, challenges, and best practices in the implementation of data strategies, with a strong focus on open data. The network meets formally on a quarterly basis, and the data.gouv.fr team (previously Etalab) participates actively in these meetings to ensure alignment and provide support. In addition to collective meetings, regular one-to-one exchanges take place between the data.gouv.fr team and ministerial CDOs or open data officers to address specific issues and monitor implementation. 2. Open Data France At the local level, the association Open Data France supports and coordinates the actions of local and regional authorities engaged in open data initiatives. It organizes regular events and working groups to foster collaboration and exchange between local actors. In 2023, the data.gouv.fr team was frequently involved in these initiatives, particularly in discussions on the future of open data in territories. These collaborations contribute to the co-construction of tools, guidelines, and policies adapted to the needs of local authorities.
2024:
**The CDO network**

The aforementioned CDO network makes it possible to include all central government stakeholders in the open data awareness and training process. It also makes it possible to track needs (data needs, formation needs etc.) from the different ministries’ division to Etalab to trigger appropriate actions. The CDO network formally gathers at regular occasions (every trimester) in order to share about their progress, difficulties and good practices over data strategy in general. The issue of open data is of  course at the center of the discussions. Moreover, one-to-one exchanges between Etalab and the ministerial CDOs and open data officers take place regularly.

**Open Data France**

The association Open Data France aims at bringing together and supporting local authorities actively engaged in a process of opening up public data, and encouraging all the steps taken by these authorities with a view to promoting open data. Open Data France regularly organises meetings to exchange knowledge and experience with local actors in the field of open data. **For instance, in 2022, Etalab was frequently associated to many meetings and committees with Open Data France, especially on the question of the co-construction of the future of open data in territories.**
