column6:
Are there any processes in place to assess if public sector bodies are charging for data above marginal cost? (please see directive (EU) 2019/1024 on open data and the reuse of public sector information).

For Explanation:
* If yes, please specify the process(es).
column13:
2025:
Yes, processes are in place in France to ensure that public sector bodies do not charge for data beyond marginal cost, in line with Directive (EU) 2019/1024. French law establishes the principle of free reuse of public information in Article L. 324-1 of the Code of Relations between the Public and the Administration (CRPA). This article states that the reuse of public information is, by default, free of charge. Previously, a few exceptions allowed cost recovery for certain datasets (e.g. meteorological data), but most of these exceptions have now been removed, and the vast majority of public data is accessible free of charge. When fees are charged, they must comply with strict legal and regulatory conditions, and their justification can be subject to oversight by the Commission d’accès aux documents administratifs (CADA).
2024:
French law states that the re-use of public information is free of charge by principle (see Article L. 324-1 of the Code of relations between the public and the administration (CRPA)).
As an exception, fees can only be charged in two cases:
- For administrations whose main activity consists of collecting, producing, making available or disseminating public information, when less than 75% of the costs related to this main activity are covered by tax revenues, endowments or subsidies (i.e. at least 25% by own revenues). For the State's administrations (including its public administrative establishments), a strict list of data likely to be subject to a re-use fee is published (D. 324-5-1 CRPA).
- For public libraries, including university libraries, museums and archives, only for information resulting from digitisation operations of their holdings and collections and, where applicable, the information associated with them, when the latter are jointly marketed (art. L. 324-2 CRPA). In short, royalties may only relate to the re-use of digitised image files and their metadata (if they are re-used jointly with them); royalties may not relate to natively digital documents.
All fees previously collected that do not comply with the legal framework now in force can no longer be claimed.
The amount of the fees shall be set according to objective, transparent, verifiable and non-discriminatory criteria. The amount shall be reviewed at least every five years. The details of its calculation shall be published in electronic form jointly on the website of the administration concerned and on data.gouv.fr.

Etalab is in charge of assessing whether the amount of the fees charged by State administrations is appropriate. The list of State bodies that can charge a fee is again published by decree, hence an eventual modification goes through a strict review process in which Etalab is involved.

In 2018, the Court of Audit (Cour des comptes) issued a summary report to Prime Minister Édouard Philippe pointing out the issues related to the economic models of three State operators charging for data and the consequences of opening such data. (https://www.ccomptes.fr/system/files/2019-03/20190311-refere-S2018-3287-valorisation-donnees-IGN-Meteo-France-Cerema.pdf).

Prime Minister Philippe replied in 2019 (https://www.ccomptes.fr/sites/default/files/2019-03/20190311-refere-S2018-3287-valorisation-donnees-IGN-Meteo-France-Cerema-rep-PM.pdf) deciding to generalising the opening of data produced by the national geographical institute IGN and Météo-France. Prime Minister Castex, in his April 2021 circular (https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/circulaire/id/45162) reiterated the aim of extinguishing fees by 2023. The Naval Hydrographic and Oceanographic Service (SHOM) met the commitment and stopped charging fees.

Article D324-5-1 of the Code of the Relations between the Public and the Administration will be modified to reflect these changes.

column6:
What are the top 3 challenges that your country is facing in the implementation of the mentioned open data policies/strategy?

For Explanation:
* Please briefly describe.
column13:
As stated above, despite the overall high level of open data maturity of all public sector organisations at national and local level, there is room for improvement in some key areas:

- Data literacy of civil servants and training in open data skills. This has been pointed out by the Open Data Mission carried out by MP Éric Bothorel (https://www.vie-publique.fr/sites/default/files/rapport/pdf/277879.pdf). The need for skills and expertise in the field of data has also been the object of a specific mission carried out by the DINUM and the national statistical institute INSEE (https://www.etalab.gouv.fr/publication-du-rapport-dinum-insee-12-recommandations-pour-dynamiser-la-gestion-et-la-valorisation-des-competences-data/) which formulates 12 recommendations.
- Although the law states that all data must be open by default, the existence of this right is not widely known among the general population, civil servants that do not work directly on data are not always trained on how to respond to access-to-information requests, and there are no sanctions for the public bodies that do not comply. The aforementioned open data mission underlined the need to improve the right of access to data and the role of the independent authority that supervises this right, the Commission for Access to Administrative Documents (Commission d’accès aux documents administratifs, CADA).
- Fragmentation of efforts and discoverability of data. Public sector organisations at national and local level are rather independent in the implementation of their own open data strategy, and local authorities are not obliged to publish data on the national portal [data.gouv.fr](http://data.gouv.fr). The main advantage of this configuration is agility and the possibility to accommodate different degrees of competence and needs. The downside is the fragmentation of efforts and the difficulty to centralise data on the national portal. Having to develop harvesters from other open data portals to data.gouv.fr, setting up the harvesting pipeline, managing the content on both a ministerial/local portal and the national one is a challenge for both Etalab managing the national portal and the other actors.

2025:
1. Improving data literacy among public servants DINUM has made the development of digital skills within the State a national priority. To support this, it launched the Campus for Public Digital Training, an interministerial initiative that consolidates and promotes digital training programs. This platform equips civil servants—particularly in the digital and data fields—with essential skills to support public service transformation and open data practices. 2. Ensuring effective implementation of the “open by default” principle Significant progress has been made, and efforts are now focused on ensuring that public actors view open data as a strategic opportunity rather than a legal obligation. Additional measures are being taken to catalogue and reference restricted data, increasing transparency even when data cannot be openly shared. 3. Reducing fragmentation and improving data discoverability The implementation of high-value datasets has helped structure publication practices and improve the visibility of important data on the national portal. France is also investing in the development of thematic data verticals—such as https://meteo.data.gouv.fr and https://ecologie.data.gouv.fr—designed to offer structured, domain-specific access points that are directly connected to data.gouv.fr. This strategy moves beyond decentralized harvesting and reinforces data.gouv.fr as the authoritative source, improving both organization and user navigation across thematic areas.

Does the national portal provide a mechanism for users to rate datasets?

For Explanation:
* If yes, please provide the direct-URL to this feature or describe how this functionality is provided.
column13:
The national portal does not offer a formal dataset rating system, such as star ratings or voting mechanisms. However, several features provide indirect signals of dataset usefulness or quality:

• Usage metrics, including reuse counts, are prominently displayed and serve as indicators of interest and relevance.
• Users can mark datasets as favorites, which acts as a form of positive feedback.
• Open discussions are available on each dataset page, where users can share critiques or suggestions.
• A reporting function is available to flag outdated or problematic content.
• Each dataset also has a metadata quality score, based on the completeness and structure of its information.

A rating system was not implemented due to several concerns. For example, widely used datasets like SIRENE may receive low ratings from users who do not fully download or understand the data. Also, essential datasets with known quality issues might receive misleadingly low ratings, even if they are the official and most relevant sources.

For Explanation:
* If yes, please explain your process for improving the portal based on user insights and feedback
* If relevant, kindly highlight some improvements made in the past year
column13:
We apologize for the confusion.

Developments on data.gouv.fr are done in an agile manner and are primarily guided by:

1. User Feedback

The platform is primarily built based on user feedback, which comes from several sources:

- User tests and interviews
- Interviews serve to:
- Conduct forward-looking research and update the vision: maintaining a broad view of the users' context, their needs, sector evolution, and usage trends, rather than focusing solely on ongoing and planned work.
- Prepare for a future project that hasn't been tackled yet, to understand current usage, identify user problems, gather test data, and validate or invalidate proposed features.

- Tests serve to:
- Identify usability issues before coding, understand how the application is used, and detect its shortcomings.
- Test planned changes at a lower cost using more or less finished and interactive mockups before coding.
- Verify, once the changes are in production, whether they work "as expected".

Both approaches are essential for prioritizing upcoming work, limiting the influence of personal biases. Ideally, multiple elements or hypotheses are tested during a session with a user (as organizing it is time-consuming), and an "interview" part is included in the tests (with questions beyond what's on the screen).

- Support feedback
- Feedback received by the support team
The support team is in direct contact with users and regularly receives valuable feedback. However, it's important to note that this feedback mostly comes from data producers, who represent only a portion of our users and whose needs may sometimes conflict with those of data reusers.
- GitHub tickets
Some users, often advanced users or partners, propose improvements via GitHub.
- Feedback from social media and specialized platforms
Insights can often be gleaned from community discussions on platforms like teamopendata, Twitter, or LinkedIn. However, it's crucial to ensure the representativeness of this feedback compared to the rest of our users to avoid responding only to the loudest voices.

2. Usage Metrics

We monitor usage metrics, such as platform activity (views, downloads, data previews) and catalog evolution (data quality improvement, resource type evolution), to identify trends and ensure that our actions are heading in the right direction. However, we place greater importance on impact indicators (see below).

3. Team Feedback

The team is also a critical source for prioritization. While user feedback and usage should remain our guiding star, it's crucial to consider team feedback, especially for:

- Understanding the complexity and technical debt induced by developments
- Facilitating the work of the team (both the development team and the support team)
- Building a shared vision and ensuring team motivation

4. Other Types of Feedback

data.gouv.fr operates in a complex environment where feedback and directives can come from many sources (political mandates, ministries, management, European partners). This feedback must also be carefully considered and sometimes addressed strategically, even if it doesn't align perfectly with the product vision.

This working methodology does not prevent data.gouv.fr from having a roadmap.

The roadmap of data.gouv.fr serves as a guiding thread for the team and facilitates interactions with stakeholders. The team aims to be agile, so the roadmap is not set in stone and is not tied to specific dates or fixed deliverables.

Mission and Impact Objectives

Above all, the team pursues a mission and impact objectives.

Our mission is to promote the reuse of public data. This mission is broken down into objectives and impact indicators.

1. Improve the discoverability of open data
2. Promote the quality of open data
3. Encourage the reuse of open data

Rituals

In practice, it is the product owner's responsibility to synthesize needs and represent the user's voice within the team.
We work in two-week sprints, where we plan the tasks to be completed.

The goal is to assume deliberate prioritization by asking, what evolution of the application will bring the most value to the user at this moment? This also involves saying no regularly (or, at worst, "later") to protect the interests of both the user and the team, and ultimately to ensure that we remain aligned with the product vision.

We also strive to design features that are as "small" as possible.

The larger a feature or evolution is:

- the more likely we are to get stuck in an endless tunnel
- the more bugs we'll have to deal with
- the longer it will take to put into production, delaying value delivery to the user
- the longer it will take to get feedback on usage
- the higher the risk of having worked for nothing

We also aim to have the shortest feedback loop possible: changes are rolled out quickly because they are small and non-parallelized, tests are systematic, and usage and impact are measured. All of this helps us learn as quickly as possible whether the change effectively improves the product, and to gain more insight into user behavior, their expectations, etc., and ultimately to learn how to improve the product.

column13:
2025:
Yes, we monitor the keywords used in search queries on the portal and track how users interact with them.

We are currently making a significant effort through UX research to redesign the search engine. This work focuses on improving relevance, performance, and overall user experience. Planned improvements include:

• Smarter filters to refine results more effectively
• A unified search across all types of content (datasets, api, reuses, organizations.)
• Improved search analytics to better understand user needs and adapt the search engine accordingly

Metrics and results can be shown on demand. 

These changes are part of a broader strategy to be implemented throughout 2025.
2024:
We track the keywords searched using our traffic monitoring tool, Matomo.

However, this is not our main priority, as we have observed that the majority of users come from search engines like Google rather than our internal search engine. Tracking the most popular datasets is often more insightful for identifying trends.

On the other hand, we display a dedicated form when a search yields few or no results. This allows us to identify datasets that need to be opened or are poorly documented and therefore don't rank well in search results, based on user feedback.

We also occasionally monitor the use of filters.

Fun fact: one year, we identified the word "goat" as one of the most searched terms on the platform. After investigating, we discovered that a question in the national digital education program PIX, mandatory for middle school students, asked them to find the number of goats in a department using data.gouv.fr.

* For informational purposes, kindly provide the URLs to the five most popular datasets on the portal
column13:
We closely monitor the most viewed pages and the most popular new content. For example, a top 10 list is displayed daily on the team's communication tool.

This allows us to identify trending topics to develop further (e.g., writing a dedicated article or highlighting specific datasets).

It also helps us determine when data exploration is relevant. For instance, some datasets are very popular because users are often looking for information rather than raw data. This insight helps us decide which datasets to redirect users to or when to create a dedicated data exploration.

For example, on the dataset of deaths, we display an information banner to redirect users who are looking for a specific death record rather than the entire database. In 2024, 38% of users who visited this dataset clicked on the link to the dedicated data exploration, allowing them to conduct a more specific search.

The five datasets that regularly appear in the top are:

- Fichier des personnes décédées (File of deceased persons)
- Demandes de valeurs foncières (Requests for property values)
- Répertoire national des associations (National directory of associations)
- Base SIRENE des entreprises et de leurs établissements (SIREN, SIRET)
- Liste publique des organismes de formation (L. 6351-7-1 of the Labor Code)

It's worth noting that some datasets may generate a lot of traffic but are strongly tied to current events (e.g., datasets on elections, fuel prices, or COVID-19 data).

We also monitor traffic on data reuses for the same reasons.

For Explanation:
*If yes, please briefly describe how your optimise the search
column13:
2025:
Yes, we take several measures to optimise the search and discoverability of both data and editorial content:

1. We continuously monitor and curate published content to ensure relevance and compliance with the platform’s terms of use. Many automated alerts are in place to detect weak signals of outdated or problematic content. Users can also report issues directly through a dedicated feature.
2. We have a team member dedicated to editorial work. This includes selecting and promoting key content through specific features, thematic pages, and regular publications. Notably, we publish a monthly summary of new datasets and dedicated articles on high-impact data. We also promote content actively on social media.
3. We regularly monitor the performance and relevance of the search engine and work on its continuous improvement to enhance discoverability.
2024:
We launch in 2021 a new search engine.
On top of that, the team is always working on the curation of the datasets on the portal and do their best to prevent inappropriate content (publicity mainly).

From the [platform's activity report](https://agarrone.github.io/public-files/moderation.pdf) which is sent to him every morning the data editor selects on a daily basis the most relevant datasets to highlight on the home page and on the different thematic pages. On top of that we work on the improvement of the search engine, for example:

- the tag system of the datasets makes it possible to optimize the search
- the "highlight" button for the platform administrator allows to bring up a data set in the ranking

We also carry out technical developments, which are based on log analysis:

[Keep track of udata search results performances](https://github.com/etalab/datagouv-search-indicator)

In order to highlight the key datasets published on the platform, we offer editorial content:

- We publish an [article every month](https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/posts/suivi-des-sorties-mai-2020/) to showcase the most important publications (datasets or reuses) during the last month
- We offer the subscription to a [newsletter](https://infolettres.etalab.gouv.fr/subscribe/r1aq92xnj) .
- We publish articles on [Etalab's blog](https://www.etalab.gouv.fr/) in order to make some popular publications visible.
- Other articles about new data sets are posted [here](https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/posts/)
- We highlight specific content on our [social network](https://twitter.com/datagouvfr)
- Users receive notifications when new data sets are available on the national portal (RSS, ATOM feeds, email notifications etc)

2025:
Yes, the national portal allows the publication of non-official data, including community-sourced and citizen-generated content.

Any user, including individuals, can create an account and publish their own datasets on data.gouv.fr. 

Non-official data is distinguishable from official data in two main ways:

1. Publisher types are clearly identified (e.g. individual, association, public institution).
2. A certification label is applied to trusted public producers to help users distinguish them from other contributors.

Additionally, users can contribute to existing datasets by publishing reuses or community resources. 

This approach encourages a collaborative ecosystem while ensuring transparency about the source of each dataset.


- Example of a media organization: Mediapart has its own organization page where it can publish datasets as a non-public actor: https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/organizations/mediapart/#/presentation
- Example of an individual: Antoine Augusti has a user profile where he publishes datasets independently: https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/users/antoine-augusti/

Metadata quality indicators: Each dataset has an integrated checklist in the admin dashboard assessing metadata quality. 

If a criterion is not met, it is clearly indicated, helping producers take corrective actions. These tools support continuous improvement and higher quality of publication across the portal.

We are planning to introduce additional indicators soon, such as the response rate and average response time of a data producer to questions asked about their datasets. column13:
data.gouv.fr offers several methods of publication:

- Direct publication
- Publication via API
- Publication through harvesting

The platform supports the harvesting of several metadata formats, including DCAT, CKAN, and GeoNetwork.

Users can set up a harvester, which must then be validated by the data.gouv.fr team.

We establish a mapping of fields for essential metadata, and some additional properties are retained for traceability purposes.

When harvesters are properly configured, we are able to retrieve 100% of the essential metadata for the data.gouv.fr model.

Harvested data represents approximately 50% of the data.gouv.fr catalog.

column13:
2025:
Yes, France has implemented several additional measures beyond the use of the DCAT-AP tag to ensure that high-value datasets (as defined in Regulation (EU) 2023/138) are interoperable with those of other countries.


These measures include:

1. Technical guidance and documentation
France has published dedicated guidance to ensure alignment with European interoperability standards for high-value datasets. These guidelines specify metadata structure, data formats, and technical modalities of publication and are available here:
https://guides.data.gouv.fr/autres-ressources-utiles/donnees-de-forte-valeur-modalites-de-rapportage
2. Dedicated reporting and monitoring platform
A platform has been developed to support and monitor the reporting of high-value datasets:
http://reporting-hvd.dataeng.etalab.studio/
This tool allows data providers to assess compliance and facilitates alignment with EU-level requirements, ensuring datasets are interoperable and usable across borders.
3. Public dashboard and coordination mechanism
The implementation and progress of high-value datasets are tracked publicly via:
https://ouverture.data.gouv.fr/donnees_de_forte_valeur
This encourages consistency, accountability, and harmonisation across sectors and ensures that France’s datasets are accessible and usable through data.europa.eu.
4. Engagement with European guidelines
France actively engages in EU-wide initiatives and working groups to ensure that national implementation aligns with European technical specifications, including the semantic and syntactic interoperability of datasets.
2024:
We ensure that the metadata is properly filled out and that it is reported to data.europa. Data producers are more than us in direct contact with other data producers from others countries to ensure the coherence.

In the context of High Value Datasets reporting, we have taken extremely good care that the national catalogue expose correct DCAT-AP description of datasets. Our first approach was to carry out extensive work to use the SEMIC ISO to 19139 DCAT-AP XSLT as our main harvesting interoperability solution for most decentralized or thematical geographical platforms. This lead to studies on common issues that we’re fixing either at the metadata or the harvesting level (licenses, data services, contact points and other responsible parties, etc). We’ve then ensured that our DCAT-AP exposition would be correctly interpreted by data.europa.eu by using the SPARQL reporting endpoints to list required metadata. This lead us to notice some wrong expositions by the national catalogue that we’ve worked on since.

We developed our [own licence](https://www.etalab.gouv.fr/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/ETALAB-Licence-Ouverte-v2.0.pdf) and provide [guidelines](https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/licences) and guides on how to choose a licence and why (see previous questions).

**Reusability** :

With our focus on data literacy and the organisation of events, we foster the reusability of data by insisting notably on [quality of documentation](https://guides.etalab.gouv.fr/qualite/documenter-les-donnees/) of data, [description of metadata](https://guides.etalab.gouv.fr/qualite/documenter-les-donnees/#description-des-metadonnees) and how [reuses are important](https://guides.etalab.gouv.fr/juridique/reutilisation/#qu-est-ce-qu-une-reutilisation) for example (see dimension 1 for more insight).

Reuses are highlighted in the same way as data [on the portal](https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/reuses/covid-19-en-france-au-06-juillet-2020-surveillance-des-entrees-hospitalieres-et-des-tests-de-depistage/) and through our [communication](https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/posts/).

**Machine readability and openness** :

A documentation is available to support producers on how to publish data sets in machine readable format: [here](https://guides.etalab.gouv.fr/data.gouv.fr/) and [here](https://doc.data.gouv.fr/a-propos/que-publier-et-comment-le-publier/).

On top of advocacy programs and [editorial content](https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/posts/) we develop tools to help producers to provide high quality data. For instance,

- The Etalab team launched in 2019 [www.schema.data.gouv.fr](http://www.schema.data.gouv.fr/) a referencing, validation and support service for the creation of public data schemas for France. From schema.data.gouv.fr and the tools attached to it, it is possible to consult the referenced data schema, to validate that a data set conforms to a schema, to generate documentation and sample data sets automatically or suggest standardized entry forms. Any actor is also free to propose the referencing of diagrams on schema.data.gouv.fr.
- Etalab has also developed a tool, [CSV-GG](https://csv-gg.etalab.studio/), that helps you create a CSV file that conforms to an existing data schema. The tool guides you through several steps to obtain a complete, valid and structured file.

**Open identifier**

Discoverability of data.gouv.fr catalog is one of our top priorities. With this in mind a lot of effort are put in the  improvement of the search engine, for example:

- the tag system of the datasets makes it possible to optimize the search
- the "highlight" button for the platform administrator allows to bring up a data set in the ranking

**Linked-data**

We wrote a [quality guide](https://guides.etalab.gouv.fr/qualite/preparer-le-jeu-de-donnees/#la-structure-du-jeu-de-donnees) to help administration in the open data strategy. This guide underlines the necessity to include “linked data” (données pivot) that facilitates the crossover between datasets. Ex. Identification number of a company, geolocalisation etc.

We are also working on a tool enabling the enrichment of resources with additional third party data available on the portal

The platform data.gouv.fr allows users to link a specific resource to a common standard / schema shared by the community. This feature allow users to access easily to all the resources depending of this specific schema.

column6:
Do you have a definition of open data reuse in your country?
 
For Explanation:
* If yes, please specify it.
column13:
2025:
In France, according to a broad definition that is commonly accepted, « reuse » refers to the use of public data by third parties for purposes other than the public service mission for which the data was produced or received (this definition has been recalled in the legal guide provided by the French open data team : https://guides.data.gouv.fr/guides-open-data/guide-juridique/reutilisateurs-de-donnees/respecter-les-conditions-de-reutilisation). This definition directly stems from the Code of Relations between the Public and the Administration : « Public information contained in documents communicated or published by the administrations mentioned in the first paragraph of documents communicated or published by the administrations mentioned in the first paragraph of article L.300-2 may be used by any person who wishes to do so for purposes other than those of the public service mission for which the documents were produced or received. » (https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/codes/article_lc/LEGIARTI000033219044)

This definition is similar to the PSI Directive definition : « Public sector bodies collect, produce, reproduce and disseminate documents in order to fulfill their public service mission. The use of these documents for other purposes constitutes reuse ».

The complexity and the need to clarify the definition of reuse has been emphasised in the literature, particularly with respect to research data, a key issue being the distinction between use and reuse. Besides that definition, more restrictive approaches have also emerged : some consider that only perennial uses of data are reuses while others consider any use of data as reuse. In our day to day operations, any exploitation of data in order to obtain information is considered as reuse, whether this exploitation is freely accessible or not : following that definition, a use of private data or a data journalist’s work to prepare for an investigation will be considered as reuse.

column6:
Are there any processes in place to monitor the level of reuse of your country's open data?
 
For Explanation:
* If yes, please (1) briefly describe these processes and (2) provide the URLs to support the answer.
column13:
2025:
In France, quantitative and qualitative processes are implemented to grasp the level of open data reuse.

Quantitative processes :
- The monitoring of datasets metrics on the national open data portal data.gouv.fr (datasets visit and download metrics, metrics on reuses published, etc.) to understand which datasets are the most popular and to follow popularity dynamics (https://stats.data.gouv.fr/). Datasets metrics on the data.gouv.fr platform are displayed here : https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/dashboard/ and on each dataset’s page.

Qualitative processes : 
- The monitoring of reuses referenced on the national open data platform data.gouv.fr (https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/reuses/) : reuses can and are incentivised to publish their reuse work on data.gouv.fr and link them to reused datasets. These publications are monitored daily by the French open data team and also allow data producers to have visibility on their published data’s uses. To this day, 4300+ reuses have been shared on the data.gouv.fr platform and we are working on engaging more Reuters to publish their work so as to track them better, for example with a custom user flow : https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/pages/onboarding/reutilisateurs/
- Surveys to gather reuse information from reusers : numerous data producers conduct surveys to better grasp who and how their published data is used. One example is from the National institute for geographic and forestry information who carries out a public consultation on the reuse of the national building standard dataset : https://tally.so/r/3xROXy
- Interviews with data producers and data reusers : the French open data team regularly interviews data producers and data reusers to identify emblematic reuse cases on important datasets and better understand their impact. The gathered information is often exposed on the data.gouv.fr platform as documented use cases : https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/pages/onboarding/liste_cas_usage/
- Social media campaigns implemented by the French open data team promoting reuse cases and encouraging reusers to share their reuse work, so as to identify more of them : https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:activity:7310984416070123520 
- Open data community animation : the French open data team creates and animates spaces for data producers and data reusers to discuss and meet, allowing for more reuse creation and information gathering about them : https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/posts/retour-sur-le-hackathon-donnees-ouvertes-meteo-france/ https://forum.data.gouv.fr/ 
2024:
In France, quantitative and qualitative processes have been implemented to grasp the level of open data re-use :

- The monitoring of datasets metrics through the national open data portal [data.gouv.fr](http://data.gouv.fr/) : datasets visit and download metrics as well as the metrics on reuses published are tracked to understand which datasets are the most popular and to follow popularity dynamics (https://stats.data.gouv.fr/). We are currently working on a new interface to showcase those metrics but also trends and dynamics : [http://activites-datagouv.app.etalab.studio/](http://activites-datagouv.app.etalab.studio/)
- The monitoring of reuses referenced on the national open data portal [data.gouv.fr](http://data.gouv.fr/) ([https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/reuses/)](https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/reuses/)) : reusers are encouraged to publish their reuse work linked to a dataset, and their publications are monitored by the [data.gouv.fr](http://data.gouv.fr/) team on a daily basis and also allow data producers to have visibility on the reuses developed from their open data. To this day, more than 3 000 reuses have been shared on the [data.gouv.fr](http://data.gouv.fr/) portal and we are working on engaging more reusers to publish their work in order to track them better, for example with a custom user flow : [https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/pages/onboarding/reutilisateurs/](https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/pages/onboarding/reutilisateurs/)
- Interviews with data producers and data reusers : the [data.gouv.fr](http://data.gouv.fr/) team regularly interviews data producers and data reusers to identify emblematic reuses on important datasets and gather information about them. Part of the learnings gathered from those interviews can be found here : [https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/posts/comment-ladministration-utilise-les-donnees-publiques-lexemple-des-startups-detat/](https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/posts/comment-ladministration-utilise-les-donnees-publiques-lexemple-des-startups-detat/) ; [https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/posts/comment-les-donnees-de-transport-contribuent-a-ameliorer-la-mobilite-et-laction-publique/](https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/posts/comment-les-donnees-de-transport-contribuent-a-ameliorer-la-mobilite-et-laction-publique/) ; [https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/posts/comment-lopen-data-devient-un-outil-de-formation-essentiel-dans-lenseignement-superieur](https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/posts/comment-lopen-data-devient-un-outil-de-formation-essentiel-dans-lenseignement-superieur) and more detailed here : [https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/datasets/r/a61e1fcc-cd61-46bd-a6c5-af94cb9f8459](https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/datasets/r/a61e1fcc-cd61-46bd-a6c5-af94cb9f8459)
- Surveys to gather reuse information from reusers : numerous data producers conduct those type of surveys, namely the Ministry of Culture who has carried out a public consultation on the reuse of cultural public data : [https://www.culture.gouv.fr/Thematiques/Innovation-numerique/Actualites/Open-data-decouvrez-les-resultats-de-la-consultation](https://www.culture.gouv.fr/Thematiques/Innovation-numerique/Actualites/Open-data-decouvrez-les-resultats-de-la-consultation)
- The animation of communities, that can be done at the level of an administration or with an interdepartmental scope.

column6:
Are there any activities in place to encourage public bodies to monitor the reuse of their own published data (e.g. incentives or obligations in place for public bodies or civil servants of national government)?
 
For Explanation:
* If yes, please (1) briefly describe these activities/incentives and (2) provide the URLs to support the answer.
column13:
2025:
French administrations have reached a certain level of maturity with respect to open data. Data publication is no longer made solely to abide by the law, and we witness more and more public bodies monitoring the reuse of their published data. They are actively encouraged to and are provided with assistance, tools and best practices to do so.

At an institutional level, the Prime Minister, in his April 2021 circular, underlined that each Ministry will need to animate their data reusers ecosystems and monitor reuse, namely in order to identify high value-added datasets and encourage more sharing : https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/download/pdf/circ?id=45162

Within this framework, the French open data team (data.gouv.fr) has deployed several initiatives to further encourage and help public sector organisations in monitoring reuse :

- It provides public bodies with useful tools to monitor reuse level : on the data.gouv.fr platform, data producers have access to metrics for each dataset (https://guides.data.gouv.fr/guide-data.gouv.fr/statistiques) and to a list of reuses published and associated to their datasets (https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/reuses/)
- It trains civil servants on measuring and stimulating data reuse with workshops organised regularly (ministerial CDOs, open data officers, data producers more generally) : https://guides.data.gouv.fr/guides-open-data/guide-qualite/ameliorer-la-qualite-dun-jeu-de-donnees-en-continu/connaitre-et-suivre-les-usages-dun-jeu-de-donnees https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/pages/webinaires
- It helps public sector organisations organise events (hackathons, etc.) to meet with reusers so as to better know them and their activities. One example : https://www.numerique.gouv.fr/actualites/hackathon-donnees-alimentaires/#:~:text=La direction interministérielle du numérique,2 et 3 décembre 2024
2024:
2024:
Yes. - First, public statistics that are available on the portal: Public Statistics Guide - Second, our strategy is to empower data producers in measuring usage. We produce recommendations and guides to this end: Improving Data Quality Continuously
2023:
Public bodies are highly encouraged to monitor the re-use of their own published data.

First, while helping data producers in opening their data, Etalab strongly advocates for the monitoring of one’s published data, emphasising the benefits of doing so. Parts of our arguments are available here : (https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/posts/quel-suivi-des-usages-des-donnees-ouvertes/).

Etalab’s strategy for the monitoring of reuses is one where we aim to empower data producers in doing so. Therefore, our efforts are dedicated to providing them with the help to measure reuse, thus incentivising them :

- We provide them with tools, namely metrics and notifications on new reuses published (https://www.data.gouv.fr/en/datasets/catalogue-des-donnees-de-data-gouv-fr/), and we are today working on making them even more accessible to them : https://www.linkedin.com/posts/antonin-garrone-8272bb154_nous-sommes-en-train-de-travailler-sur-la-activity-7043991572467601409-LvWL/?utm_source=share&utm_medium=member_desktop.
- We provide them with methodological guidelines on how to measure reuse : https://etalab-2.gitbook.io/guides/publier-des-donnees/guide-qualite/ameliorer-la-qualite-dun-jeu-de-donnees/connaitre-et-suivre-les-usages-dun-jeu-de-donnees

To deepen this approach, we interviewed data producers to understand how we can better help them follow their open data reuses. Insights are in this study : https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/datasets/r/a61e1fcc-cd61-46bd-a6c5-af94cb9f8459.

We also have programs that promote the measurement of reused data.

Etalab supports administrations in measuring data that is reused on a daily basis. In addition, specific programs for transforming public administration through data enable the importance of open data to be introduced and the need to measure reuse :

- The program “[Entrepreneurs d’intérêt général](https://entrepreneur-interet-general.etalab.gouv.fr/)” creates new opportunities to hire civil servants with high level digital skills within the administration, to improve public service mission and to transmit new skills in public organisation. The proposed challenges are often based on the use of data to better implement public policies. Many challenges have an open data component. In this perspective, the EIG programme emphasises the need to monitor the reuse of open data.
- The “Lab IA” program assists administrations in the use of their data thanks to data sciences and artificial intelligence. Some of the projects have an open data component. In this perspective, the programme emphasises the need to monitor the reuse of open data.

Does your country have processes in place to monitor and measure the level of reuse of high-value datasets ((EU) 2023/138)?
 
For Explanation:
* If yes, please specify how and highlight challenges if any. 
* If you are an EFTA or a candidate country to the EU, please select 'not applicable'.
column13:
2025:
In France, there is an established process to monitor and measure open data reuse level (see question I2). A specific version of this process has been implemented to track the reuse of high value datasets in particular. It namely relies on using high value datasets metrics (dataset visit and download statistics, statistics on the number of reuses associated, etc.) to assess interest in datasets and direct uses, and on examining big reuse cases. Obtaining measurement data, such as identifying the big bulk of high value datasets reuses, can be challenging.

This process is continuously carried out. An example here with the February 2025 analysis and indicators : https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/datasets/r/78e7885a-279f-4344-abb8-b00d7d7619d3
2024:
We monitor the usage of high-value data by relying on statistics and reuses. We plan to conduct surveys by data theme, as we have done for the Public Data Service.

column6:
Has your government specified what 'impact of open data' means (e.g. in a strategy document)?
 
For Explanation:
* If yes, how do you define the impact of open data in your country? 
* If possible, please provide a URL to a public document describing it.
column13:
2025:
The report « For a public data policy, algorithms and source codes » led by MP Eric Bothorel clearly defines what « impact of open data » means. It is defined as such : « for citizens, it is a matter of transparency of public life and of simplification of procedures ; for businesses, it fosters innovation and modernises the economy ; for public actors, it informs decision making and improve the quality of public services ; for research, it enhances activity and promotes collaboration » (https://www.info.gouv.fr/upload/media/default/0001/01/2020_12_rapport_-_pour_une_politique_publique_de_la_donnee_-_23.12.2020_.pdf - from p.22).
2024:
2024:
We have implemented specific impact indicators to measure the impact of data.gouv.fr, which is an indirect way of measuring the impact of open data.
2023:
The Open Data Mission led by MP Eric Bothorel defines four impact areas for open data : scientific as a vector of knowledge, economical as a driver of innovation, democratic to improve public service and political to restore people’s confidence in public action (https://www.gouvernement.fr/upload/media/default/0001/01/2020_12_rapport_-_pour_une_politique_publique_de_la_donnee_-_23.12.2020_.pdf) : p.22-23). This view is in line with the ministerial strategy on open data, which is focused on openness i.e. more public open data to foster innovation and transparency, to enhance the external evaluation of governmental policy and the democratic debate. In this regard, the final report of the Open Data Mission recommends to assess the economical, social and scientific impact of the opening and sharing of data and source codes (https://www.gouvernement.fr/upload/media/default/0001/01/2020_12_rapport_-_pour_une_politique_publique_de_la_donnee_-_23.12.2020_.pdf) : p.13).

The vision previously detailed is embraced within Etalab, as we consider that open data impact is manifold and can be measured through different ways.

The four impact areas can be translated in three kind of audiences :

- Administrations that improve the delivery of public services
- Citizens who benefit from greater transpaency
- Companies, NGOs, researchers, etc. who use data to gain knowledge and create new innovative products and services.

As a final remark, the impact of open data can be measured both qualitatively and quantitatively, in a complementary way : we thus carry out both an analysis of quantitative metrics on our national open data portal data.gouv.fr and of qualitative impact by interviewing portal users, data producers and reusers.

In the official interministerial data administration framework (https://static.data.gouv.fr/resources/politique-publique-de-la-donnee-des-algorithmes-et-des-codes-sources-15-feuilles-de-route-ministerielles/20210927-160143/cadre-interministeriel-donnee.pdf), the interministerial director for digital affairs outlines the vision and challenges of data-driven public action. Data is said to be « the strategic asset of the digital revolution », and its impact on public action is broken down into five areas : transparency, production of better public services, efficacy, supportiveness, creation of economic value.

At the request of the Prime Minister, an unprecedented mobilisation has taken place in all ministries about data, algorithms and source codes : together, within a shared interministerial framework, each ministry has defined its strategy in this area and has broken it down into a plan of concrete actions to be implemented over a period of 2 to 3 years. The 15 ministerial roadmaps on data, algorithms and source codes are available here (https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/datasets/politique-publique-de-la-donnee-des-algorithmes-et-des-codes-sources-15-feuilles-de-route-ministerielles/) and the list of actions decided by the ministries in the framework of the ministerial roadmaps is available in open data here (https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/datasets/liste-des-actions-prises-par-les-ministeres-dans-le-cadre-des-feuilles-de-routes-ministerielles/). Each ministerial roadmap specifies the impact of open data in their respective field : for example, the Ministry of Justice has defined a list of impact indicators, the Ministry of Ecological Transition has outlined the specific impact of open data on the environment, etc.

column6:
Do you have a methodology in place to measure the impact of open data in your country?
 
For Explanation:
* If yes, please briefly describe the key points of this methodology.
column13:
2025:
The French open data team (data.gouv.fr) has developed a methodology to measure the impact of open data. It is based on examining four levels, for which data use is assessed :
1. Raw data itself : dataset visits, dataset downloads, etc.
2. Direct uses of data : number and nature of dataset reuses
3. Indirect uses of data : use of reuses
4. Externalities : broader social and economic impact

We measure :
Level 1 and level 2 using metrics provided by the data.gouv.fr platform
Level 3 and 4 by identifying and measuring the impact of open data use cases.

Our approach alignes with and follows the work currently being carried out by data.europa.eu to design a shared methodological framework for assessing the impact of open data : the Use Case Observatory and Indicators for an open data impact assessment. 

This methodology is set and thoroughly described in this study : https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/datasets/r/b647386b-b143-4fa3-891e-1ad9d31a19ab
2024:
2024:
In addition to the platform's impact indicators, we now rely on the outputs, outcomes, and impacts methodology, which is quite similar to our level-based evaluation.

We then break it down by theme.
2023:
Etalab has developed a systematic impact assessment methodology. This methodology proposes to estimate the impact of open data by examining four different levels or layers :

- First level : raw data itself : number of datasets published, downloaded, etc. For this first level, we analyse visits to dataset pages, datasets downloads, etc. by using data.gouv.fr metrics available on [stats.data.gouv.fr](http://www.stats.data.gouv.fr/). We are then able identify datasets with the highest impact and the ones that are highly demanded. The [data.gouv.fr dataset catalogue](https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/datasets/catalogue-des-donnees-de-data-gouv-fr/) also provides visibility on published datasets with their associated metadata and metrics. This provides a more global knowledge on user behavior on the national platform.
- Second level : direct uses of the data : number of reuses on datasets. For this second level, we examine how many reuses are known for each dataset and their nature.
- Third level : indirect uses of raw data : usages of the reuses developed from open data. For this third level, we investigate how much open data reuses are themselves used (this is sometimes impossible to know).
- Fourth level : externalities : societal and economic impacts of open data. For this fourth level, we document the impacts on the datasets for which we have observed high impact in a structured assessment report : general description, reuser, value proposition, datasets used, partners involved, results, next steps and learnings, etc.

This methodology is presented and detailed in a working paper exploring how to measure open data impact : https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/datasets/r/a61e1fcc-cd61-46bd-a6c5-af94cb9f8459

We are continuously trying to improve this impact assessment methodology by integrating other countries’ best practices. We have participated in several working groups on this topic and have already presented our approach on numerous occasions, namely [data.europa academy webinar ´Measuring open data Impact in Europe](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Cp7-qSNLR1U)

column6:
Is there collaboration between government and civil society or academia to create open data impact in your country?

For Explanation:
* If yes, please provide an example
* If possible, URLs to such projects and collaborations.
column13:
2025:
Central government bodies have several formal partnerships with civil society organisations and academia to create open data impact. Here are a few examples :
- The French open data team (data.gouv.fr) has partnered with Latitudes, an association promoting tech for good, to develop the Open Data University program through which teachers in universities make their students work on projects reusing open data to develop their skills. In 2024, 2000 students from 30 universities have participated to the program and worked on projects such as « how to promote access to culture ? » or « is the distribution of charging infrastructures for électricité cars in France appropriate ? » : https://www.opendatauniversity.org/ https://www.latitudes.cc/
- The Interministerial Directorate for Digital Affairs leads the « Citizen Initiatives Accelerator » (https://communs.beta.gouv.fr/), a program that aims at supporting general interest projects led by civil society organisations, so as to accelerate their development and impact. It provides them with access to public data, a coaching offer, connections with the right representatives within public administration, networking opportunities, etc. In 2024, through this program, the Interministériel Directorate for Digital Affairs has partnered with : Open Street Map (a free, open map database updated and maintained by a community of volunteers) to develop uMap based on Open Street Map data (https://umap.openstreetmap.fr/fr/), Open Food Facts (a non profit that develops a free, online and crowdsourced database on food products) to develop an eco score on food products by reusing ecobalyse open data (https://fr.openfoodfacts.org/) or Pyrenean (a non profit organisation developing an open spruce solution for early detection of fire outbreaks by reusing open data https://pyronear.org/)
- The Ministry of Ecological Transition developed Green Data for Health, a service offer that facilitates the use of environmental data to serve health-environment for national and regional public servants, researchers, private professionals and health-environment related civil society organisations. It is based on 3 components : an online data catalog, legal assistance and a French health-environment data community (with call for projects, challenges, etc.) with more than 450 active members (https://gd4h.ecologie.gouv.fr/)
- The Ministry of Ecological Transition, through its Adaptation program, has helped associations in developing their projects related to climate change adaptation through the reuse of open data. In 2024, it has helped the association « Observatoire de l’immobilier durable » in developing a decision-support tool for climate risks based on IPCC scenarios through an analysis that cross-references exposure and vulnerability (https://www.innoverpourlatransitionecologique.fr/fr/challenges/open-booster/pages/rejoindre-une-equipe?lang=f)
2024:
2024:
Among projects in France, we can mention:

OpenStreetMap
OpenFoodFact
The Open Data University project
2023:
We are very lucky to have a strong and active civil society in France on open data.

The COVID-19 crisis has been a catalyst for collaboration between government and civil society. Open data made it possible for impactful tools to be built, for example ViteMaDose [https://vitemadose.covidtracker.fr/](https://vitemadose.covidtracker.fr/) that checks for available slots in vaccination centres and is based on the list of said centres, pharmacists and GPs that administer vaccines. The development of the COVID-19 dashboard on the Government website was also a coordinated effort from different actors to create impact : [https://www.etalab.gouv.fr/comment-les-administrations-ont-collabore-a-louverture-des-donnees-du-coronavirus-le-cas-francais](https://www.etalab.gouv.fr/comment-les-administrations-ont-collabore-a-louverture-des-donnees-du-coronavirus-le-cas-francais).

Within the framework of the Open Government Partnership [https://www.modernisation.gouv.fr/nos-actions/gouvernement-ouvert/ouvrir-laction-publique-construisons-ensemble-le-plan-daction-gouvernement-ouvert-2021-2023-de-la-france](https://www.modernisation.gouv.fr/nos-actions/gouvernement-ouvert/ouvrir-laction-publique-construisons-ensemble-le-plan-daction-gouvernement-ouvert-2021-2023-de-la-france), the next French Action Plan is being developed together with governmental actors such as the DITP, Etalab, and cada.fr, civil society associations such as madada.fr and ouvre-boite.org, and journalists. This action plan aims to create impact on important themes for French people : transparency of public action results, environmental issues, local public action, users at the heart of public action, citizen participation, digital inclusion, etc.

In 2022, Etalab has collaborated with Latitudes, a non-profit promoting « Tech for good », to design an « Open Data University » : [https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/pages/odu/home/](https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/pages/odu/home/). This program, that aims at teaching higher education students how to reuse open data, provides teachers with high impact open data projects for their students to work on and create impact. This year, 5 projects on high value added datasets have been designed and led to impactful reuses :

- Cycling infrastructures : Students are being asked to find out where to build cycling infrastructures to reduce cycling accidents and improve road safety [https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/pages/odu/defi_infrastructures-cyclables/](https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/pages/odu/defi_infrastructures-cyclables/)
- Energy issues in France : Students are being asked to analyse and make predictions to better understand the possible impacts of the Ukrainian crisis on energy in France : [https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/pages/odu/defi_energie/](https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/pages/odu/defi_energie/)
- Middle school sectors : Students are being asked to design a tool to make it easier for parents to know which middle school to enroll their child in : [https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/pages/odu/defi_carte-scolaire/](https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/pages/odu/defi_carte-scolaire/)
- French recovery plan after the COVID-19 crisis : Students are being asked to assess the extent to which the aid distributed by the State as part of the recovery plan has had an impact on economic activity and/or ecological transition in France : [https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/pages/odu/defi_france-relance/](https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/pages/odu/defi_france-relance/)
- Electric vehicles : Students are being asked to find out whether the distribution of charging infrastructures on the territory correspond to a logic of population distribution and/or road traffic : [https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/pages/odu/defi_vehicules-electriques/](https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/pages/odu/defi_vehicules-electriques/)

Through the Accelerator of citizen initiatives [https://citoyens.transformation.gouv.fr/](https://citoyens.transformation.gouv.fr/), Etalab has collaborated with Infoclimat to create impact with weather data and make them more accessible to all : [https://www.infoclimat.fr/](https://www.infoclimat.fr/)

column6: Automated feedback mechanisms tracking users´ access to datasets
column13:
2025:
The French open data team (data.gouv.fr) and many data producers have implemented automated dashboards to track users’ access to datasets. They include usage metrics such as : number of views on datasets, number of downloads on datasets, number of reuses linked to datasets, etc. The indicators selected were inspired by data.europa.eu « Indicators for an Open Data Impact Assessment ». They are openly displayed here : https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/dashboard/ and on each dataset’s page : https://guides.data.gouv.fr/guide-data.gouv.fr/statistiques. Data producers also have access, through the data.gouv.fr platform, to a consolidated view of their datasets usage metrics. 

A synthesis of these automated statistics as of 2024 is available here : https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/datasets/r/b647386b-b143-4fa3-891e-1ad9d31a19ab 
2024:
In 2023, the data.gouv.fr team conducted an extensive survey on the impact of open data.

This survey is based on the French methodology for impact measurement and is inspired by European work, particularly the "Indicators for an Open Data Impact Assessment."

The study outlines the outputs, outcomes, and impacts for the four dimensions of impact (governmental, environmental, social, economic).

Regarding the outputs, a selection of indicators among those identified by the Commission were selected, including:
- Number of datasets on the theme
- Number of new datasets on the theme in 2023
- Number of views on these datasets in 2023
- Downloads of these datasets in 2023
- Number of discussions
- Number of reuses on the theme
- Number of new reuses on the theme in 2023
- Reuses by type
- Number of views on the reuses in 2023
- Discussions on the reuses

Regarding the outcomes and impacts, the use cases examined were selected from three main sources:
- The reuse catalog of the data.gouv.fr platform;
- The catalog of digital public services developed within beta.gouv.fr;
- The catalog of research publications on scanr.

And according to three criteria:
- High potential impact;
- Availability of resources and information;
- A balanced distribution in the four impact categories defined by the Open Data Maturity Report.

For each use case, a literature search was conducted and interviews were sometimes conducted with their designers to document the services, the data used, and the impacts created.

The results of this study will be published in 2024 in the form of six articles on data.gouv.fr and consolidated into a more comprehensive paper.

This is not the only study; we can notably mention the work of OpenDataFrance (DataImpact: new edition of the study on the reuse cases of environmental data - Open data france https://opendatafrance.fr/dataimpact-publication/) as well as the book by Dr. in Sociology Samuel Goëta “Les données de la démocratie: open data, pouvoirs et contre-pouvoirs” (https://cfeditions.com/donnees-democratie/) which provides a critical assessment of the impact of open data.

Mes Aides Reno (https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/reuses/calculateur-des-aides-a-la-renovation-energetique/) is a digital public service, developed within the Interministerial Directorate for Digital Affairs, that simplifies access to energy renovation subventions for everyone. With a target of 700 000 renovations per year, the resources allocated by the French government to the renovation of private housing reached 4 billion euros in 2024.
Mes Aides Reno helps users build their home’s energy renovation project by assisting them in assessing and requiring national and local aid so that more people engage in renovation projects. 

500 000 simulations were carried out every month in 2024 and 10% led to appointments with a France Renov counselor to go further into the process. 

Some of the open datasets used : https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/datasets/liste-espaces-conseil-france-renov-1/ https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/datasets/perimetre-espaces-conseil-france-renov-1/ 
2024:
We focused on two applications that converge towards more effective and efficient public action:

Zero Vacant Housing

Developed by the Ministry of Ecological Transition, Zero Vacant Housing (ZLV) is a tool that helps local authorities identify vacant housing in their territories and then mobilize owners to put these properties back on the market. It was built using the National Buildings Database and the National Condominium Registration Registry. Since its launch, ZLV has facilitated the return of vacant housing to the market with:

- 7,605 housing units that are in the process of being vacated or have already been reoccupied;
- 7,570 municipalities using the solution, with 27,655 updates to files already carried out.

This return to the market helps create an affordable housing supply, boosts local economic activity related to the construction industry, and reduces the need for new construction.

Go Rénove Bailleurs

Go Rénove Bailleurs is a public service that assists with the energy renovation of buildings for social landlords. It provides them with:

- An overview of their building portfolio and its energy performance;
- Indicators to assess the opportunity and impact of renovations.

The solution relies heavily on the National Buildings Database. It promotes more renovations, a key public policy priority of the Government (Climate Resilience Law).

Link to the report : https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/datasets/r/b647386b-b143-4fa3-891e-1ad9d31a19ab

The Directorate General of Public Finances (DGFiP) developed a tool modeling the State’s accounts and their movements over ten years (https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/reuses/datavisualisation-des-comptes-de-letat/), so as to increase transparency and accessibility to the State’s financial data. The interface offers a comprehensive view of the State’s balance sheet and income statement, with granularity enabling fine-grained analysis by accounting item and sub-item. This tool allows to better inform a wide audience : from September 2024, it has already been consulted more than 110 000 times.

The open dataset reused : https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/datasets/donnees-de-comptabilite-generale-de-letat-sur-10-ans/
2024:
On the transparency and accountability of public administrations, we focused on three uses:

Barometer of the Application of Laws

The Barometer of the Application of Laws, designed within the National Assembly, formats open data such as "Laws and Decrees of the Official Journal" to make them more accessible. This service promotes greater transparency regarding the application of laws by allowing measurement of the proportion and timeliness with which the decrees required by a law are published. In 2024, the service recorded:

- 145,538 views of the application rate of a law from its legislative file;
- 4,188 unique visits to the list of laws.

Camerci

For Camerci, the "Video Surveillance – Camera Placement" data was used by a citizen to create a map that allows individuals to request a copy of the surveillance footage in which they appear. This use facilitates the exercise of one's rights and awareness of current legislative provisions.

Responsible Public Procurement and Local Purchasing: Lessons from French Open Data

In this research work, open data from public procurement was utilized to analyze local public purchasing. The results suggest that local purchasing may have protectionist foundations and may not necessarily be the result of environmental concerns. Such analyses align with the issue of citizen oversight of administrative actions enabled by open data.

Link to the report : https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/datasets/r/b647386b-b143-4fa3-891e-1ad9d31a19ab

2025:
Datalma (https://beta.gouv.fr/startups/datalma.html) is a digital public service developed within the French Presidency. It aims at supporting decisions taken by the Presidency, the Prime Minister and the ministries based on relevant and recent data, thus allowing for data-driven decision making. It provides thematic dashboards following relevant indicators. An MVP dashboard has been developed regarding health matters, and used numerous open datasets such as some listed here : https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/pages/donnees_sante/.
2024:
Examples abound regarding the use of open data in the development of public policies. We have selected three to be examined:

Cartofriches

Developed by Cerema, Cartofriches helps local authorities and other project leaders locate and characterize brownfield sites for reuse. Its features include:

- Visualization of brownfield sites in the territory;
- Detailed information about each site.

Cerema uses BASIAS and BASOL data to pre-identify brownfield sites. The tool facilitates the reuse of brownfields and thus contributes to reducing land artificialization, with 10,385 brownfields identified.

Banning Cars to Promote Bikes? A Study on the City of Tours

This research article on mobility in the city of Tours uses daily bicycle counter data and climate data to study the effect of closing a bridge to cars on bicycle traffic. The result provides a diagnosis that the local government can use to adapt its mobility policies: the closure is associated with a 7.23% increase in bicycle traffic.

A History of Political Conflict – Elections and Inequalities in France (1789-2022)

The work of two economists (Thomas Piketty and Julia Cagé) combines data on election results (legislative, presidential elections, and referendums for the 36,000 French communes from 1789 to 2022) with socio-demographic indicators to propose an analysis of the social structure of the electorates of different political currents. The reflections developed have greatly contributed to public debate: who votes for whom and why? What are the consequences for democracy?

Link to the report : https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/datasets/r/b647386b-b143-4fa3-891e-1ad9d31a19ab

In 2023, the data.gouv.fr team conducted an extensive survey on the impact of open data.

The study outlines the outputs, outcomes, and impacts for the four dimensions of impact (governmental, environmental, social, economic).

Regarding the outputs, a selection of indicators among those identified by the Commission were selected, including:
- Number of datasets on the theme
- Number of new datasets on the theme in 2023

- Number of new reuses on the theme in 2023

- The reuse catalog of the data.gouv.fr platform;

And according to three criteria:
- High potential impact;
- Availability of resources and information;
- A balanced distribution in the four impact categories defined by the Open Data Maturity Report.

Mon Logement Etudiant (https://monlogementetudiant.beta.gouv.fr/) is a digital public service developed by the Ministry of Higher Education and Research, that facilitates access to housing for students. Access to independent housing is still difficult for many students, leading some of them to drop out of school, not have a stable home or self-censorship in career choices. Mon Logement Etudiant seeks to centralise as many housing offers as possible from social landlords and to provide students with a housing aid simulator.

Two use cases illustrate how open data can be mobilized to address urban housing issues:

Résorption bidonvilles

Résorption bidonvilles is a digital public service that enables state services, local authorities, and others to identify, share information, and take action to eliminate slums. It allows users to:

- Consult the list and characteristics of all sites in a territory;
- Learn about the actions taken;
- Assist each other with a directory of all users and a forum;
- Visualize platform data.

Through simplified operational monitoring for public officials and better coordination among stakeholders, the tool accelerates the eradication of slums and improves support for affected populations. Since the platform's launch in 2019, more than 4,000 people have been rehoused (17 sites eliminated in 2022, 28 in 2021, 16 in 2020) and in 2022:

- 3,566 minors were enrolled in school through the school mediation program;
- 5,461 people received health support in 2022;
- Over 1,000 people gained employment.

Aux Alentours by MAIF is a tool developed by the mutual insurance company. It aggregates and maps numerous open data sources (risks, facilities, transport stops, noise exposure, etc.) to enable individuals to better understand the risks associated with their environment and take preventive measures with appropriate advice.

As of now, these internships were often found through students’ network. The tools thus gives students from middle schools in priority education networks access to quality internship offers. Over 70 000 students have already benefited from it, with 37 000 offers already published and 11 000 internships completed.

2024:
Examples abound regarding the use of open data in the field of education and skills. We have selected four for examination:

DiagOriente

DiagOriente is a digital public service that helps young people formalize their skills and professional interests, discover corresponding professions, and find training and/or employment more easily. It relies on data such as job operational requirements, labor market data, and job offers. The service currently has 432,000 users, among whom:
- 85% realized they had many skills;
- 75% discovered professions they would like to pursue;
- 65% completed the process with an engaged professional project.

SupTracker

A personal project by two citizens, SupTracker formats open data related to Parcoursup to allow users to:

- Get information on a training program: applications and admissions, profile of admitted candidates, selectivity indicators, etc.;
- Compare training programs;
- Analyze orientation by high school specialties;
- Explore the distribution of candidates based on their profile: honors in the baccalaureate, scholarship status, etc.

Thanks to the application, students can better inform themselves about the training programs they consider joining (recruitment and selectivity) to formulate coherent orientation projects.

- Analyses based on the social position indices of schools, colleges, and high schools

The social position index of an institution is an indicator summarizing the socio-economic and cultural conditions of the families of the students it welcomes. The associated data, published in 2022 by the Ministry of National Education, have rekindled and enriched the debate on the lack of social mixing in schools. For example:

The newspaper Le Monde wrote an article highlighting socio-economic disparities between public and private middle schools, as well as some neighboring public middle schools;
The Department of Prospective, Evaluation, and Performance of the Ministry of National Education conducted a study on social disparities between middle schools, in light of the objective of social diversity.

Open Data University Challenges
As part of the Open Data University, open data becomes a training tool for developing skills and civic engagement among young people. The Open Data University is a program that offers higher education institutions the opportunity to have their students work on open data challenges addressing social and environmental issues. The program is run by the association Latitudes, which collaborates with 100 higher education institutions to integrate social and environmental dimensions into their curricula. In 2023-2024, more than 650 students from 16 institutions were trained by working on open data challenges related to elections, culture, and energy.

France Chaleur Urbaine (https://france-chaleur-urbaine.beta.gouv.fr/) is a digital public service developed by the French Agency for Ecological Transition that seeks to accelerate the connection of buildings to district heating networks, an ecological and economical way of heating. As of February 2025, more than 5100 requests have been submitted and 1460 connections to networks were in progress or effective, representing around 78 000 tonnes of CO2 that will potentially be avoided every year.

Regarding ecological cities, we focused on two use cases: Registre de preuve de covoiturage Designed by the Ministry of Ecological Transition, the Registre de preuve de covoiturage (RPC) helps regions encourage short-distance carpooling. By using a registry that aggregates completed carpooling trips (open) and their certification, it facilitates the distribution of incentives to promote this practice. The service supports the implementation of public policies to develop daily carpooling, addressing several issues: - Environmental issues: each kilometer carpooled per passenger avoids the emission of 195g of CO2 equivalent (Ademe); - Economic and social issues: carpooling provides a solution for the 13 million French people facing "mobility poverty." Since 2019: - 20,303,882 trips have been recorded; - 7.4 million incentivized trips were generated from campaigns configured on the RPC; - With an average of 2.21 people per vehicle. Analysis and Prediction of Pedestrian Flows in a Multimodal Transport Hub Using Multi-Source Data This research leveraged open mobility data to understand the dynamics of pedestrian flows in the transport spaces of the La Défense district and forecast short-term crowding. These forecasts could enhance passenger information for public transport users or enable "on-demand" regulation of transport services, guiding their usage effectively.

2024:
Examples abound regarding the use of open data in adaptation to climate change and related disasters. We have selected three for examination:

Pyronear

Pyronear is an association that aims to democratize open solutions for combating forest fires. It is developing a forest fire risk score using various open data sources such as meteorological data, soil moisture index, and forest fire databases in France. This risk score aims to enable early detection of fires, allowing for faster and more effective intervention by fire and rescue services.

VigiFrance

VigiFrance is a personal project by a citizen. The tool centralizes and synthesizes a set of open data related to natural, technological, and health risks to provide clear and localized information quickly. It includes data on air quality from Atmo France, the National Address Database, and weather alerts from Météo-France. Citizens can thus monitor risk evolution near their location, stay informed during a disaster, and adopt appropriate behaviors.

Projects conducted during the Météo-France Open Data Hackathon
The data.gouv.fr team, in conjunction with Météo-France, organized a hackathon on public meteorological data in April 2024. During this event, numerous projects related to climate change were developed:

- OpenGustMap: Estimation of observed wind speed at any place and time in the past to help insured individuals assert their rights under storm guarantees;
- Franceinfo: Comparison of current weather with historical temperatures over the past decades in Overseas France;
- ClimateViz: Public platform for creating customizable indicators based on historical weather data and climate forecasts;
- SafeCoast: Alerts and analyses of extreme events at observation stations for better protection of French coasts against climate risks;
- Voyageurs du climat: An exploration tool that allows observing the evolution of weather phenomena in France and comparing certain indicators over time.
