* If yes, please provide an example
* If possible, URLs to such projects and collaborations.
column13:
2025:
The collaboration between government and civil society takes place in the context of the OGP IT Community and the 6° National Open Government Plan (6NAP – see https://open.gov.it/governo-aperto/piano-nazionale/6nap) where also activities on Open Data are included also with reference to their impact.
One of the objective of the above-mentioned Plan is indeed to strengthen transparency and openness of data to create public value and open the NRRP to citizens. This objective includes two commitments:
- Promoting technology and data as a common good to encourage open government practices (see https://open.gov.it/governo-aperto/piano-nazionale/6nap/azione-3/impegno-6)
- Promoting a new model of transparency focused on public value and civil society participation (https://open.gov.it/governo-aperto/piano-nazionale/6nap/azione-3/impegno-7). 

The activities included in the commitment C6 of the Plan are listed and described at this link: https://open.gov.it/governo-aperto/piano-nazionale/6nap/azione-3/impegno-6#attivit- 
One of those activities is aimed at improving access to information and decisions on public investment decisions registered with the Unique Project Code (Codice Unico di Progetto – CUP) that create value in the OpenCUP portal (see https://www.opencup.gov.it/), also by improving data interoperability.
The impacts of these activities are: the improvement of the decision-making process and the accountability of public administrations; a better data quality, accessibility and interoperability also thanks to a specific ontology and controlled vocabularies that are being created.

Besides the 6NAP, there are other initiatives of collaboration between government and civil society or academia. The project “Open Government Data: Understanding Society Through Public Administration Data” (see https://ogd.sociologia.unimib.it/) is funded by the Ministry of University and Research and is implemented by the University of Milan-Bicocca, also through agreements with specific public administrations.
The key activities planned in the project are:
- Public Administration Open Data Observatory, aimed at creating a hub to transform public data into resources ready for research;
- Development of New Lines of Research, aimed at guiding data-driven policies and promoting a deeper understanding of social phenomena;
- Multimedia Laboratory, aimed at disseminating knowledge and providing resources for interactive learning, also involving the non-academic community.
The impact created by the project is at a scientific, technological and socio-economic level. Scientific Impact: the research contributes to the creation of new scientific knowledge. Technological Impact: production of accurate data and development of innovative methodologies for analysing data from different sources. Economic and Social Impact:in the short term, creation of jobs and purchase of goods to improve teaching; in the medium to long term, contribution to advanced training, strengthening human capital and promoting the use of data by citizens to create economic opportunities and influence policies.
2024:
The co-creation process involving representatives of PAs and CSOs (civil society organizations) belonging to the OGP IT Community continues with the aim of defining the 6° National Open Government Plan (6NAP) where also activities on Open Data are included also with reference to their impact.

The policy of Open Data in Ukraine includes the following basic documents that regulate Open Data sphere:
Law of Ukraine "On Information" https://zakon.rada.gov.ua/laws/show/2657-12#Text  
The law defines the basic principles of access to information, and establishes the categorization of information that is in the possession of state bodies                                                                                                                                                                                       The Law of Ukraine "On Access to Public Information" https://zakon.rada.gov.ua/laws/show/2939-17#Text which contains a separate article on Open Data, and establishes the general principles of access to public information.
Resolution of the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine dated October 21, 2015 No. 835 "On approval of the regulation on data sets that are subject to publication in the form of Open Data" https://zakon.rada.gov.ua/laws/show/835-2015-%D0%BF#Text 
The regulation defines the procedure for publishing  Open Data, requirements for its metadata, and a list of sets of data that must be published in the form of Open Data.
In addition, the provision contains implemented principles of the International Open Data Charter                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Resolution of the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine dated November 30, 2016 No. 867 "Some issues of public information disclosure in the form of Open Data" https://zakon.rada.gov.ua/laws/show/867-2016-%D0%BF#Text. The regulation contains basic information about the functioning of the national Open Data portal, and the obligations of data providers in working with portal
Resolution of the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine dated September 22, 2016 No. 686-r "Some issues of joining the International Open Data Charter" https://zakon.rada.gov.ua/laws/show/686-2016-%D1%80#Text. Resolution establishes Ukraine's accession to the International Open Data Charter and imposes an obligation on data providers to use the principles of the charter during the process of publishing datasets
The implementation of Directive 2019/1024/EU regarding Open Data was carried out in 2021 with the adoption of Resolution No. 407 of the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine dated March 3, 2021 "On Amendments to Resolutions No. 835 and No. 30 of the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine dated October 21, 2015 November 2016 No. 867"

The Law of Ukraine "on Access to Public Information" provides for the possibility of publishing information provided by individuals or legal entities under private law.
However, if a natural or legal person under private law is a provider of information of significant public interest or concerns the environment, protection of life and health of citizens - such publication is mandatory. NGO "Save Dnipro" publish its own data on the National portal https://data.gov.ua/organization/9b012670-b499-4923-a3c9-4c23f1d86f8f.
Moreover, the draft of the Strategy for the Development of Open Data for 2025-2027 also defines measures to increase the intensity of publication and access to data generated by citizens. This is defined in Strategic Goal 5 (page 9). This task is aimed at building relationships between business and government regarding the sharing of machine-readable data, which will facilitate the effective use of this data. Such exchange will promote the development of the digital economy, innovation and the implementation of modern technological solutions, and can also lead to insufficient interaction and exchange of data between sectors.
The expected results of the implementation of Strategic Goal 5 will be the creation of a basis for the development of a regulatory framework that regulates B2B (business-to-business) and B2G (business-to-government) relations in the field of machine-readable data exchange. Strategic Goal 5 of the Strategy for the development of Open Data for 2025-27 envisages building interaction between stakeholders in the Open Data sphere to realize the social and economic potential of open data. One of the tasks for implementing this strategic goal is: supporting programs that promote the use of open data (page 9): https://data.gov.ua/uploads/files/2025-05-01-150336.772070OD-Strategy.pdf 
2024:
2024:
One of the goals of new Open Data Strategy is the high level of re-use of public information in the form of Open Data, which also includes re-use of Open Data by the private sector. It will include the following subgoals: the functionality of the Portal allows ordinary users to use its capabilities having basic technical skills; the Portal has implemented several channels of user interaction with data providers and the holder of the Portal; dynamic data, which is in high demand in society, is updated at the time of creation and measures to achieve those subgoals.
https://data.gov.ua/uploads/files/2022-06-15-102752.7196282150222.pdf

The "Open Data Advocacy" series was also launched https://osvita.diia.gov.ua/courses/open-data-advocation.
 
In addition, the draft of the Strategy for the development of Open Data for 2025-27 provides for the provision that the revision of the current legislation on Open Data, including legislative acts regulating, in particular, the reuse of data, should become a key stage in the implementation of the Strategy. In order to implement this task, it is planned to prepare systemic changes to the legislation to eliminate obstacles to access to public information and its use as Open Data. Reuse will also be ensured by increasing the quality, interoperability, quantity and volume of Open Data sets and associated metadata, which is Strategic Goal 2. Also, Task 6 of Strategic Goal 5 is to facilitate hackathons, competitions and support programs for projects based on on Open Data. Does the national strategy/policy mandate carrying out and maintaining a data inventory by public bodies, whether at national or local level?

For Explanation:
* If yes, please briefly specify.
column13:
2025:
According to legislation, all public bodies must publish the result of data inventory on data.gov.ua. 
Legislation establishes the definition of the term "information audit" - the process of analysis by the data provider on the availability, status, formats, management processes and use of all information in his possession. An information audit is mandatory and is performed at least once a year.
The methodology of information audit is approved by the central executive body, which ensures the formation and implementation of state policy in the field of Open Data - Ministry of Digital Transformation.

Support for local initiatives is provided by the Ministry of Digital Transformation of Ukraine inter alia by concluding memorandums of cooperation with local councils. Within the framework of these memoranda, the Ministry supports local authorities in conducting information audits, adopting the internal legal framework of data providers, and grants a license for the deployment of local Open Data portals. Also, training on Open Data is mandatory for such bodies.
Thus, the Ministry of Digital Transformation is actively stimulating the development of regional Open Data policy, in particular to systematize work with administrators at the regional level and simplify citizens' access to Open Data. The Data+ communication platform was created with the assistance of the Ministry of Digital Transformation of Ukraine, which was publicly presented on May 29, 2024. Within the framework of the operation of Data+, regular meetings are held with stakeholders in the field: the Ministry of Digital Transformation of Ukraine, the Ombudsman of Ukraine, data providers, experts, civil society, etc. 
During 2024, 7 Data+ community meetings were held. An online discussion on the challenges and opportunities in the open data sector took place in connection with the first reading of Draft Law No. 8153 "On Personal Data Protection." Other key topics included the discussion of Draft Law No. 11533 of August 29, 2024, concerning access to information from individual electronic registers; the challenges of verifying and publishing data from the Unified State Register of Addresses; and the methodology for ranking cities based on the level of open data publication. Public consultations were also held on the draft Open Data Development Strategy for 2025–2027. Additionally, an online training session titled “Using Artificial Intelligence in the Field of Open Data” was conducted, along with the inaugural meeting of the communication platform, where participants were introduced to the objectives of the initiative. A detailed description of all events is available on the Facebook community page of the Data+ communication platform: https://www.facebook.com/share/g/1Fe51a26NU/.

column13:
The full-scale war waged by Russia against Ukraine has a significant impact on the Open Data sphere and the implementation of strategies and plans for the development of the Open Data sphere. To ensure the interests of national security and defense, till August 2022 the work of national and local portals was temporarily suspended, as well as activities related to improving the level of skills in Open Data. In addition, due to the war, funding for IT development, including Open Data, has been significantly reduced.
At the same time, despite the full-scale invasion of the Russian Federation into Ukraine, the Ministry of Digital Transformation in every possible way ensures the safe opening of data, access to which has been restricted due to military operations. For this, it is necessary to find a balance between transparency and security, taking into account all the challenges of war. For this purpose, a method of conducting a three-part test is currently being developed (https://www.facebook.com/mintsyfra/posts/pfbid0aMQXFMTP8sk84qRa8YcF1pgV7xtC4J2RV8WfW7Lk48unLrBLz45g23TJmXeNTSStl), constant consultations are held with data providers and other stakeholders. Ministry of Digital Transformation of Ukraine proactively takes measures to renew access to datasets of high social interest, for example the Unified State Register of Legal Entities and Individual Entrepreneurs and Public Organizations, Register of Damaged and Destroyed Property in the form of Open Data taking into account security interests.
Another serious challenge for the development of open data was the termination of USAID funding for projects. Many activities in the field of open data were implemented with the support of the DTA project, which was funded by USAID and UK dev.

During dataset moderation (checking by an authorized person of the portal holder of data sets uploaded to the portal for compliance with the requirements specified in the Regulation on data sets to be made public in the form of Open Data), incorrectly created sets are rejected with appropriate comments, then these comments must be made by the data provider corrected. In addition, the strategic goals of the new strategy for the development of Open Data are to strengthen an ecosystem of education in the field of Open Data, to improve the quality and interoperability of published datasets. In addition, the Ministry actively stimulates the development of the regional Open Data policy by concluding memorandums of cooperation with local self-government bodies and, accordingly, providing support to these bodies during the implementation of the Open Data policy.
Moreover, from the end of 2023, the Open Data Academy is implemented. This is an initiative aimed at training the regional civil servants on Open Data. column13:
2025:
Portal users, if they possess socially necessary information, can become data providers and publish created datasets on the portal. 
For example, the public organization "Save Dnipro" publishes data on hourly concentrations and the air quality index for fine dust of the 2.5 micron fraction in populated areas of Ukraine, and data on radiation background monitoring in Ukraine: https://data.gov.ua/en/dataset/b1b08d68-52b8-48db-a9ef-5546c49a9e00, https://data.gov.ua/en/dataset/80c116f5-9826-4e8e-87f8-ff5d5342da94.
This data is updated monthly, while information providers can choose the frequency of updating datasets: more than once a day, daily, weekly, monthly, quarterly, semi-annually, annually.
Enriched datasets can also be published by adding new versions to the created datasets by the data provider.
Additionally, the National Portal provides functionality for users to contribute datasets by users in the following ways: each page of datasets has a "Propositions" section, for example https://data.gov.ua/en/dataset/198185ea-44d6-48f0-877c-44251c413f64/issues, as well as "Proposed datasets" https://data.gov.ua/requests/all.

Instruction (https://bit.ly/3dq9MYZ) and other materials helping data providers with their publication process are published at the portal https://data.gov.ua/pages/835-rec-index. 
To ensure the support of data providers, the Ministry constantly consults the responsible persons of data providers. During dataset moderation (checking by an authorized person of the portal holder of data sets uploaded to the portal for compliance with the requirements specified in the Regulation on data sets to be made public in the form of Open Data), incorrectly created sets are rejected with appropriate comments, then these comments must be made by the data provider corrected. 
Also, an "Open Data Technical Support" chat has been created in WhatsApp for information providers, where they can ask practical questions about creating datasets.
Moreover, from the end of 2023, the Open Data Academy is implemented. This is an initiative aimed at training the regional civil servants on Open Data. So far, such trainings have been carried out for such employees of Chernivtsi, Lviv, Zakarpattia, Vinnytsia, Kirovohrad, Rivne, Ivano-Frankivsk, Zhytomyr, Kyiv, Odesa, Ternopil, Chernihiv, Cherkasy regions https://academy.data.gov.ua/.

During the entire existence of this series, more than 60,500 civil servants have reviewed and successfully passed it.

For Explanation:
* If yes, please explain the measures in place to ensure complete series of datasets
column13:
The Unified State Web Portal of Open Data ensures the preservation of previous versions of published resources. These versions can be found on the dataset webpage. Example: https://data.gov.ua/dataset/2a746426-b289-4eb2-be8f-aac03e68948c/resource/e43a82da-89e1-4bbb-820c-bd04ab7a0c89  
Versioning of datasets as a functional possibility of the portal is defined in Resolution № 867. In addition, Resolution № 835 defines the fundamental principle of publication of datasets - openness by default, which consists in ensuring the release of all public information by data providers in the form of Open Data, which is in their possession, except for information that is classified by law as information with limited access, as well as information that is not subject to publication in accordance with the Law of Ukraine "On Access to Public Information".
Also, the Ministry of Digital Transformation provides a guidance and support for ensuring the data we receive is of an acceptable quality. The ministerial team has developed recommendations for the publication and updating of datasets by data providers: https://data.gov.ua/pages/835-rec-index.
Moreover, during the moderation of the dataset by an authorized person of the Ministry as the holder of the portal, the description of the set, the number of keywords, and the correct selection of the name of the set are checked. In addition, in case of inconsistency in the quality of the already published version of the dataset, the authorized person of the Ministry can reject the already published version and send it for revision.
Thus, the dataset undergoes repeated moderation, the possibility of which is determined in Resolution № 867.
In addition, the ministerial team constantly provides advisory support to information providers, conducts trainings to ensure that all versions of datasets are of appropriate quality.
Moreover, information providers independently choose the frequency of updating the datasets. When choosing the frequency of updating datasets, information providers shall ensure the maximum possible frequency of their updating and maintenance in an up-to-date state on the Unified State Web Portal of Open Data. The information provider receives a push notification to his email from the portal about the need to update a certain dataset.

The goal of this project is to develop unified requirements for the interoperability of open data sets and to form rules for the formation of sets and standards, which should significantly affect the quality of data, their use and machine readability.
The collection will consist of 4 parts:
1. Dictionary of variable and attribute names, their list (namespaces).

3. Recommendations for managers and software developers - so that the software being developed is interoperable and allows uploading public information in the form of Open Data (guidelines).

The portal supports work with the DCAT dictionary (https://www.w3.org/TR/vocab-dcat/) and DCAT-AP, as a standard solution on the CKAN architecture and as extensions. In particular, metadata of datasets and resources are distributed using the API procedure. The portal uses typical CKAN procedures for working with API.
Transmitted through the portal's API metadata can be translated to DCAT and DCAT-AP using a typical dictionary that uses the ckanext-dcat extension (https://github.com/ckan/ckanext-dcat?tab=readme-ov-file#schemas).
The DCAT and DCAT-AP models are also supported at the level of harvesting datasets from other open data portals based on the CKAN architecture or another architecture. In this case, RDF is used. The Ministry has developed instructions for setting up the harvesting procedure, including using the DCAT and DCAT-AP models. (https://data.gov.ua/uploads/files/2021-06-29-135404.275118-.pdf).
The portal uses the common extension ckanext-dcat (https://extensions.ckan.org/extension/dcat/) which adds the following functionality for using DCAT and DCAT-AP (https://data.gov.ua/api/3/action/status_show):
- dcat - Adds DCAT (Data Catalog Vocabulary) support to CKAN. This extension allows you to describe datasets according to the DCAT-AP standard, which provides better interoperability with other data catalogs.
- dcat_rdf_harvester - This extension is used to collect RDF data (Resource Description Framework) from other portals that support DCAT and import it into CKAN.
- dcat_json_harvester - An extension for collecting and importing DCAT-compliant JSON data from other sources into CKAN.
- dcat_json_interface - An interface for working with data in JSON format that conforms to the DCAT standard. This extension allows you to interact with DCAT data by saving it in JSON format.

column13: The Ministry of Digital Transformation employ a framework to measure the impact of Open Data. We have utilized international best practices such as NYU’s GovLab project https://odimpact.org/ . Qualitative approach to its Open Data impact measurement is used . Typical Open Data impact research involves pre-screening of potential subjects either from a bottom-up approach (a large number of Open Data products found in a specific domain or from a specific Open Dataset) or a top-down one (research into a specific governmental body or domain, e.g. ecology, state regulatory commission, health, etc). The research relies heavily on interviews and focus-groups with parties involved in opening the data (state officials, data scientists), creating and using products based on these data (NGOs, civil activists, journalists, etc). The impact is measured by analysis of several key categories, namely: does it help prevent or detect corruption; does it provide new tools for civil impact; how many users of the Open Data and tools created on the basis of the Open Data? and does it improve social standards? Interviews with the before-mentioned parties allow to gain as much of an objective view of Open Data impact as possible.

In Ukraine, the basis for confirming the case of reuse of a data set is a software product (application) that uses data sets in its work.  Ministry of Digital Transformation maintains a complete list of all applications/visualizations/dashboards and analytical panels in a special section of the Open Data Competence Center Diia.Open Data.

https://openbudget.gov.ua/analytics/incomes

The study "Gender component in Open Data of Ukraine" outlined the fact that human beings and their needs are placed at the center of state decision-making. Open data, disaggregated by gender and other social indicators, helps to obtain valuable information about the current state of rights and opportunities for women, men and their various groups, including the vulnerable, to see gender gaps and possible discrimination. Such data is an important tool for the development, implementation and monitoring of gender-responsive policies, inclusive solutions and services in various spheres of life. In Ukraine, the economic effect of Open Data is divided into direct and secondary. Direct economic impacts include the economic value created by enterprises that provide services using Open Data, as well as the corresponding employment. Employment is considered to have a direct economic impact if the organization bases its business or activities on Open Data (for example, a startup that would not be able to operate without Open Data, or a civil servant working with a national portal). The creation of economic value in the macroeconomic sense involves the creation of gross value added. The latter includes three components: gross profit of the enterprise, wages of employees and taxes paid on products and taxes related to production (excluding subsidies). In other words, the business generates certain profits for its investors, employees and the state. Open data companies, like any business, also create gross value added - it is a direct economic contribution of such companies. https://kse.ua/wp-content/uploads/2021/11/Open-data-methodology-2021-11-04.pdf. 

Responce to reviewer:
Report on Economic Impact of Open Data in Ukraine has been developed (https://tapas.org.ua/wp-content/uploads/2022/08/Economic-impact_report.pdf).
The report analyzed three key indicators: 1) the impact of Open Data on the Ukrainian economy; 2) the number of jobs related to Open Data in the country; and 3) the sectors of the Ukrainian economy that benefit the most from Open Data. 
The information presented in the report is based on the pace of economic development and advancement in the Ukrainian Open Data sphere until Russia invaded Ukraine on February 24, 2022. 
One of its findings was that Open Data contributed between 0.62-1.19% of Ukraine’s gross domestic product (GDP) in 2020. 
The Open Data sphere could contribute between 0.78-2.08% to Ukraine’s economy i.e., UAH 49.9 billion ($167 million) by 2025 through a combination of direct and indirect benefits. 
The research also found that the number of Ukrainians working directly with Open Data is between 4,400 - 6,700. In 2025, somewhere between 23,600 to 50,800 people could be working with Open Data. 
Top sectors working with Open Data in Ukraine include: IT and telecommunications; scientific and technical activities; public administration; real estate, transportation; and postal and courier services. This was TAPAS’ second study on the impact of Open Data on Ukraine’s economy.

Open data has an impact on the level on employment. Today more than 100 available open data services help Ukrainians to check business partners, receive free medicines and medical services, safely invest in real estate, etc. Such services create new jobs for citizens of Ukraine (source: https://tapas.org.ua/all-uk/news-uk/mintsyfra-prezentuvala-viziiu-rozvytku-vidkrytykh-danykh-v-ukraini/). The total employment in the field of open data in 2020 was 15.9-24.5 thousand people. According to the State Statistics Service, in 2020 there were about 7.5 million full-time workers in Ukraine. Since Ukraine is part of the cluster of "fast developing countries", the share of direct employment related to open data is about 0.09% of all employees. Accordingly, under the implementation of the optimistic scenario, direct employment in the field of open data amounts to 6.7 thousand people. If employment grew in accordance with the growth of the general open data market, then under a conservative scenario, direct employment amounts to 4,400 people. However, in addition to direct employment, open data also provides indirect employment. According to research by Shakespeare and Vickery, the indirect open data market is 250-278% of the direct market. Taking into account the average value of these studies, indirect employment related to open data is 11.5-7.8 thousand people (according to research https://tapas.org.ua/wp-content/uploads/2022/08/Economic-impact_report.pdf)

Updated answer:
Lithuania has a national open data policy and has reached tangible results in amending legislation in this regard recently. 
Main legislation on open data policy:
1) The Law on the Right to Receive Information and Re-use of Data
https://e-seimas.lrs.lt/portal/legalAct/lt/TAD/TAIS.94745/asr 
Amendments to the Law on the Right to Receive Information and Re-use of Data entered into force in July 2021 transposing provisions of the Directive (EU) 2019/1024 on open data and the re-use of public sector information as well as establishing a Model for data opening which obliges institutions to inventory their data to know what data are owned by the state and open the data on user demand. The Law was revised on 23/04/2024 establishing that the Law would apply to all 274 private joint-stock companies and joint-stock companies managed by the state or municipalities from November 1 of 2024. Their open data will be inventoried and published for reuse on the Lithuanian Open Data Portal.
https://eimin.lrv.lt/lt/ziniasklaidai/naujienos/eimin-iniciatyva-atveriama-dar-daugiau-svarbiu-duomenu/
2) The Law of the Republic of Lithuania on Reuse of Health Data
https://e-seimas.lrs.lt/portal/legalAct/lt/TAD/72c77a52626411ecb2fe9975f8a9e52e/asr
This law regulates the process of using re-usable health data for public purposes, ensuring the right to privacy and protection of personal data. The legal act enables the use of health data collected in information systems for scientific research, experimental development, innovation, education, knowledge management in health and other purposes. Also for data-based decision-making both at the political and health system regulatory level - for the effective management process of health care institutions, quality assessment of health services, etc.
3) Description of data opening procedure was approved by the Minister of Economy and Innovation on 01/04/2022
https://e-seimas.lrs.lt/portal/legalAct/lt/TAD/327dd210495011ebb394e1efb98d3e67/asr
https://eimin.lrv.lt/lt/naujienos/viesojo-sektoriaus-duomenu-atverimo-procesas-bus-bendras-ir-aiskus
It ensures the overall data opening process of institutions, the quality of the open data, and favorable conditions for the reuse of data. It determines the data opening activities of institutions: appointment of persons responsible for organizing data opening, data inventory and creation of data sets to be opened, preparation of descriptions of data structure, usage of the State Data Management Information System for data anonymisation, data sets publication on the Lithuanian open data portal and ensuring feedback to open data users. 
4) Amendments to the Regulations of Lithuanian open data portal were made by Lithuanian Government on 25/03/2022
https://e-seimas.lrs.lt/portal/legalAct/lt/TAD/6e0d9154391911eabd71c05e81f09716/asr
https://eimin.lrv.lt/lt/naujienos/verslui-paprastesnes-galimybes-gauti-trukstamu-duomenu
The essence of these changes is simpler and faster communication between data users (business) and data holders (public sector), as all communication takes place on the portal itself, without the need to write separate requests or inquiries. The business is able to request the missing data directly on the portal, if it cannot be found here. Thus, the data opening process becomes faster and of higher quality .

Lithuanian strategy and action plan for open government data are part of the following strategic management documents:
1) The 4 year's Programme of the Nineteenth Government of the Republic of Lithuania was approved on 12/11/2024 (https://www.e-tar.lt/portal/lt/legalAct/0b418dc0b89811ef88c08519262548c4). The Programme outlines the strategic directions for open government data: 
80. We will open up and harness data, including health data, for public governance decision-making, thereby achieving greater quality and efficiency of those decisions.
269. We will improve laws to integrate personal healthcare services and clinical trials, attract innovative clinical trials, and reduce the administrative burden of biomedical research. Together with the State Data Agency, state and private partners, we will create conditions for secondary data use and big data projects.
492. We will pursue policies based on scientific research and data.
634. We will establish repositories of genetic resources for biodiversity and ensure their long-term funding and data availability. We will strengthen the maintenance and development of national databases for monitoring the state of biodiversity and ecosystems, ensuring data availability for all interested parties.
719. We will create a smart pollution monitoring system that would provide real-time data on pollution levels and their sources.
736. We will improve public information about the processes of territorial planning, construction, use and maintenance of structures by opening up data stored in information systems and presenting them to the public in a form that is understandable and accessible.
769. We will utilize digital databases. We will strive to create a single system for collecting and using data, and we will strive to use the available data for planning, risk assessment, modeling support measures or providing support, and modeling future decisions.
2) Activities, funding and indicators for open government data are approved in the Ministry's of the Economy and Innovation Progress Measure for 2021–2030 "Promoting data accessibility and re-use" (https://e-seimas.lrs.lt/portal/legalAct/lt/TAD/6cd26880021911edbfe9c72e552dd5bd?jfwid=ng0fm2s6a):
Activity 1. Preparation and adoption of the draft Law of the Republic of Lithuania on Official Statistics and State Data Management (completed in 2023)
Activity 2. Preparation and adoption of draft implementing legal acts of the Law of the Republic of Lithuania on the Right to Information and Data Re-use (completed in 2023)
Activity 3. Development of a metadata standard and API development and management model (the project is being implemented 2023-2026)
Activity 4. Development and implementation in institutions of a software tool that will generate a description of the data structure (metadata) and which will be transferred to a centralized metadata storage database (API repository) (the project is being implemented 2023-2026)
Activity 5. Implementation of API interfaces between at least 376 information systems and registers (the project is being implemented 2023-2026)
Activity 6. Populating the API repository with metadata from at least 376 information systems and registers (the project is being implemented 2023-2026)
Activity 7. Integration of state information resources into the data lake (the project is being implemented 2023-2026)
Activity 8. Development of a data exchange tool (completed in 2024)
Activity 9. Corporate investments in the creation of new innovative solutions and digital services using open data (calls for tender in 2024, 2025, 2026)
 Total funding - 66 millions Eur

The Programme outlines the strategic directions for open government data including measures related to real-time data: 
719. We will create a smart pollution monitoring system that would provide real-time data on pollution levels and their sources.

POLICY:
The Law on the Right to Receive Information and Reuse of Data (https://e-seimas.lrs.lt/portal/legalAct/lt/TAD/77d2b640dd6711eb866fe2e083228059?positionInSearchResults=0&searchModelUUID=cc1dc85c-32fd-4295-a64c-b3ba508bc7fe) transposes the provisions of Directive (EU) 2019/1024 on open data and the re-use of public sector information and includes concrete provisions on the dynamic and real-time data (please see Articles 3(10), 13(5)(6)(7)).
 The concept of dynamic and real-time data is defined in the law (Article 3(10)). The law also contains provisions on the provision of information and data: 
•	Access to variable data is provided through API that allows downloading this data in one go (Article 13(5))
•	The institution or state-run entity must ensure that the possibility to use dynamic data is provided as soon as it is collected or updated, with the exception of the exception established in paragraph 7 of this article (Article 13(6))
•	If an institution or a state-controlled entity ensures the possibility of using dynamic data immediately, as soon as it is collected or updated, the financial and technical burden would disproportionately increase, the possibility of re-using these variable data must be provided during such a period or by applying such technical restrictions that would not cause disruptions repeatedly use variable data (Article 13(7))

When implementing centralized data opening through a "Data Lake", the principle is followed that the opened data is updated when it is updated in the primary source.

The Regulations of the Lithuanian open data portal sets conditions for opening data and managing requests on this portal. The Lithuanian open data portal https://data.gov.lt/ allows businesses and the public to conveniently receive and use data managed by public sector institutions on a one-stop basis. It is envisaged that data not published on this portal will be mandatory to open if such a request from data user is received and such data is not confidential. The responsible institution has to answer the requester within 5 working days from the date of submission of the request, what decision has been taken regarding the opening and submission of the requested data to the portal. 2025:
Businesses often request data (to be opened to public) through the State Data Agency. There were ~10 in-person meetings with individual businesses to discuss their needs.
Data Ambassador events provided excellent opportunities to learn from citizens, journalists, non-government organizations about their needs.

ACADEMIA. The State Data Agency organized 7 lectures at Lithuania's largest universities, including Vilnius University, LSMU, and Vilnius Tech. Students enrolled in data science programs were invited to attend. These lectures focused on demonstrating how open data can be utilized in scientific research, particularly for writing bachelor's and master's theses. The presentations featured 40 illustrated examples showcasing real discoveries made using Lithuanian open data. Each lecture was conducted for a single group of students, with a total of approximately 400 students participating across all sessions.

CITIZENS. The State Data Agency launched a competition challenging participants to solve a complex data engineering puzzle based on open data. The puzzle received approximately 600 attempts, with around 50 successful solutions (winners). Each winner was contacted personally and invited for an individual visit to the State Data Agency, with the option to bring colleagues and friends who share an interest in data. A total of 30 such meetings were held, each attended by 3 to 8 guests. During these 1-2 hour sessions, participants were given an inside look at how open data is created and used. As a result of these meetings, five new employees were hired to work with open data, while many others expressed strong interest in its potential applications—how it can be requested on demand (free of charge) and integrated into their work or studies.

JOURNALIST. Journalists regularly ask State Data Agency for certain official statistics. Each time we encourage them using open data (which can be used to derive same statistics but with greater customisation and granularity) .

2025:
Lithuania’s model is hybrid, with central oversight and policy direction (top-down) combined with decentralized data publishing and user engagement (bottom-up). This approach helps ensure consistency and strategic alignment while encouraging innovation and responsiveness to local needs. It also solves the fragmentation of data opening and data maturity.

BODIES:
•	The Ministry of the Economy and Innovation is the main actor in charge of open data policy making including the following activities: 1) preparation of legal acts setting up principles and processes in the field of open data, 2) construction of financial measures for data opening and promotion of the use of open data (RRF reform, EU Structural Funds investments for the period 2021-2027, the state budget), 3) providing political messages on open data, 4) work with stakeholders, 5) coordination of Data opening coordinators network activities (Open Data club), 6) international cooperation, etc.
https://eimin.lrv.lt/lt/veiklos-sritys/skaitmenine-politika/atviri-duomenys-1
•	State Digital Solutions Agency is a body under the Ministry of Economy and Innovation, which is in charge of implementing open data policy including the following activities: 1) maintenance and development of the Lithuanian open data portal, 2 administrative and technical consultations and help for institutions on data opening process, 3) promotion of open data, 4) cooperation with institutions’ Data opening coordinators and open data users, 5) ensuring the opening of the requested data, 6) analysis of the impact of open data, etc. 
https://vssa.lrv.lt/lt/veiklos-sritys/duomenu-atverimo-koordinavimas/
•	State Data Agency is responsible for a centralized data opening scheme. Data sets of state institutions are processed and opened centrally through the State Data Management Information System managed by the Agency, which ensures standardized anonymization and quality of data (https://duomenys.stat.gov.lt/atviri-duomenys/). Furhermore, the State Data Agency was appointed as the competent authority under Article 7 of DGA to assist the public sector institutions which grant or refuse access for the re-use of certain categories of protected data (https://e-seimas.lrs.lt/portal/legalAct/lt/TAD/01106654590311ee8e3cc6ee348ebf6d?positionInSearchResults=16&searchModelUUID=b7458ac9-1946-4098-aeb1-39c07692931e).
•	In addition, all public bodies are obliged to appoint a person responsible for organizing the opening of the authority’s data, the “Open data Coordinator”. The assigned coordinator has to ensure the process of opening of data, its supervision and compliance with the requirements laid down in the legislation.  

Under the Model for opening data (https://eimin.lrv.lt/lt/veiklos-sritys/skaitmenine-politika/atviri-duomenys-1) all institutions are obliged to open data on user demand registered at the Portal as well as on their own decision. In case there is no data opened on the Portal, Users are encouraged to register their request here https://data.gov.lt/requests/submitted. Institutions are obliged to open data on User demand and all communication related to open data goes through the Lithuanian open data portal and is publicly visible under the updated law’s provisions. 
Ministry of Economy and Innovation and the State Digital Decisions Agency are responsible for promoting the Model for opening data and encouraging institutions to open data as well as data Users to register their needs at the Portal this way obliging institutions to open most valuable data.

column13:
2025:
Lithuania's national governance structure does support local and regional open data initiatives  through centralized policies, guidance, and a national portal. The national government provides methodological and technical support for local institutions on how to publish data.

The State Data Agency is implementing the project “Integration of State Information Resources into the State Data Lake” , during which it cooperates with institutions and together inventories and opens up data from all state information systems and registers. Since the beginning of the Project in 2023, 188 municipalities and municipal enterprises have been inventoried. The main areas of data processed by municipalities are: application processing (admission to schools, kindergartens, various supports), waste management, heating networks, cemeteries, green spaces, geographic data and salary payment/financing. To date, 114 municipal datasets have been opened within the scope of the Project .

Also, in 2024 the State Data Agency introduced a new data analysis tool to local government representatives - the Municipal DataLab application . The data provided in the application allows for various analyses to be performed when solving daily relevant municipal issues, planning strategic goals, and, if necessary, managing crises and emergency situations. By creating the Municipal DataLab , the agency wants to show that important state data not only could, but should be used to solve daily municipal issues, plan strategic goals, and, if necessary, manage crises and emergency situations. (https://vda.lrv.lt/lt/naujienos/pristatytas-savivaldybems-skirtas-duomenu-analizes-irankis-savivaldos-datalab/)
The State Data Agency has launched regular DataLab trainings for municipal representatives. This is a unique opportunity to deepen practical knowledge about the Municipal DataLab tool, which allows for data-driven decision-making in various areas, from emergency management to infrastructure planning (https://vda.lrv.lt/lt/naujienos/savivaldybiu-darbuotojai-kvieciami-i-reguliarius-datalab-mokymus/)
2024:
Under new Model for opening data (https://eimin.lrv.lt/lt/veiklos-sritys/skaitmenine-politika/atviri-duomenys-1) established in 2021, all institutions are obliged to open data on user demand registered at the Portal as well as on their own decision. In case there is no data opened on the Portal, Users are encouraged to register their request here https://data.gov.lt/requests/submitted. Institutions are obliged to open data on User demand and all communication related to open data goes through the Lithuanian open data portal and is publicly visible under the updated law’s provisions. 
Ministry of Economy and Innovation and Information Society Development Committee are responsible for promoting the Model for opening data and encouraging institutions to open data as well as data Users to register their needs at the Portal this way obliging institutions to open most valuable data.

column13:
2025:

Does the governance model include the appointment of official roles in civil services that are dedicated to open data (e.g. open data officers)?

For Explanation:
* If yes, please describe how this task is fulfilled at public body level.
column13:
2024:
POLICY:
According to Article 7(1)(2)(3) of Description of data opening procedure approved by the Minister of Economy and Innovation 01/04/2022, (https://e-seimas.lrs.lt/portal/legalAct/lt/TAD/327dd210495011ebb394e1efb98d3e67/asr), all public bodies are obliged to appoint a person responsible for organising the opening of the authority’s data, the ‘Data Opening Coordinator’. The designated coordinator has to ensure that the process of opening data is carried out, together with its supervision and compliance with the requirements laid down in the legislation.
According to the Law of the Republic of Lithuania on State Information Resources Management (https://e-seimas.lrs.lt/portal/legalAct/lt/TAD/TAIS.415499/asr):
- State Digitization Commissioner simultaneously performs the functions of the Ministry's Institutional Digitization Commissioner and assists the Minister in formulating political provisions, setting priorities and making decisions regarding the need to ensure the reuse of data and changes in its legal regulation (article 13 (3));
- Institutional Digitization Officer together with the person or persons responsible for the organization of data reuse, specified in the description of the procedure for data preparation and publication for reuse, approved by the minister, ensures the reuse of data (article 14 (3));
- Data Management Commissioner together with the person or persons responsible for organizing data reuse, organizes data reuse, monitors and analyzes data reuse processes, provides the data manager with the results of the monitoring and proposals for the necessary decisions on data reuse issues (article 15 (2)).

yes, the State Data Agency shares information about newly opened datasets on their website: https://duomenys.stat.gov.lt/naujienos/. There are ongoing workshops for public sector bodies and open data reusers about the available data. The Agency organizes at least two annual events where open data stakeholders participate and exchange ideas and best practices.
The State Data Agency regularly organizes meetings and consultations aimed not only at the public sector but also at the academic community and researchers. We continuously present information about the State Data Lake and the possibilities for data use to interested user groups.
In 2024, several events were held to promote awareness of data usage practices and opportunities. Among them were dedicated sessions on the DataLab tool for representatives of municipalities, during which the tool and its capabilities were introduced.
Good practice seminars and Palantir training sessions were also organized, providing a platform to share knowledge and experience in data management and usage. The Agency participated in the conference “New Generation Lithuania: A Plan for Success”, where the use of data in the public sector was discussed.
A special event for municipalities attracted around 300 participants and focused on the data inventory process and its achievements. In addition, the annual data event—the Annual Data Conference: “The Dialectics of State Data: The Struggle of Opposites and the Search for Unity”—was held to explore the complex interplay of perspectives in public data governance.
An event specifically designed for researchers was also organized. This event targeted physicians, scientists, researchers, students, data analysts, biostatisticians, bioinformaticians, and anyone interested in the practical use of health data. The State Data Agency hosted an information day at the Lithuanian University of Health Sciences titled “Health Data and Their Practical Use.”
Additionally, the seminar “Data for Science: Presenting Data Analytics Opportunities at the State Data Agency” was held for the academic community. During this event, opportunities for analyzing state data were presented, and participants were informed about current topics in state data inventory, mature national data sets, health data access, and potential areas of cooperation between the Agency and academia.

The National Audit Office carries out studies and assesses whether the efficient and secure opening and re-use of data is ensured, e.g.  https://www.valstybeskontrole.lt/EN/Post/17855/quality-and-easy-access-to-data-is-essential-to-strengthen-public-data-governance?utm_source=chatgpt.com
2024:
Existing legislation and processes are reviewed and updated as needed. 
On May 2024 the Parliament of Lithuanian Republic has confirmed the amendments of law on the right to receive information and data reuse (https://e-seimas.lrs.lt/portal/legalAct/lt/TAD/9203a7a2017111ef8e4be9fad87afa59?jfwid=-7i0sbj2e9). The first main amendment is to expand the scope of the law, i.e. to apply the law to all state and municipally managed enterprises and companies that provide public services (currenlty till 01.11.2024 the law is only applied to state and municipally managed enterprises and companies operating in the areas covered by the directive (EU) 2019/1024. The second amendment is to define high-value datasets and their publication and reuse procedure, i.e. provide a link to regulation (EU) 2023/138 (currently till 09.06.2024 it is regulated that the list of thematic categories of high-value data and the list of high-value data sets are approved by the Government).

Are there any processes in place to assess if public sector bodies are charging for data above marginal cost? (please see directive (EU) 2019/1024 on open data and the reuse of public sector information).

For Explanation:
* If yes, please specify the process(es).
column13:
According to Article 10 of the Law on the Right to Receive Information and Reuse of Data, data for re-use shall be provided to applicants free of charge, unless otherwise provided by the laws of the Republic of Lithuania or the legal acts of the European Union.
 Where a charge is made for the re-use of data, it shall not exceed the marginal cost of reproducing, providing and publishing the data, as well as depersonalising and taking measures to protect confidential business information.
The Communications Regulatory Authority of the Republic of Lithuania (https://www.rrt.lt/en/ ) is responsible authority in assesing if public sector bodies are charging for data above marginal cost.

What are the top 3 challenges that your country is facing in the implementation of the mentioned open data policies/strategy?

For Explanation:
* Please briefly describe.
column13:
1. Our main challenge and goal is to increase use of open data. The process of opening up data is significantly intensified (more than 1500 data sets are opened and published on data.gov.lt + other data sets that are opned on other national portals), therefore we encourage our data users to use open data or request new data for opening so that data could be basis for their new products and technologies. The estimate shows that the efficient use of data can generate an additional 2% of national GDP.
2. Ensuring data confidentiality is also a challenge. Lithuania is a small country with a low population density, so the more detailed the data, the higher the risk of disclosure. For example, opening Covid-19 data on deaths, especially young people, by gender, age and age dimensions in practice ment identifying the relatives of such a person and escalating the relevant history in public, in violation of the privacy of the relatives.  On the other hand, the ongoing debate on data has led to a better understanding of it.
3. Ensuring national security by opening up public sector data. It is being discussed more and more often that open national data can be used by Lithuania's unfriendly neighbors-states to carry out various provocations or military actions in our country. Therefore, Lithuania and other EU members must assess which data is not safe to open

column13:
2025:
Most public sector data providers contribute data to the portal, either directly or indirectly through centralized publication by national authorities.
The agreed approach is based on a centralized coordination model, where certain datasets (especially from municipalities and smaller institutions) are published by a central government entity on their behalf. This ensures that relevant data is still made accessible through the portal, even if the originating institution does not upload it directly.
In cases where data providers are not contributing directly, the primary reasons include:
Lack of technical capacity or readiness, particularly in smaller municipalities.
Limited awareness of open data obligations or the benefits of data sharing.
Some entities do not hold relevant datasets or are not required by national law to publish specific types of data.
Ongoing efforts are being made to improve awareness and build technical support, particularly for smaller or less-resourced institutions, to increase participation in the future.

2025:
1.As mentioned in Question I3 (Answer 2), the National Open Data Portal includes a feature that allows civil society to request new open datasets. This functionality is actively promoted during conferences, workshops, and presentations in which the State Data Agency participates.
2.The State Data Agency regularly engages with higher education institutions—including both students and faculty—to discuss available open datasets and explore opportunities for research based on public sector data.
 - https://vda.lrv.lt/lt/naujienos/valstybes-duomenu-agentura-ir-vilniaus-universitetas-stiprina-bendradarbiavima/
 - https://vda.lrv.lt/lt/naujienos/pasirasyta-bendradarbiavimo-su-vilnius-tech-sutartis/
 - https://vda.lrv.lt/lt/naujienos/valstybes-duomenu-konferencija-priesybiu-kovoje-vienybes-paieskos/

3.The State Data Agency offers secure virtual environments that allow safe analysis of sensitive anonymized data. In some cases, requests for access to sensitive data are redirected into the creation of publicly accessible, demand-driven open datasets rather than being granted as private access.
4.As the national statistics bureau, the State Data Agency frequently receives public inquiries about statistical indicators. It has established a practice of converting these one-off requests into reusable, demand-driven datasets. These datasets offer more detailed insights than simple statistical indicators and are designed for broader reuse.
5.In the context of an RRF-funded project to centralize national data into a single Data Lake, the State Data Agency systematically interviews each potential data provider. One goal is to encourage data providers to make datasets open by demonstrating how this can reduce the volume of individual public inquiries. Institutions are asked about the types of data most frequently requested by the public, which serves as an indirect public survey. The insights gained inform the publication of datasets that are most useful to society.
6.Transparency International Lithuania, in collaboration with the Lithuanian Parliament, developed the political integrity monitoring tool Manoseimas.lt. This platform features MPs’ agendas, meetings with interest groups, and registered lobbyists, allowing for comparisons between MPs and political groups. 2024:
1. As mentioned in question I3, answer 2, the National Open Data Portal includes a feature for the civil society to request new open data. This functionality is promoted at every conference, workshop, and presentation in which the State Data Agency participates.
2. The State Data Agency frequently meets with higher education institutions (both students and teachers) to discuss available open datasets and explore potential research topics. We are aware of at least three master's level students using our open data in their theses.
3. The State Data Agency offers virtual environments with sensitive anonymized data for safe analysis. Some requests for sensitive data access are redirected to a different track, resulting in the creation of demand-driven open data collections accessible to everyone instead of private access.
4. The State Data Agency, as the national statistics bureau, frequently receives inquiries about statistical indicators. Recently, the agency has developed a practice of converting individual single-indicator requests into universal demand-driven open datasets, allowing for wider reuse and more nuanced analysis, as this data is more detailed than simple statistical indicators.
5. As the State Data Agency leads an RRF-funded project aimed at centralizing national data into a single Data Lake, one of its tasks is to systematically interview every potential data provider. So far, approximately 300 in-depth interviews have been conducted. Data providers are incentivized to share their data with the promise that making some data open will significantly reduce the burden of individual requests from the public, such as custom statistical indicators. Institutions are asked about the most frequent public requests, and these responses are treated as an indirect public survey ("what do people want to know"), leading to the publication of more useful datasets.
6. "Transparency International Lithuania," in collaboration with the Parliament, created an online political integrity monitoring tool called Manoseimas.lt. This tool includes the agendas of Members of Parliament, their meetings with interest groups, and registered lobbyists, allowing for comparisons between individual MPs and different political groups. Permit data was also matched with parliamentary committee meetings to track permit usage for committee discussions.

The LT72 platform is a government initiative that uses open data to inform citizens about emergency shelters, evacuation points, and safety protocols in the case of extreme events, such as natural disasters or military threats. This reuse of open data has significantly enhanced public preparedness and response to emergencies. By making this critical information easily accessible to the public, the government has improved the effectiveness of its civil safety services, ensuring that citizens can quickly find shelter and respond appropriately in emergencies. This, in turn, strengthens overall public safety and helps to reduce the damage caused by unforeseen crises.

The Vaccination Dashboard, created by the State Data Agency, is based on open data regarding seasonal flu and COVID-19 vaccinations. The dashboard provides updated data on vaccination coverage by institutions, showing statistics on vaccine types, age groups, and gender of vaccinated individuals.
Impact:
This tool allows public health authorities to monitor vaccination efforts in real time and make evidence-based decisions regarding vaccination campaigns, resource allocation, and public outreach. By making the data accessible to the public, the dashboard helps enhance transparency and provides crucial insights to ensure informed public health interventions.
2024:
Road traffic information system of state importance, called EIS. The purpose of creating this system is to enable road users and road maintenance companies to use traffic data collected automatically and stored in one place. Data is collected into the EIS from several automatic weather stations, called KOS stations. These are roadside devices with sensors that measure parameters needed to determine road condition and traffic conditions (road surface temperature, air temperature and relative humidity, dew point, wind direction, speed and gusts, intensity and type of precipitation, visibility, road surface condition, frozen depth of road structures, etc.). The system also collects video data, which is collected from cameras installed and additionally installed at KOS stations. Another and no less important goal of EIS is to inform road users about traffic conditions, traffic disturbances, applied traffic management measures on roads and to provide users with the opportunity to perform automated traffic data analysis.

State agencies can monitor the potential for further use of high-value datasets primarily through the national public data portal, for which the 2023 CI Act makes it mandatory for all public bodies to make metadata available. The National Data Agency also provides a one-stop information point and contact service on the national public data portal where requests for the reuse of high-value datasets can be submitted. 2025:
As mentioned last year, there is a slight difference in approach here. In Hungarian law, open data refers to the "classic" transparency system, according to which the functioning of public institutions must be transparent and all related data must be freely accessible. Hungary has made great efforts in this area. We have one of the strictest freedom of information laws in the EU. The Infotv. obliges public institutions to publish certain information about themselves in a specific format on their websites. In this respect, yes, open data has had a huge impact on transparency, as a lot of information about the functioning of the public sector is freely available on the internet. However, the reuse of public data is a different issue, also from a legal point of view. Freedom of information does not extend to the accessibility of public databases or data sets. The reuse of PSI is governed by different laws and different systems. When we talk about data policy, we focus primarily and almost exclusively on issues related to reuse, and it has no direct impact on "classic" transparency or freedom of information. Therefore, although there may be an indirect link between freedom of information and reuse, freedom of information is constitutional, while reuse is socio-economic in nature, which means that one cannot directly influence the other.

A Norwegian Official Report (NOU 2024:14) proposes new legislation. The proposal will establish common rules for how public sector entities should make data available in ways that create value for others and contribute to an open and democratic society. The proposal will implement three EU legal acts aimed at facilitating the reuse of data from public entities: the Open Data Directive (EU) 2019/1024, the Implementing Regulation on High-Value Datasets (EU) 2023/138, and the Data Governance Act (EU) 2022/868.: https://www.regjeringen.no/no/dokumenter/nou-2024-14/id3046520/
2024:
Guidelines for making public data available - https://www.regjeringen.no/no/dokumenter/retningslinjer-ved-tilgjengeliggjoring-av-offentlige-data/id2536870/. Transposition of the Open Directive is still in progress: https://www.regjeringen.no/no/sub/eos-notatbasen/notatene/2018/juni/endring-viderebruksdirektivet/id2604081/

The Government has trough "Data as a resource" (https://www.regjeringen.no/en/dokumenter/meld.-st.-22-20202021/id2841118/?ch=2) set the following principles for its data policy:
1. Data must be as open as possible and as closed as necessary.
2. Data should be findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable (FAIR).
3. Data must be shared and used in ways that create value for the private sector, the public sector and society.
4. Data must be shared and used in ways that respect fundamental rights and freedoms and preserve Norwegian social values.

The Norwegian government has established a public committee to assess the appropriate implementation of the directive (https://www.regjeringen.no/no/dep/kdd/org/styrer-rad-og-utvalg/viderebruksutvalget/id2926740/). The committee's proposed regulation of the reuse of data will be based on the Public Access to Information Act with regulations and EU Directive (EU) 2019/1024 on open data and reuse of information from the public sector. The above-mentioned directive is a minimum directive, and therefore the committee is asked to consider whether Norway should go beyond the thematic categories that follow from the directive when it comes to datasets of high value, and also include other datasets than those covered by the EU's implementing act on datasets of high value.

column13:
2025:
"A study of the Norwegian data economy has been carried out over the past year. The purpose of the study has been to identify key challenges and opportunities related to the public sector's role and tasks that manage and provide public data for further use. The issue of charching for data above marignal cost are discussed, and some measures are proposed. https://www.regjeringen.no/contentassets/cb9240c57f8b4c5cb916e86ebee32ecb/rapport-utredning-av-dataokonomien-i-offentlig-sektor-ak-l80868.pdf 

A Norwegian Official Report (NOU 2024:14) proposes new legislation. The proposal will establish common rules for how public sector entities should make data available in ways that create value for others and contribute to an open and democratic society. The proposal will implement three EU legal acts aimed at facilitating the reuse of data from public entities: the Open Data Directive (EU) 2019/1024, the Implementing Regulation on High-Value Datasets (EU) 2023/138, and the Data Governance Act (EU) 2022/868.: https://www.regjeringen.no/no/dokumenter/nou-2024-14/id3046520/

column13:

column13:
Datasets: 
* The source must contain at least one resource of the type dcat:Catalog
* The source must contain at least one resource of type dcat:Dataset
* None of these may be blank nodes. 
* All datasets must be pointed to from a catalog using the predicate dcat:dataset. 

API/data service: 
* The source must contain minimum one resource of the type dcat:Catalog
* The source must contain minimum one resource of the type dcat:DataService. 
* None of these may be blank nodes. 
* All APIs/data services must be pointed to through the predicate dcat:service

column13:
2025:
In 2023, the Office of the Auditor General conducted an investigation into data exchange within the public administration. The report was addressed by the Norwegian Parliament (Storting) in February 2024. The investigation focused particularly on the exchange and use of data to enhance efficiency, improve services, and user experiences.
https://www.riksrevisjonen.no/rapporter-mappe/no-2023-2024/myndighetenes-tilrettelegging-for-deling-og-gjenbruk-av-data-i-forvaltningen/
2024:
Norway does not have a general report on the effects of open data on governmental challenges. Use of data and analyzes of effects are largely linked to use cases, and essentially the data used is a mixture of open data and data with restrictions. A recent report (2022) concludes that measuring effects and gains from a single data set, especially into services, is difficult and that there are few feasible methods.

We have several reports relating to the effect of various use cases. For the example used in the answer, the White Paper on Readily Available and Accessible (Open) Marine Geospatial Information can be referred to. 

In 2020, an assessment was made of the societal benefit of BarentsWatch. In the report presented, it is concluded that they fulfill an important societal need. Furthermore, the report points out that measuring the usefulness of information sharing is demanding as it is not the information itself, but the use of it that possibly creates value for society. Of benefit to society, the following are highlighted:
• Cost savings in the public sector
• Increased profit for business
• Reduced environmental costs
• Reduced accident costs
• Reduced crime (increased safety)
• Increased trust

Within different sectors there are several different reports and analyses. Examples:
• Faster response time with geographical analysis (planning of ambulance services): https://geodata.no/bransjer/raskere-responstid-med-geografisk-analyse
• The value of free map and property data: https://www.regjeringen.no/globalassets/upload/kmd/plan/verdien-av-gratis-kart-og-eiendomsdata.pdf
•The environmental sector is characterized by extensive data collection activities and monitoring of the environment and natural resources, as a basis for decisions and trade-offs between different considerations. The Norwegian Environment Agency, in its capacity as the national coordinator for environmental data, has conducted a systematic review of opportunities and challenges for increased use of environmental data. A key aspect is  environmental data as a basis for decision-making: https://www.menon.no/wp-content/uploads/2021-153-Hovedrapport-KVU-Fremtidens-miljodata.pdf
• Value and effect of data sharing: https://www.digdir.no/datadeling/verdi-og-effekt-av-datadeling-en-kartlegging-av-norske-virksomheters-praksis/3925

"The national statistics bank is used for various purposes. One example is The Technical Calculation Committee for Income Settlements."The Technical Calculation Committee for Income Settlements uses statistical data in several ways in its work:

Analysis of Economic Trends: They use statistical data to analyze economic trends, including inflation, wage development, employment, and other economic indicators. This provides them with a picture of the current economic situation.

Reference Data: Statistical data serve as reference data to compare current income levels and working conditions with previous years. This helps them assess changes over time.

Modeling and Forecasts: They can use statistical models to create forecasts for future economic conditions, including wage growth, price inflation, and other economic variables. This is important for planning income settlements.

Insight into Sectors: Statistical data provide insight into various sectors of the economy, such as industry, services, the public sector, etc. This allows them to assess how changes in income settlements will affect different parts of the economy.

Comparisons with Other Countries: They can also compare Norwegian data with statistics from other countries to assess how competitive wage and working conditions are compared to international standards.

Language use is increasingly dependent upon a wide range of digital applications, and (lack of) access to such applications will essentially govern the possibilities linguistic minorities have to use their languages. Dictionary resources are freely abailable for others to use, not only in open interfaces (https://sanit.oahpa.no/, etc.) but also the content. As a result, the dictionary has been reused both for machine translation, pedagogical applications, and other dictionary providers, such as dinordbok.no and others. The core data are structured, machine-readable grammatical models: https://giellalt.github.io/LanguageModels.html. The language models and documentation and source code are openly available. The key factor is to build, document and share language models that makes reuse possible. These resources have changed the prerequisites for use of minority languages. Earlier, North Saami newspapers were e.g. publised every second day, at most. With the spellchecker it was possible to publish the newspaper http://avvir.no daily. The availability of proofing tools in standard word processors, a functionality taken for granted by all majority language users, is now either in place or within reach for the Nordic national minority languages. The source code is available under an open license:
https://github.com/apertium/apertium-sme-nob

In some municipalities, air quality data is utilized to assess the level of air pollution, particularly in terms of particulate matter (PM) and pollutants such as nitrogen dioxide (NO2) and carbon monoxide (CO). When air quality deteriorates to a certain extent, these municipalities may implement restrictions on activities that contribute to air pollution, such as:

Driving Restrictions: They may impose temporary driving restrictions, particularly on vehicles with high emissions or during periods of high pollution, like smog or haze events. This can include measures like alternating license plate numbers allowed on the road on specific days.

Wood-Burning Bans: During periods of poor air quality or high pollution, some municipalities may ban or restrict the use of wood-burning stoves or fireplaces to reduce the emission of particulate matter and other pollutants from burning wood.

These measures aim to improve air quality and protect public health by reducing exposure to harmful pollutants. The specific restrictions and their enforcement can vary from one municipality to another, depending on local air quality conditions and regulations.

column13:
The Open Data Directive was transposed into Irish Law on July 22nd 2021 through Statutory Instrument 376/2021, the European Union (Open Data and Re-use of Public Sector Information) Regulations 2021.  These regulations fully transposed the Directive in to Irish law.  They also include the request regime for accessing open datasets and the appeals process a requester can utilise if they are not provided with the data requested. SI 376/2021 is the basis for Irish Government policy on open data.
The regulations may be accessed at https://www.irishstatutebook.ie/eli/2021/si/376/made/en/html

An official government Circular which provides instructions and guidance for all public service organisations on implementing the Open Data Directive was issued in December 2021.  This Circular sets out the actions public bodies and public utilities need to carry out to meet their obligations under the Directive.  Circular 20/2021 – Open Data Directive https://www.gov.ie/en/circular/523a7-circular-202021-open-data-directive/  

Our Open Data policy is to encourage and drive the publication, uptake and use of Open Data and in doing so add value to the economy by increasing transparency, stimulating new business applications, building trust in Government and improving the lives of citizens by delivering better services.
This is being achieved by:
• Encouraging the release of all appropriate high value government data as Open Data by default 
• Building a value driven economy by making it publicly available and freely reusable 
• Engaging with a broad community of stakeholders to promote and encourage the use of Open Data
