Are there any processes in place to assess if public sector bodies are charging for data above marginal cost? (please see directive (EU) 2019/1024 on open data and the reuse of public sector information).

For Explanation:
* If yes, please specify the process(es).
column13:
2025:
The difference between the 2024 and 2025 responses is due to a different interpretation of the question regarding the nature of the process.
The 2024 answer describes a legally established mechanism, which is triggered when specific circumstances arise — such as a request or notification from stakeholders. In these cases, an analysis is conducted, meetings are held with the parties involved, and the relevant legal framework, including tariffs and fees, is reviewed.
The 2025 response reflects a narrower interpretation of the question — assuming it refers to a centrally coordinated, regularly conducted, and proactively scheduled review process for all cases of potential overcharging above marginal cost.
We clarify that a legally grounded process exists and functions when triggered by specific input or events, and is fully aligned with the applicable national legislation. This provides the correct context for the 2024 response, which accurately reflects how such cases are handled in practice.


2024:
In accordance with the current legal framework in Bulgaria and through the Law on Access to Public Information, information from the public sector is provided for reuse free of charge or after payment of a fee, which cannot exceed the material costs of reproducing and providing the information. There are certain exceptions to this principle.
The processes used to identify Public Sector Organizations that charge data fees beyond marginal costs are a result of data requests received from interested parties.
The data department team analyzes the processes of pricing and payment of the data above the marginal costs, identifies the high value data according to the competence of the relevant administration, which should be published in an open machine-readable format on the Portal. A connection is established between the data holders, the interested parties requesting the data and the data department as a mediator, and meetings are organized to establish the details of the method of providing the data and the legal grounds for their provision at the present time.
Once meetings are organized between the relevant departments or working groups are formed, the purpose of which is to review the legal basis for the creation, maintenance and dissemination of the relevant data sets. The relevant regulations and documents defining the tariffs and fees are reviewed and, after assessing their importance and significance for users, a decision is made to provide the data with free access or up to marginal costs.
As a result, they are included in the annual list of data sets by priority areas, approved by a Ministerial Council Decision. The responsible administrations, for their part, should change their legal grounds for collecting fees for those included in the list of data approved by the decision of the Council of Ministers.

* What is the technology stack of your portal (e.g. based on uData, CKAN, etc.)
column13:
Technology Stack:
3.6.1. Fluentd
Fluentd is a service for collecting data from log files and forwarding them through a specialized protocol to a centralized repository.
License: Open source software, distributed under Apache License v2.0.
3.6.2. Firewall
Configuration via iptables and Linux kernel firewall. It serves to block Internet traffic and allow defining services, ports, protocols, and traffic sources. It is used to increase information security.
License: open source software, distributed under the GNU GPL.
3.6.3. Load balancer
Optional item, in case of installation on more than one server with application software. It serves to distribute the load between multiple servers with an identical configuration. If needed, implementation is provided via Apache 2 and mod_proxy_balancer.
License: Open source software, distributed under Apache License v2.0.
3.6.4. Database (Master / Slave)
A relational database management system. The project envisages the use of MariaDB to store user profiles and other specific data required for the implementation of the Open Data Portal. This DBMS will not be used to store datasets.
License: open source software, distributed under the GNU GPL.
3.6.5. ElasticSearch node
ElasticSearch is a full-text search and data analysis system. It offers possibilities for storing and processing large volumes of information. The system supports the construction of clusters of single installations, which increase productivity and guarantee the impossibility of work.
This component will be used to store, search, process and analyze datasets.
License: Open source software, distributed under Apache License v2.0.
3.6.7. Greylog
Centralized storage of data collected from log files. It allows automated processing of the collected data, as well as preparation of various statistical reports and visualizations. In addition, the system allows for automated output when events are initiated.
License: open source software, distributed under the GNU GPL.
3.6.8. Web application
It represents an application server on which an open data portal is installed.
3.6.9. Data migration tool
Represents an installation of the automated data entry tool.
3.6.10. Automated data entry tool
The automated data entry tool is designed as a set of components located in the so-called "container" which is a system running on different operating systems. The installation of the automated data entry tool requires the installation of a special pad that implements the support of this container. For the base of work, choose Docker Community Edition. The open data tool will run seamlessly on any hardware capable of running the pad.

column13:
Open data is the public information collected, created and maintained by public sector organizations and published in an open machine-readable format (CSV, RDF, XML, JSON, etc.), allowing re-use for commercial or non-commercial purposes.
Reuse of public sector information is the use also for commercial or non-commercial purposes other than the original purpose for which it was created within the powers or functions of a public sector organization. The provision of public sector information to a public sector organization in connection with the exercise of its powers or functions is not reuse within the meaning of Access to Public Information Act. (Article 2a, APIA).

The system for electronic budget payments (SEBRA) is a system for monitoring payments initiated by budget enterprises included in it and managing payments within pre-set limits. The implementation and improvement of SEBRA is a major component of the budget reform and, in particular, of the reform of the payment system for the budget sector, through which the following main goals are achieved:
- improvement of the budget payments and rationalization of the payment process by centralizing the monetary resource in BGN in the Bulgarian National Bank and decentralized management and control of the payments of the individual systems, through the relevant primary administrator;
- implementation of aggregated control and management of payments by setting a general limit for payments to the relevant budget appropriations, with a view to ensuring rhythmicity in the financing of state expenditures.
Achieved results:
- modernization, simplification and rationalization of cash management and budget execution;
- improving efficiency in the management of budgetary resources;
- limiting cash payments to the maximum extent;
- increasing fiscal transparency;
- improvement of fiscal discipline.

It represents a single, central, public web-based information system that provides electronically the entire process of submitting and considering an application for access to information, referral by competence if necessary, provision of a decision and publication of the relevant information by those obliged under the Law on Access to Public Information entities subject to the protection of the applicant's personal data according to the Personal Data Protection Act.

The Open Data team maintains an ongoing dialogue with multiple users and owners of open data to improve the access and impact of this data.
An internship program was announced at the beginning of the year, which supported an intern to work with the open data team.
 
The impact on government open data challenges can be seen in the way government policy has changed to take open data requirements into account.

Several entities foster these data ecosystems to provide services to the community and contribute to science. Examples of such projects are: IPMA (https://www.ipma.pt/) and CIIMAR (https://www.ciimar.up.pt/), which have a project for monitoring jellyfish on the Portuguese coast, GelAvista (https://www.cienciacidada.pt/project/15); and CCMAR (https://ccmar.ualg.pt/en/our-strategy), which has several projects for citizen data sharing related to the marine environment (https://ccmar.ualg.pt/en/citizen-science). column13:
2025:
The National Digital Strategy: The Key to Simplification (Action Plan 2025–2026), under Initiative #13 – “Data Available for Everyone”, emphasizes the development of a common data model for Public Administration. This model establishes clear standards for how data should be stored, managed, shared, and analyzed, ensuring its secure and responsible use. A structured framework is essential to unlock the full value of public sector data and should include practical examples to guide improvements in data quality and reuse.
As part of this initiative, Action 13.3 focuses on the creation of a National Data Catalogue, built upon the common data model. This catalogue will include both open and restricted (closed) datasets, enhancing transparency and discoverability while respecting legal and ethical constraints.

Furthermore:
Public sector entities are required to maintain inventories that clearly indicate which datasets cannot be made openly available, along with the justification for such restrictions. These datasets are typically labeled as “Com Restrições” (i.e., Not Open Data) in national catalogs—for example, in the https://snig.dgterritorio.gov.pt/rndg/srv/eng/catalog.search#/search?fast=index.

The site in dado.gov, https://dados.gov.pt/pt/pages/faqs/terms/ provides detailed guidance in its FAQs section, outlining the types of data that can or cannot be released, and the legal, ethical, and technical considerations involved.

Several legal instruments govern these practices:
Law No. 26/2016, of 22 August, as amended by Law No. 68/2021, defines the framework for access to administrative and environmental information and the reuse of public sector documents. It also provides indirect guidance on when data should not be released in open formats (https://www.pgdlisboa.pt/leis/lei_mostra_articulado.php?nid=2591&tabela=leis&ficha=1&pagina=1).
Article 27 of Law No. 58/2019, of 8 August, which ensures the application of the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), requires entities to support the National Data Protection Commission in preparing and regularly updating a general inventory of data processing activities (https://diariodarepublica.pt/dr/detalhe/lei/58-2019-123815982).

Also, The Council for Digital in Public Administration, abbreviated as CDAP, created by Council of Ministers Resolution no. 94/2024, of July 25, is the project group that aims to promote coordination and decision-making between all government areas, in order to ensure that there is a single vision regarding technological development and administrative simplification of public services in Portugal, allowing the coordinated implementation of the National Digital Strategy. 
The CDAP has an Operational Committee with different Working Groups responsible for different areas and one being precisely Data. The group is made up of members of Public Administration bodies who have extensive knowledge of the indicated topic with the aim of ensuring alignment with other working groups and the Operational Committee. The Data Governance Technical Working Group of the Council for Digital in Public Administration (CDAP) has been developing activities in three distinct subgroups:
• The first subgroup is focused on updating the National Digital Interoperability Regulation (RNID)
• The second subgroup seeks to create a common basis that facilitates the sharing and reuse of data between sectors, promoting a collaborative approach supported by instruments such as Mosaic and national data and services catalogues. This group has been consolidating proposals for methodologies and governance practices for the creation of common spaces for sectoral data, including the use of tools such as controlled vocabularies and data and service catalogs.
• The third subgroup aims to support public entities in the secure sharing of data, promoting a structured approach that allows mitigating risks and strengthening trust in the interoperability ecosystem. The activities of this group, among others, include the preparation of a roadmap of good practices focused on data security and privacy, based on four dimensions: data purpose, data knowledge, anonymization methods and relevance of interoperability between entities.

Under Initiative #13 – “Data available for everyone”, the strategy defines four concrete actions:
13.1. Definition of a Public Administration Data Model: Establishes a unified framework for structuring and managing data across entities.
13.2. Update of the National Digital Interoperability Regulation: Ensures consistent data exchange standards.
13.3. Creation of a National Data Catalogue: Centralizes metadata and improves discoverability and reuse.
13.4. Development of a plan to create common sectoral data spaces: Promotes harmonization across domains 

2. Data Literacy
The strategy’s “People” dimension aims to enhance digital skills across the population and public sector:
Targets include increasing the share of the population with basic digital skills to 80% and ensuring that 7% of the employed population are ICT specialists, with at least 30% being women 3.
Awareness campaigns, training programs, and guidelines are also being deployed to support open data understanding and use.

3. Qualified Human Resources
The strategy acknowledges the shortage of skilled professionals and addresses it through:
Capacity-building initiatives embedded in the action plan.
Collaboration with academia and training institutions to develop tailored programs.
Public consultation and stakeholder engagement to align workforce development with real needs
2024:
There are two major pillars on which we are working to respond to these three major challenges: a) Law No. 68/2019, b) Recovery and Resilience Plan/Digital Transition (Specific projects aimed at open data).
Several projects are being developed to address some of the challenges, this process has enforced the Political and institutional support/adherence, and more HR were outsourced to execute the palnned tasks. 2024:
We collect several insights from the portal usage and needs that we strive to address. Typically, we include these improvements in our backlog after a thorough analysis of the effort and impact. These improvements must wait for their inclusion in the next project, or in urgent cases, the current project. An important step in this process is interacting with the uData framework development team to determine if some of these improvements are also in their roadmap.

From these insights, we can provide three concrete examples that were included in the previously mentioned backlog. The first was the need expressed by users to have a preview tool for structured data. This feature, developed by us, is already operational on dados.gov. The second was the need for a simple way for providers to check compliance with quality standards. This was implemented in due time by the uData team and is already functional on dados.gov. The last one addresses numerous complaints about the loss of thematic organization of the datasets in the new version of uData. To mitigate this problem, we are in discussions with the uData team to understand how we can provide users with a thematic approach to finding datasets. In summary, we collect feedback and take action to improve.

2024:
As explained in question P2, the National Data Strategy has been finalized and is awaiting publication in the coming months. The effort to create data inventories/catalogues is progressing for most of the important entities that also represent many other entities. Both of these aspects will serve as leverage for the implementation of data governance in the Public Administration.
2023:
Develop a governance structure, implement an Open data National Strategy, make data inventories/catalogs (that include information about data, data that cannot be opened, and data that can be opened and is not yet published), send a survey to the entities on data maturity (to each of the government agencies and the departments within), create awareness initiatives (webinar on open data concept and benefits, and the open data directive), and make a portal improvement. Also define methodologies to monitor/evaluate the impact of open data in areas such as government efficiency / public policies; reduction of operating costs; quality of public service provided; environmental impact; social impact; macroeconomic and microeconomic impact, etc. Design a user satisfaction survey.
Public sector data providers still demonstrate some reluctance, there is some cultural tightness, low awareness and data literacy, some departments have limited technological and human resources, and, most basilary, the lack of a general governance structure, in Portugal.

2024:
In addition to all the initiatives implemented by the Portuguese Public Administration (PA) to maintain and evolve the portal, and with the intention of securing the portal’s relevance and importance, AMA has decided to assign a critical role to the portal. Leveraging the importance and impact that the “Portal Mais Transparência” (https://transparencia.gov.pt/pt/), a reuse of open data, has on transparency, citizen awareness, and participation, AMA decided that dados.gov will be the single point of access and aggregator for the high-quality data needed to update the “Portal Mais Transparência” in near real-time. This strategy, agreed upon by 9 entities (2 more to come), makes dados.gov a critical part of this reuse, which is internationally recognized and has a significant impact on the media and society (see attached document “Reuse_portal mais transparencia.pdf”). Without the option to participate in a marketplace where data monetization is a reality, we have concluded that the only strategy is to increase the positive impact and relevance of the portal to ensure its future financial sustainability.
Another contribution to the sustainability of the portal is the publication of open data from public service and feedback from citizens, which are the basis of an internal service of AMA, GIAP (see attach document "TICAPP202203_Guia de Utilização do Portal do gIAp_V2.0.pdf"), which contributes to the following objectives: Improve citizen satisfaction; Contribute to the continuous improvement of the quality of public service delivery, combining different channels: in person; voice and digital; Simplify administrative processes; and Evaluate the quality of services, taking into account the expectations of citizens.
Another relevant strategic decision is that it was decided to use an open source framework, uData, to improve sustainability.

2024:
The ongoing project entitled "Open Data - Impact Assessment Model Definition" (URL: https://www.base.gov.pt/Base4/pt/detalhe/?type=contratos&id=9601046) has implemented systematic methods for collecting (re)use cases, incorporating best practices (while also accounting for the cautionary lessons) from reports such as "Rethinking the Impact of Open Data," "The Economic Impact of Open Data," and "The Use Case Observatory Volume I" available on data.europa.eu. The first reports of the project can be consulted here for more information [Please check the file attached to this survey_Relatório Casos de Estudo.pdf]
The systematic methods for gathering eligible entities for building use cases about the impact they create when (re)using open data are the following prioritization rules:
a) having ongoing or scheduled data platforms, explicit data policies, data quality control procedures, and/or general knowledge of its platform users
b) the data platform is in the form of a website, data portal, or web application
c) entities can be classified as private, public (government) or academic institutions
d) entities can maintain regular and effective communication with the Administrative Modernization Agency, I.P. (AMA)
e) entities can underpin if their operational influence is in at least one of the following sectors: social, governmental, environmental or economic
f) entities can be classified into at least one of the following positions of the open data value chain: data reuser, data portal, data intermediary
Upon their acceptance of the collaboration, they were provided with an impact assessment questionnaire.

The study from AMA, "Projeto Impacto dos Dados Abertos. Casos de Estudo", categorizes the information of the use cases in different topic areas. 
The reuse cases and their impacts are assessed and classified by data providers and reusers under four possible areas or dimensions: governmental, economic, social, and environmental. The project is implementing surveys to the entities to assess different metrics related to the knowledge and evidence of the impacts of the reuse cases in each of the four dimensions. This allows the measure of the impact of the open data in each dimension and to perform a global analysis, from which the cases can be classified considering their impacts. This was already applied in a set of reuse cases, and future plans include applying it to a larger set. [Please check the file attached to this survey Relatório Casos de Estudo.pdf]
The metrics that are being produced in the context of this project were inspired on “Rethinking the impact of open data” (Ooijen et al., 2023), “The Use Case Observatory” (Carsaniga, Dogger e Regeczi, 2022), “European DATA Market Study 2021–2023” (European Commission, 2023a), “Creating Value through Open Data” (Capgemini Consulting et al., 2015) e “The economic impact of open data” (Huyer e Knippenberg, 2020).

column13:
2025:
The Ministry of Health in Portugal is responsible for the open data initiative known as the "Transparency Portal". The primary objective of this initiative is to ensure full access and transparency to a wide range of data concerning the operations and transactions of the National Health System (SNS). This involves information from different organizations involved in providing healthcare nationwide. This portal has a significant impact on health:Access to detailed health data allows for better monitoring of health outcomes, identification of trends, and early detection of issues, enabling timely interventions and also, Policymakers and health administrators can use this data to make informed decisions regarding healthcare policies, resource allocation, and management of healthcare services.
Other examples:
1- The "Resposta Sazonal em Saúde" (Seasonal Health Response) is a platform with interactive dashboards of the daily updates on the progression, accessibility, and use of healthcare services by citizens, namely primary Healthcare, hospital healthcare, and emergency healthcare. It provides timely information to the populace and healthcare sector stakeholders, facilitating their effective preparedness for response https://www.sns.gov.pt/plano-de-contingencia-sazonal/
2- The Daily Evolution of Emergency Calls seeks to inform the public on health initiatives, resource allocation, and the development of preventive measures.URL: https://transparencia.sns.gov.pt/explore/dataset/acionamentos-de-meios-de-emergencia-medica/table/?sort=periodo
In particular, it allows to monitor the response times relative to the number of daily emergency events and determine the nation-wide average response time as well as allow nation-wide media outlets to create awareness on the public to sub-optimal response times https://expresso.pt/sociedade/2022-10-23-INEM-demorou-uma-hora-ou-mais-a-acionar-meios-em-mais-de-mil-chamadas-d36ee608 
3 - The "Centro de Saúde Fora de Horas" (After-hours Healthcare Centers, URL: https://www.arslvt.min-saude.pt/centros-de-saude-fora-de-horas/#14) is a data visualization map of healthcare centers with extended working hours. Its primary goal is to reduce the demand for hospital emergency services among patients who, while experiencing an acute illness, do not require such specialized care. This tool has been featured in national-level media outlets, e.g., https://www.publico.pt/2022/11/23/sociedade/noticia/portal-sns-passa-informacao-centros-saude-abertos-ate-tarde-2028846

There exist several particular data publication plans and corresponding workflows :
- all of Luxembourg's INSPIRE datasets are made available via a central INSPIRE platform with a well defined workflow starting with the obligation for the data owner to first publish the data in its "AS-IS" state on the open data portal, where it is retrieved by the ETL backoffice and integrated into the INSPIRE data warehouse. From here it is made available through the legally mandatory services and it is then described in the central catalog https://catalog.inspire.geoportail.lu/geonetwork/srv/eng/catalog.search#/home. Here the datasets as they are displayed on the open data portal following the automatic publication workflow https://data.public.lu/fr/datasets/?q=INSPIRE
- the national geoportal map viewer https://maps.geoportail.lu contains a large amount of map layers (around 1500, a great part of which are open to the public) and an ongoing project aims at implementing a workflow to automatically publish any geoportal layer with the correct metadata and via bulk download opportunities as well as webservice / API access as open data on the national open data portal

column13:
2024:
The responsible team at SIP / division open data and access to information constantly monitors the national open data portal in terms of its contents, the announced data and documents, the metadata quality, the licenses as well as re-uses that document potential public interest in some of the data.
The roadmap document https://data.public.lu/en/pages/5yearplan/ specifies more concrete measures that allow to meet the strategic objectives. With regard to the Open data law https://legilux.public.lu/eli/etat/leg/loi/2021/11/29/a836/jo and the Freedom of Information law https://legilux.public.lu/eli/etat/leg/loi/2018/09/14/a883/jo, the national open data team assists data owners in publishing (more) data by providing technical and legal assistance, while focusing on data quality considerations, interoperability issues, legal constraints and licensing as well as possible automation of data publication.
Like the European Interoperability Framework, the National Interoperability Framework https://mindigital.gouvernement.lu/fr/dossiers/2019/NIF-2019.html  adopted in 2019 by the Luxembourg government covers open data by its very first principle “openness”. Under the principle of openness, this strategic document recommends to “Publish own data as open data by default, unless restrictions (security, data protection, etc.) apply”.
The open data team also contributes to the Ministry for Digitalisation’s three call for projects aimed at government administrations and services: NIF4Gov to further develop interoperability in the public sector domain; DATA4Gov to promote the use of data within the public sector; as well as,  AI4Gov to foster the use of artificial intelligence within the public sector. All three subject matters benefit greatly from an open data approach.
An important aspect is the consistent professional training for public sector employees, to help them be more aware of open data topics and become an active part in the open data ecosystem.
It should also be mentioned that the Ministry for Digitalisation works on several national projects - in collaboration with the open data team as well as the Luxembourg National Data Service (LNDS) - that are important contributions to the open data strategy:
- a national general data strategy is being finalised and due for publication soon. The data strategy reiterates the National Interoperability Framework’s approach of openness by default.
- a common and generalised data inventory effort is ongoing, together with the open data team at SIP, the above mentioned LNDS and all the other public sector organisations that work on cataloguing data: national library BNL, university and national archive etc
2023:
The responsible team at SIP / division open data and access to information constantly monitors the national open data portal in terms of its contents, the announced data and documents, the metadata quality, the licences as well as  re-uses that document potential public interest in some of the data.

With regard to the Open data law https://legilux.public.lu/eli/etat/leg/loi/2021/11/29/a836/jo  and the Freedom of Information law https://legilux.public.lu/eli/etat/leg/loi/2018/09/14/a883/jo, the national open data team assists data owners to publish (more) data by providing technical and legal assistance, while focussing on data quality considerations, interoperability issues, legal constraints and licensing as well as possible automation of data publication.
In this context the open data team closely collaborates with the Luxembourg government's interoperability programme and the governmental AI4Gov programme to foster the availability of open datasets that can be used for AI. Both programmes consist of yearly call for projects at the level of government administration and services, where data and opendata should be an important aspect.
An important aspect is the consistent professional training for public sector employees, to help the be more aware of the opendata topics and become an active part in the open data ecosystem.

- we regularly write own harvester scripts, after discussing with the data owners and obtaining their feedbacks and consent about licence, description, validity etc

column13:
The portal is acknowledged as the central national platform for open data, which is manifested by its increasing notoriety in projects and strategic texts. To continue fostering it, the open data team regularly undertakes promotion and sensibilisation activities.
On the public sector side, we have built a group of open data representatives of all ministries, administrations and other public sector organisations, with the intention to enhance their knowledge about the importance of their data being available as opendata and the opportunities provided by the portal in this context. We have started a series of dedicated open data meetups, where they can better understand how to use the portal and how to represent their organisation on the portal. The agenda of the first event of this series contained presentations about the basics of the open data portal https://data.public.lu/en/posts/le-premier-open-data-meetup-du-gouvernement/ as well as  insights aboiut ongoing inventory and High Value Data projects.
On the general public side, we traditionally organisie hackathon events, at least once per year, about topics focussing on opendata that already exists on the portal and where we encourage the participants to create user accounts and to publish their reuses. When we discover in the media eventual re-uses of open data, we generally get in touch with the reusers to invite the to also use the portal functions to publicly announce their reuse case.
These activities contribute to the constantly rising number of portal users.

column13: The datasets that are created and updated automatically basically concern the following categories : geodata from the geoportal and/or the INSPIRE portal, geodata from the Greater-Region-Atlas project, national statistics and  statistical data from the national social security system. The geodata are all integrated via scripts on the producer (data owner) side, invoking the API of data.public.lu to create the datasets, create and update the metadata and the corresponding resource. For the statistical data the open data team has written dedicated harvesting scripts that scan the data owners' sites to retrieve the data and the descriptions. For the data from the national statistics office, this data harvesting happens with active mutual collaboration.

Do you undertake efforts to ensure that published data covers the full period from when it was first published until today, for example, the complete time series?

For Explanation:

column13:
The open data team checks the whereabouts of new datasets and  gets in touch with the data producers to see whether former time series can be added. Sensibilisation for the importance of long time data series is often necessary as most data producers tend to focus on the actual figures / data. In some cases the actual data can be delivered automatically whereas the retrieval of former series may need manual actions. Generally we sensibilise the data owner to implement an update procedure that keeps older data intact and available. We also advise them to consider a posteriori packaging of yearly data into one-year-archive files to prevent an excessive amount of resources in the datasets and allow an easier bulk download, or depending on the technical resources, to consider implementing an API.
Here an example : from the very beginning of Luxembourg's open data project, the quarterly anonymised extractions of statistics from the national person register RNPP are important datasets https://data.public.lu/fr/datasets/?q=rnpp .

column13:
On the portal a dataset can only be published if certain key metadata fields have been filled (or options been selected). This accounts for a certain minimum metadata quality. Among the mandatory fields on a datasets are the title, a description, an update frequency, a creation date and an author. Here we are stricter than DCAT-AP on the frequency and author fields. For a distribution, the mandatory fields are the title, the URL and the format. Here we are stricter than DCAT-AP for the format.
In our opendata strategy we insist on the importance of choosing an open licence and strongly advocate the use of CC0. At the opendata team we regularly manually check the datasets to add tags. There are also written guideline-documents like https://data.public.lu/fr/pages/fact-sheets/data-quality/ and https://data.public.lu/fr/pages/fact-sheets/licenses/

* If yes, please explain the support you provide?
column13:
There is a 3 tier approach to achieve good or at least continuously better public sector open data quality in Luxembourg : 
- the first concerns chapters dedicated to public sector open data, the national portal, and related topics in the regular trainings proposed to any public sector agent at the training institute INAP
- the second is the (recently built) group of open data representatives at the public sector organisations. This group has been mentioned in other questions above, and has been created following the Prime Minister's order to officially name such representatives, in his letter https://data.public.lu/fr/datasets/lettre-circulaire-aux-departements-ministeriels-administrations-et-services-de-letat-donnees-ouvertes/ , where several practical measures have been outlined to fulfill the obligations of the open data directive and corresponding national laws. The idea behind this permanent group is to intensify exchanges, best practices, technical help and general open data related information between the responsible persons via regular meetings. The first meeting of this series has taken place in April 2024 https://data.public.lu/fr/posts/le-premier-open-data-meetup-du-gouvernement/
- the third is the 1-to-1 approach we already mentioned before : the open data team usually is in touch with each individual data owner and helps with advice or technical assistance when data is published. Due to this good connection to the data owners, we are able to help focussing on quality aspects like updates, resource formats, problems in the data itself, metadata etc. This has proven to be of great value for the general data quality on the portal. In this context we should name our link checking programme : To avoid presenting data which is not available anymore, we have automated tests in place to check the availability of data, for all the data which is not hosted directly on the portal. Every month, an automatic check is conveyed, which is filtered manually to avoid false positives, then the team of the open data portal contacts all the organisations which have an availability issue (dead links), and try to find a solution with them to have the data back online as soon as possible. It can range from simple url fixes to more complex operations such ass setting up an automated synchronisation with the open data portal. This has been the case for example with our national weather data provider, Meteolux: 
https://data.public.lu/fr/datasets/present-weather-condition-at-luxembourg-airport-ellx-decoded-from-metar-message/

Do you investigate the most common causes for the lack of DCAT-AP compliance?

For Explanation:
* If yes, what are the main causes for the lack of DCAT-AP compliance?
column13:
The main causes of DCAT-AP non-compliance:
-	The DCAT-AP endpoint is part of the core platform we use for our portal, which we have to update regularly. This can be a costly update, because we have to keep some customisations and settings, so we are not doing it every year. In the meantime, the DCAT-AP standard is constantly updated. It could be interesting to have a more stable standard, which would be less frequently updated, giving us the time to catch up. On our side, we analyse regularly our compatibility with the DCAT-AP standard (see the gap analysis here https://data.public.lu/fr/datasets/r/f6097aa5-fbfd-4aa3-94a2-d6fd8d5a8882 and we discuss possible improvements of its implementation with the upstream (udata) project https://github.com/opendatateam/udata/issues/2854 )
-	Moreover, we don’t have any known user of our DCAT-AP endpoint except the european data portal.  We have not received any feedback about our DCAT-API endpoint implementation so far. This lack of feedback does not help us to prioritise fixes on the DCAT-AP endpoint.

« réutilisation » : l’utilisation par des personnes physiques ou morales de documents détenus par :

column13:
The use of the open data portal and of its data sets is monitored in detail, which allows to gain insights about re-use cases and their impact. In the portal, the internal statistic dashboard which renders key information about every dataset, is a good way to track the popularity of datasets, from the perspective of the data producers.
We keep an eye on the exchanges between data users and providers in the corresponding portal sections, to deduce possibly interesting re-use cases, and - as far as possible with the available means - we try to know more in order  to properly document the re-use to evaluate it's impact as well as to use it as an example to trigger further visibility for open data.
A particular case are API's where it is possible to require the use of a personal key, which obliges re-users to  be identified and the data providers to get detailed information about the uses. This is also the case of the geoportal API, which is used a lot at the national level, or the  public transport API for example.
Currently however these insights are not yet handled in a coordinated way.

The OGD master plan sets out the principles, goals and measures for open government data and defines implementation priorities for the federal administration. The publication and use of OGD give rise to new questions relating to law, ethics, governance and others, as well as new responsibilities. It is not an incentive, but the EMBAG regulation states that OGD data must be published in accordance with the OGD principles, one of which is to publish as soon as possible, if possible even in real-time (see p. 8).
This is particularly important for dynamic data (including environmental data, traffic data, satellite data, meteorological data and data generated by sensors), which are constantly changing and whose economic value depends on their availability without delay and with regular updates. Dynamic data should be made available through an application programming interface ("API") immediately after acquisition or creation or, in the case of a manual update, immediately after the dataset has been modified, in order to facilitate the development of Internet, mobile and cloud applications based on such data.

column13:
2025:
The activities to support open government data (OGD) in Switzerland are organised by various bodies, including the specialist body for data management and interoperability, the OGD forum and two operational working groups (legal and portal).

The specialist body for "data board confederation"  is responsible for coordinating data management and interoperability throughout the Federal Administration. It also coordinates open government data and OGD activities.

The main function of the OGD forum is to facilitate the sharing of expertise on open data and support stakeholder debate on this topic in Switzerland. It also provides support for the implementation of the OGD activities set out in the 2024‒2027 OGD master plan. To this end, it sets out recommendations for the development of OGD in Switzerland, supports the coordinated implementation of OGD throughout Switzerland and raises awareness throughout the Federal Administration of the OGD principles in accordance with the federal act (EMOTA). Additionally, it encourages multistakeholder participation and debate on OGD matters at every level of the Swiss federal system. The members of the OGD forum have the power to set up independent working groups.

Two working groups have been set up to support delivery of the OGD master plan. The portal working group oversees the operation and development of the opendata.swiss portal. This group is open to all opendata.swiss contributors. The legal working group ensures that OGD activities have a solid legal basis and that conditions for the use of OGD keep pace with new developments.

2025:
We are currently working on DCAT-AP CH 3.0.0. It will come into force by the end of the year and will be fully compatible with DCAT AP 3.0.0
2024:
2024:
We have DCAT-AP CH in version 1, which was created in 2018 and builds on DCAT-AP version 1. Version 2.0.0 has recently been approved by eCH. The definition area is https://dcat-ap.ch/. There you will find both versions of the DCAT-AP CH. The portal is mainly based on the DCAT-AP conformance, but also on the version 1 of the DCAT-AP CH, as it contains some Swiss fields used by the community. The decision to create a version 2 of DCAT-AP CH and to keep a national application profile was a difficult one. We decided to keep it because there are particularities in the use of the standard, there are properties such as distribution coverage that the Swiss community relies on and that can't be found in DCAT-AP. The vocabulary also needs Swiss adaptations. Licences are used in a different way than in DCAT-AP. We felt that it would better support the Swiss community if Switzerland maintained its own profile and explained how classes and properties are adapted to the Swiss context. While version 1 of DCAT-AP CH was not DCAT-AP compatible with version 2.0.1 of DCAT-AP. DCAT-AP CH V2 is now compatible with DCAT-AP v2.0.1. The process of collecting and reviewing showcases is now much easier. The OGD Office encourages at every opportunity (e.g. events, Twitter, LinkedIn) to upload showcases. It encourages the collaboration between public bodies and students. They are looking for data coaches every year. The students reuse open data from different public bodies, one example is from the canton of Thurgau: https://ogd.tg.ch/anwendungen/open-data-vorlesung-2022.html/14316. The research institute Sotomo analysed the ideological orientation of members of the Grand Council in canton Basel-city, based on their votes, which were recorded and published in machine-readable form at opendata.bs.ch. This study revealed that there was sometimes discrepancies between ideologies and voting behavior. - In the example of the Sotomo study, the impact of open data is qualitative rather than quantitative. The study uses publicly available voting records (published on opendata.bs.ch) to analyze discrepancies between the ideological positions of elected officials and their actual voting behavior. While this enhances transparency and informs public discourse, the project does not include a formal quantification of open data's effect on governmental efficiency, effectiveness, or decision-making capacity.

- In addition to the previously mentioned case, the DigiPartIndex (DPI) offers a concrete, quantified example of how open data contributes to addressing governmental challenges such as transparency, citizen participation, and evidence-based decision-making in Switzerland. Developed by researchers at the University of Zurich, the index evaluates all 26 Swiss cantons based on the availability and use of digital tools for political participation - including e-transparency, where the publication of machine-readable government data plays a key role. The index explicitly measures how openly accessible data on parliamentary proceedings, political processes, and government decisions enable citizens to monitor public institutions and engage meaningfully. Cantons are scored on a 0–100 scale, with Geneva leading at over 58 points and others scoring below 10, reflecting substantial variation in open data-driven transparency and participation. By linking these scores to socioeconomic and institutional variables through regression analysis, the study demonstrates that open data is not only a foundation for digital democracy, but also a measurable driver of more transparent and participatory governance.
Full report (in German): https://digipartindex.ch/docs/DigiPartIndex_2023_de.pdf ; Website: https://digipartindex.ch/en/project/  
https://digipartindex.ch/docs/case_studies_icegov_2023.pdf 
- A complementary study using the DPI, “Case Studies on Digital Political Participation in Austria, France, Canada, Germany, Italy, Japan and Switzerland", illustrates how open data enables participatory governance through real-world examples, such as public consultation platforms and machine-readable parliamentary records. In the opinion-formation dimension, Switzerland scores a strong 70 points - reflecting, among other factors, the country’s open data strategy and the existence of a national open data portal, both of which are included as indicators in the assessment. 1. Impact Monitoring Framework for Open Data: https://boris.unibe.ch/75031/1/CeDEM2016%20-%20Impact%20Monitoring%20Framework%20V06.pdf
The paper introduces an Impact Monitoring Framework that applies the Social Return on Investment (SROI) methodology to assess the social and environmental value of open data initiatives. The framework links the four SROI steps—input, output, outcome, and impact—with the 14 high-value data categories outlined in the G8 Open Data Charter. This approach aims to provide a structured way to evaluate the effectiveness of open data in delivering tangible benefits to society. While the paper does not provide specific case studies or quantified results, it emphasizes that environmental data, such as information on air quality, water resources, and biodiversity, can lead to significant positive outcomes when made openly accessible

2. Sustainability through Open Data: https://www.academia.edu/2452512/Sustainability_through_Open_Data_Examples_from_Switzerland
The article highlights several Swiss open data initiatives related to environmental sustainability but notes that most impacts are illustrated qualitatively through project descriptions and applications rather than systematically quantified. While the open data-driven projects (such as those visualizing energy consumption or nuclear energy information) improve public awareness and transparency, the article does not provide explicit metrics or comprehensive evaluations quantifying their direct impact on environmental outcomes or policy effectiveness.

There is still uncertainty wrt the scope of the environmental data. Wrt company register there has been uncertainty wrt the inclusion of personal data. There is a national level register (aanmerkingsregister.nl) that indicates which agency is responsible for HVD sources. The national open data portal is yet to add a HVD category to it, which is dependent also on a few outstanding metadata issues over all HVD themes.

2025:
The Ministry of Digital Affaires (MDA)  pursues an open data policy in Poland based on several documents: Open Data Programme and the Open Data Act (regulations), but also Open Data Projects, Open Data Standards and the projects of the National Repository of Scientific and Cultural Resources.
1. Open Data Programme: 
a. Open Data Programme 2016-2020 (pol.: Program Otwierania Danych Publicznych na lata 2016-2020).
In 2016-2020 MDA implemented first Polish open data strategy: Open Data Programme 2016-2020 (completed). The five Programme evaluation reports and one Programme finale research are published on dane.gov.pl.
b. Open Data Programme 2021-2027 (pol.: Program otwierania danych na lata 2021-2027).
The programme is a continuation of the open data strategy implemented by the MDA under the previous Open Public Data Programme 2016-2020. The new programme was adopted by a resolution of the Council of Ministers in February 2021. The Programme complements the Open Data Act and concentrates more on practical and technical mechanisms for opening data at the government level. Its main goal is among other to improve the quality and increase the amount of public data made available in an open manner. Examples of the planned activities include: increasing the amount of data resources made available by API on the dane.gov.pl portal, in particular dynamic data and high-value data and strengthening cooperation with data providers (e.g. conferences, hackathons, workshops, working meetings), increasing re-use and exchange of data, education, consolidation of Network of Open Data Officers. The Programme is addressed to the government administration but can also be implemented by other entities, e.g. public bodies at local level (cities/municipalities and regions) or private sector.      
An evaluation study (on-going) of the Programme was conducted in December 2023, and the results were published on data.gov.pl.                                                   
URL: 
Open Data Programme 2021-2027: 
https://dane.gov.pl/pl/knowledgebase/useful-materials/program-otwierania-danych-na-lata-2021-2027                                                       
2. Regulations:
a. Act on access to public information.
b. Open Data Act.
In Poland constitutional right to the information is realised by Act on access to public information (Act of 6 September 2001 on access to public information). Moreover in accordance with the new Polish Open Data Act (Act of 11 August 2021 on open data and the re-use of public sector information) every person shall have the right to re-use public sector information (the right to re-use) (previously Act of 25 February 2016 on the re-use of public sector information). The Polish Open Data Act implement Directive 2019/1024 and introduces the foundations for opening and re-use data. As a general rule, all public sector content can be re-used free of charge and without any conditions (or under minimum requirements). Among the new developments, the Act emphasizes the automated and real-time provision of data via the portal and through the application programming interfaces (API), and introduces the foundations for data sharing by new entities, like public undertakings and research and scientific institutions and also data sharing by private sector on dane.gov.pl portal.       
In 2023 MDA conducted an ex-post evaluation of the Open Data Act (one year after its entry in force), and its results were presented in the report. The report also contains proposals regarding the Open Data Directive.                                                                                                                                                           
URL:
Act on access to public information: https://www.dziennikustaw.gov.pl/DU/rok/2022/pozycja/902 
Open Data Act: https://dziennikustaw.gov.pl/DU/2021/1641
Report on the ex-post evaluation of the Open Data Act:
https://dane.gov.pl/pl/knowledgebase/useful-materials/prawo
3. Projects completed:
a.  Open data - access, standard, education. 
b.  Open data plus.
c. National Repository of Science and Culture Objects (KRONIK@).
Open data projects supported implementation of Open Data Programme 2016-2020/2021-2027. Main goal was to provide open data in manner that facilitates re-use of PSI; API development; open data portal development (dane.gov.pl); Open Data Laboratory (support data providers in the legal, technical and security areas of opening data); education; promotion open data in Poland.   
Project: National Repository of Science and Culture Objects (KRONIK@)  (completed)
KRONIK@ (kronika.gov.pl) is a platform that collects Polish culture, science and administration heritage dispersed until recently in the digital space. It has been equipped with a multi-search engine so that it is possible to search the collected resources in both simple and advanced way, as well as on the OCR text layer. In addition, KRONIK@ provides a free repository for archiving resources and their long-term storage, securing them against removal or loss. The successive increase in the number of entities that will make their resources available on the KRONIK@ will contribute to the increase in the number of digitally available science and culture works. 
The project also developed a metadata standard introducing uniform data management rules enabling the exchange of information and integration between digital sources.
URL:
https://www.gov.pl/web/cyfryzacja/otwarte-dane-dostep-standard-edukacja2
https://www.gov.pl/web/cyfryzacja/otwarte-dane-plus
https://www.gov.pl/web/cyfryzacja/kronik-krajowe-repozytorium-obiektow-nauki-i-kultury 
https://kronika.gov.pl/

a. open data (general): Data 3.0_exchange, value - continuation and development of the projects: Open Data - Access, Standard, Education and Open Data Plus 
b. open data (science and culture ): Kronik@ 2.0 continuation and development of the project: National Repository of Science and Culture Objects (KRONIK@)
The new project is expected to increase the quantity and quality of public sector information available for re-use, in particular high-value data and dynamic data made available via API. 
c) educational projects (from 2025)

a. first version of the standards (2018)

Programme provides strategic tasks for 7 years.
Examples of the planned activities include: increasing the amount of data resources made available by API on the dane.gov.pl portal, in particular dynamic data and high-value data and strengthening cooperation with data providers (e.g. conferences, hackathons, workshops, working meetings), increasing re-use and exchange of data, education, consolidation of  Network of Open Data Officers. 2025:
Public bodies at local level (e.g. cities/municipalities and regions) purse independent open data policy, many of them have a policies for open data and run open data portals. Also entities al local level are actively encouraged to publish data on dane.gov.pl. Moreover Open Data Programme 2021-2027 can be voluntary implemented by public bodies at local level, e.g. cities will be able to develop an annual schedule for opening selected data and making relevant data sets available at dane.gov.pl. Dane.gov.pl plans to harvest a new datasets from other local open data portals. 
The MDA also successively conducts training/education for staff of public bodies at the local level. An example is the online workshop on data opening. Within this framework several hundred employees of public bodies at the local level were trained (2023-2025).

* If yes, please briefly describe the measures.
column13:
MDA issued a second edition of the handbook of open data to promote re-use culture among public sector as well as business and NGOs.
The updated handbook is intended to more help build a culture of data re-use in offices. This handbook is a response to the information and education needs of the many offices that MDA has worked with the last 5 years. This edition introduces new categories of data, the use of regulations in the development of open data policies and ready-made solutions for data sharing such as the data.gov.pl and kronika.gov.pl services. Similarily to the previous edition, the current handbook does not explicitly foresee measures, but indicates the steps necessary to build an appropriate organizational structure, responsibility for opening data in the office (company) and re-use. These steps constitute a checklist for building a culture of re-use in an office (company).
In addition Open Data Standards (in particular Legal Standard) play such role ("openness template"). Also the Open Data Programme 2021-2027 and the Legal Standard introduced the Pillars of Openness (see. p. 58-59 Open Data Programme 2021 -2027). Meeting the these guidelines on public data sharing should mean giving data the attribute of openness. The Pillars of Openness was implemented to the Open Data Act  - definition of open data and principle of openness (Article 2.11 and Article 10.1). Appendix to the Legal Standard is also Check list (data providers can check that their data is open and in line with the Pillars of Openness). Moreover expert group (including MDA and Institute of Urban and Regional Development) developed a handbook "Data management in cities. Handbook for local governments

Do these data inventories include the data collected by public bodies that cannot be published as open data (e.g. in relation to the EU Data Governance Act (EU) 2022/868)? 

For Explanation:
* If yes, please briefly specify.
column13:
2024:
As a rule, this can happen. Data sets are subjects to validation. In case when the data cannot be published as open data, Open data team from MDA and Open data portal administrators support data providers to improve data quality (data sets at least at the 3rd level of openness). No matter if data sets can be published as open data, data sets published on dane.gov.pl always have an informative value. Moreover Open Data Act implemented the principle of openness – each public entities is obligate to shall make a data (public sector information) as open data (if it possible) (Article 10.1). Open Data Act defines the public sector information definition (any content or part thereof, regardless of the format used for recording, held by public entities - all data) (Article 2.8) and the open data definition (Article 2.11). MDA opened a Polish single information point (Article 8 DGA) in the data portal (dane.gov.pl). The single information point shall make available a searchable asset list containing an overview of protected data held by public sector bodies.
In addition, the MDA has also started  a series of training courses for public administrations on protected data (DGA) . The first training (for voivodeship offices - 16 regions  and  the biggest cities ) was held in November 2023.

column13:
2025:
MDA monitors the progress of public sector bodies in the work related to the implementation of Regulation (UE) 2023/138 on high-value data sets (including an inventory of data they hold - in particular high-value data sets from Regulation (UE) 2023/138). Specific high-value data sets inventoried in this way can be divided into two groups.
The first group includes datasets that are already being made available in accordance with the requirements of the Regulation (UE) 2023/138. The second group includes datasets on which work is underway or planned in order to make them available in accordance with the requirements of the Regulation (UE) 2023/138. The first group may include, for example, datasets on geospatial data, statistical data, or data on companies and company ownership. The second group may include, for example, certain data sets on Earth observation and environmental data.
MDA launched another project “Data 3.0 - exchange, value”, under which it is planned to increase the amount of high-value data published with an API on the data portal (dane.gov.pl). The project will be implemented in partnership with a number of public sector bodies, such as the Ministry of Economic Development and Technology, the Statistics Poland and the Chief Inspectorate of Environmental Protection.
In addition, European Funds for Digital Development 2021-2027   will provide for, among other things, Unit 2.3, “Digital Accessibility and Reuse of Information.” Support will include, among others, projects that prioritize increasing the quantity and quality of public sector information available for reuse, particularly high-value and dynamic data.
Some public sector bodies are already carrying out their own work to bring these datasets into compliance with the Regulation. Such bodies include, for example, the Ministry of Climate and Environment and the Ministry of Justice. In most cases, this work primarily involves technical aspects (for example it involves modifying the system or adding a new API). As such, in addition to being time-consuming, they also require a lot of money. Therefore, they will be co-financed under the new financial perspective of the European Funds Program for Digital Development 2021-2027.

column6:
Is there a governance structure in place that enables the participation and/or inclusion of various open data stakeholders? 

For Explanation:
*  If yes, please briefly describe the governance structure and its operating model
column13:
Stakeholders from the public and private sectors can participate in open data policy at the local and national levels. This ranges from being consulted on drating new open data regulations,  participating in research and various initiatives such as conferences, training, to making their own data available as open data or through the reuse of open data on national or local data portals.
Stakeholder participation can be divided into indirect and direct. 
Indirect participation
Already at the stage of drafting national/local laws and other regulations on data openness, stakeholders can participate in consultations on such drafts. Every public and private stakeholder has the opportunity to comment on the proposed regulations. 
Consultation on the Open Data Act:
https://legislacja.rcl.gov.pl/projekt/12337400 
Public pre-consultation of the new Open Data Programme 2021-202: 
https://www.gov.pl/web/cyfryzacja/program-otwierania-danych-na-lata-2021-2027--ruszaja-prekonsultacje-spoleczne
Evaluation of the Open Data Act and Open Data Programme 2021-2027:
https://dane.gov.pl/pl/knowledgebase/useful-materials/program-otwierania-danych-na-lata-2021-2027 
In addition, there are permanent legal mechanisms for requesting changes to laws already in force, such as the universal right of petition. Under these mechanisms the stakeholders can make requests not only to, for example, change open data regulations, but also to take action on open data. 
Furthermore, various stakeholders are regularly invited to participate in surveys on the open data reuse market. Depending on the purpose of the survey, these can be public sector and/or private sector stakeholders. The results of the surveys can be the basis for open data actions, such as educational or legal regulatory actions.
See the research reports here:
https://dane.gov.pl/pl/knowledgebase/useful-materials/raport-z-badania-wsrod-przedsiebiorcow-na-temat-wielkosci-i-charakterystyki-rynku-ponownego-wykorzystania-danych-publicznych-w-polsce
Besides, stakeholders are also invited to participate in various national/local initiatives, such as conferences, trainings, which, in addition to their educational value, provide a space for the exchange of views faced by both obligated entities and data users.
Direct participation 
Stakeholders can also directly participate in the open data reuse market through, among others, the national data portal (dane.gov.pl), as well as local portals (for examples of local portals see q. 3) , as open data contributors and as open data users. 
In addition, the Open Data Act introduces the basis for private sector stakeholders to share data on the data.gov.pl portal (e.g., businesses, NGOs) (see q. 6).
As an example of another space that allows stakeholders to participate in data openness policy, one should mention participation in the working group on strategic directions for data management (see q. 4). 
In addition, one can mention:
Open Data Officers Network (see q. 19):
https://www.gov.pl/web/cyfryzacja/pelnomocnicy-ds-otwartosci-danych
Task force for the implementation of the  Open Data Programme 2021-2027:
http://www.gov.pl/web/cyfryzacja/zespol-zadaniowy-do-spraw-programu-otwierania-danych-publicznych
 The Future is Data Conference (see q. 20).

column13: The MDA is a central hub for open data policy in Poland. MDA pursues public policy in open data at governmental level. Open data activities addressed to local and regional bodies supporting them in their endeavours are carried out by open data team as part of our strategy. (see for example Measure 3– p. 36 https://dane.gov.pl/en/knowledgebase/useful-materials/program-otwierania-danych-na-lata-2021-2027). Open data team carries out this task within its normal governance structure. Specific focus in put on such activities as trainings, promotion, information and knowledge dissemination.
A example of targeted support we give to local and regional initiatives is the letter of intent with the Górnoślasko-Zagłębiowska Metropolia (eng: Metropolis GZM), which already resulted in its local resources being made available on the data.gov.pl portal at the highest levels of openness.
https://metropoliagzm.pl/2024/05/17/metropolia-i-ministerstwo-cyfryzacji-zainicjowaly-wspolprace-w-dziedzinie-otwartych-danych/
Apart from supporting local initiatives, we also try to actively promote them and ensure the presence of the topic of open data at events addressed to local and regional participants. At this conference representatives from our open data team and cities’ data integrators initiative together promoted open data.
https://dane.gov.pl/pl/article/o-otwieraniu-danych-na-forum-we-wrocawiu
Apart from these targeted activities we also offer within our governance structure more general support to local and regional initiatives in form of trainings. An example of this type of training are cyclical online workshops organised by MDA for local government employees. The training programme includes a theoretical part focusing on explaining to participants the basic concepts and regulations of data openness. The practical part consisted of exercises on how to prepare data for release on the data.gov.pl portal and the publication process.  Within this framework several hundred employees of public bodies at the local level were trained (2023-2025).

Does the governance model include the appointment of official roles in civil services that are dedicated to open data (e.g. open data officers)?

For Explanation:
* If yes, please describe how this task is fulfilled at public body level.
column13:
The Open Data Act provides a legal basis for appointing official roles in civil service as part of open data governance and policy implementation. it is further developed by the Open Data Programme 2021-2027 that elaborates in more details on these implementation system and governance structure:
1. Task force for the Open Data Programme 2021 - 2027 - policy level (in each ministry a management member is assigned to the Task force)
2. Programme Implementers and Network of Open Data Officers – operational level.
The implementers of the Programme are members of the Council of Ministers and the President of the Statistics Poland, supported by Open Data Officers. Each ministry (and Statistics Poland) appoints civil servants responsible for implementation of the Programme, but also as a target for open data policy in institution. Their role is to remain in constant contact with Open data team in MDA and recommends new data sets to be released on the open data portal. They monitor among other:
- timely publication of public data on portal according to a defined roadmap 
- quality of data – the Programme sets standards and guidelines of data formats.
Every year the Implementers of the Programme (supported by Open Data Officers) are obliged to file a report on the implementation process and realized undertakings in the area of open data. On this basis MDA (Programme Coordinator) elaborates final report that is approved by ministerial task force and filed to the Council of Ministers. The final report is open to the public. 
3. Programme Coordinator – MDA 
4. Open data team from MDA (Data Management Department)
Open data team from the MDA constantly offers legal and technical support for Open Data Officers. 
See: Unit 6.2 in Open Data Programme 2021-2027
https://dane.gov.pl/pl/knowledgebase/useful-materials/program-otwierania-danych-na-lata-2021-2027
Moreover part of issues concerning significant tasks on open data field civil service was regulated in Open Data Act (see: Chapter 6 - "Open Data Programme", chapter 7 - "Data portal", Chapter 8 - "Open Data Officers").

Are there processes to ensure that the open data policies/strategy previously mentioned are updated and revised as needed?

For explanation:
* If yes, please describe the process and any recent updates made to strategy/policy
column13:
2025:
In addition to ongoing monitoring process of the national open data policy, MDA also conducts activities focused on evaluating its individual elements (such as documents, data portal - data.gov.pl). 
The course of the evaluation process depends on the type of open data policy element under examination. The evaluation includes, for example, research, analysis, public consultations, or commissioned expert reports.
Examples of such activities: 
1. Evaluation research on the Open Data Programme 2021-2027: 
The Open Data Programme 2021-2027 is subject to ongoing evaluation: the evaluation and the review is planned after two, four and then seven years after its adoption Two years after the adoption of the Programme, an evaluation was carried out evaluated as part of an evaluation research (on-going). The evaluation research consisted of two research studies (an in-depth interview and a questionnaire research) conducted among those responsible for the implementation of the Programme and other stakeholders (representatives of local administration, the private sector, the scientific community, NGOs, individual users). The main objective of the research was an overall evaluation of the Programme and its implementation process, as well as identification of areas that need to be changed in order to increase the effectiveness of the utility and relevance of the Programme's activities.
Based on the assessments and opinions of the respondents, the Programme, including the direction chosen by MDA regarding the expansion of the data portal (data.gov.pl), was generally positively assessed. The final report included recommendations  regarding in particular conducting an information campaign on new possibilities and benefits of opening data and conducting long-term and cyclical training for employees of public sector bodies, especially at the local level. 
Moreover, the report indicated the need to implement activities promoting the policy of open access to data aimed at gradually increasing the number of users and resources on the portal dane.gov.pl
The next edition online workshops on data opening are a response to these recommendations (see q. 3). Another project “Data 3.0 - exchange, value” also aims, among other things, to increase knowledge and skills among officials in preparing data for sharing and using data in work.The actions taken after the evaluation research of the Programme, including their impact on the open data policy, require a longer time perspective.

2. Ex-post evaluation of the Open Data Act
When designing the Open Data Act, we assumed an ex-post evaluation of this act at least one year after its implementation into the national legal order. 
As part of the evaluation, the provisions of the Open Data Act were analyzed and two studies were conducted: a study among public sector entities and a study of non-governmental organizations (22 non-governmental organizations were invited to participate). The evaluation results showed that, in general, the Open Data Act functions properly. The main area requiring intervention is primarily the issue of correct of applying the provisions of the Act. Therefore, MDA has undertaken extensive non-legislative activities, in particular information, educational and promotional activities. The implementation of these activities, as well as their impact on open data policy, requires a longer-term perspective. 
Examples of such activities include online workshops on opening data. Within this framework several hundred employees of public bodies at the local level were trained (2023-2025).
In addition, MDA launched another project: “Data 3.0 – exchange, value”. One of the planned activities is to expand knowledge and skills of administration employees, including at the local level, in the field of preparing data for sharing and using data in official work.

3. Update of the open data standards document 
The revision of open data standards was preceded by public consultations. As a result of the consultations and evaluation of the existing standards, the need to update the document was diagnosed. The effect was to supplement the standards with new issues (e.g., based on experience) identified by NGOs, entrepreneurs, law firms, citizens, local administration, etc.

column6:
Are there any processes in place to assess if public sector bodies are charging for data above marginal cost? (please see directive (EU) 2019/1024 on open data and the reuse of public sector information).

For Explanation:
* If yes, please specify the process(es).
column13:
2024:
In accordance with the Open Data Act public sector information might be re-use for any purposes, commercial or uncommercial. Data is released on line free of charge, while data on request is distributed as a principle free of charge or only direct cost  might be calculated (in Polish national law marginal cost was implemented as direct cost). The only exception is for state museums and local government museums. When making available or providing public sector information for re-use with purpose other than non-commercial research, scientific or educational purpose, these entities may charge fees higher than charges established under direct cost (Article 19 Open Data Act). Minister of Culture and National Heritage establish, by way of an ordinance, the maximum charges for re-use imposed by state museums and local government museums. 
Previously, we indicated that possibility of charging for data above marginal cost is limited and rarely used. In 2023 MDA developed report and large research/survey on implementation Polish Open Data Act by public sector bodies. Research covered over 2.5 thousand entities (various types: local governments, courts, central administration, central institutions etc.). Surveys were completed by over 1,300 entities. According to the results of the surveys in practice public sector bodies don't charge.

Are there any activities in place to assist data holders with publishing their data as open data (i.e. to help them with the data opening process)?

For Explanation:
