column13:
There are a number of activities to help data holders publish their data as open data. 
1.The new Open Data Act, which implements Directive 2019/1024 and introduces the foundations for opening and re-use data. The Act includes a definition of open data and the principle of openness (Article 2.11 and Article 10.1). 
URL: https://dziennikustaw.gov.pl/DU/2021/1641
2.Implementation of the new national Open Data Programme 2021-2027, which complements the Open Data Act and concentrates more on practical and technical mechanisms for data opening at the government level. Its main goal is, among others, to improve the quality and increase the amount of public data made available in an open manner (see q. 1). The programme is addressed to the government administration, but can also be implemented by other entities, such as public bodies at the local level (cities/municipalities and regions) or the private sector.  
URL: https://dane.gov.pl/pl/knowledgebase/useful-materials/program-otwierania-danych-na-lata-2021-2027        
3.Projects, in particular, on data opening to support national Open Data Programmes (see q. 1). This includes the Data 3.0 - exchange, value project currently being prepared for start-up, which is a continuation and development of previous projects: “Open Data Access, Standard, Education” and “Open Data Plus”. The main goals of these projects are to provide open data in the manner that facilitates re-use of PSI; API development; open data portal development (dane.gov.pl); the functioning of the Open Data Laboratory (support for data providers in the legal, technical and security areas of opening data); education; promotion of open data in Poland.
URL:https://www.gov.pl/web/cyfryzacja/otwarte-dane-dostep-standard-edukacja2
https://www.gov.pl/web/cyfryzacja/otwarte-dane-plus
https://www.rozwojcyfrowy.gov.pl/strony/dowiedz-sie-wiecej-o-programie/o-programie/
4.Open data standards (legal, security, technical and API)(see q. 1 and 8)
The Legal Standard (“openness template”) plays a special role.  Open Data Programme 2021-2027 and the Legal Standard introduced the Pillars of Openness (see pp. 58-59 of Open Data Program 2021-2027). Meeting these guidelines on public data sharing should mean giving data the attribute of openness. As an appendix to the Legal Standard, the Check list is also provided (data providers can check whether their data is open and in line with the Pillars of Openness).
URL: https://dane.gov.pl/pl/knowledgebase/useful-materials/standardy-otwartosci-danych
5.Open Data Officers Network (see q. 19-20)
Network of Open Data Officers functions in all ministries and Statistics Poland. Open Data Officers are public officials designated in their respective entities who are responsible for the implementation of open data policy. They are among other responsible for publication of new datasets on the portal dane.gov.pl and they supervise data quality and compliance with standards. They prepare annual schedules for opening and sharing selected data sets on the portal and they report on the Open Data Programme implementation and other open data activities to the Prime Minister. Open data team from the MDA constantly offers legal and technical support for Open Data Officers (see: Unit 6.2 in Open Data Programme 2021-2027).
URL: https://www.gov.pl/web/cyfryzacja/pelnomocnicy-ds-otwartosci-danych
6.reports prepared by the Open Data Laboratory with expert knowledge on open data related issues addressed to practitioners in public sector bodies (e.g. Report with recommendations on the use of contract marks in datasets made available on data.gov.pl)
URL: https://dane.gov.pl/pl/knowledgebase/useful-materials/raporty-laboratorium-otwartych-danych
7.  developing the dane.gov.pl portal and adding new functionalities (for example: DCAT compatibility, notifications for editors about the need to update data; see q. 7)
8. Regular exchange of knowledge or experience between MDA, and data holders, including Open Data Officers (see q. 20). For example: regular meetings with Open Data Officers (see q. 20). 
9. Regular exchange of knowledge or experience between public sector bodies (i.e. providers) and users of open data (e.g., academia, citizens, businesses) (see q. 21). For example: a meeting with the municipalities of the Metropolis GZM (see q. 21)

For Explanation:
* What is the technology stack of your portal (e.g. based on uData, CKAN, etc.)
column13: Dane.gov.pl as a whole is a system based on a microservices architecture, with clearly defined layers of presentation, business logic and data. From the perspective of system components, these are three-layer monolithic applications in a classic client-server architecture. Most websites operate as containers, which allows them to be easily scaled, deployed and managed later. The dominant interface for communication between services is the REST API. The system portal, i.e. the frontend element, is written using TypeScript using the Angular framework, while backend services are written using Python 3 frameworks including: Falcon, Django, RDFLib, Wagtail CMS. Depending on the type of user, individual pages are rendered on the client side (CSR) or server side (SSR). The system components are located on the VMware vSphere virtualization platform.

Additionally, internal work at the MDA regarding general interoperability of public IT systems and data has a significant impact on the HVD transborder interoperability as they are part of this wider framework.
Ongoing amendment of the Act on computerization of the activities of entities performing public tasks includes:
- legal obligation to maintain public registers only using IT systems,
- imposition of a requirement to make data from public IT systems available via standardized API,
- development of the public IT systems API catalogue, as well as information on the structure and meaning of data stored in all public registers, expanded to include information on dictionaries, classification schemes, taxonomies and code lists in public registers.
Therefore interoperability of public registers or public IT systems containing HVD will be increased by providing machine-to-machine interfaces to such a data.

Do you have a methodology in place to measure the impact of open data in your country?
 
For Explanation:
* If yes, please briefly describe the key points of this methodology.
column13:
By creating the methodology of a nationwide study on the size and characteristics of the public data re-use market in Poland, (more on the study here https://dane.gov.pl/pl/knowledgebase/useful-materials/raport-z-badania-wsrod-przedsiebiorcow-na-temat-wielkosci-i-charakterystyki-rynku-ponownego-wykorzystania-danych-publicznych-w-polsce) we defined the parameters of the impact of open data on the area of entrepreneurship, which - after some modifications and further tests - can be used to measure the impact of open data on various other aspects related to the economic and socio-cultural functioning of specific social groups, or society as such.
We measured the parameters by means of a quantitative survey, carried out using the CATI technique (computer-assisted telephone interviews) among representatives of companies responsible for data management and/or data analysis, or with people best informed about the company's situation and the area of data use. In order to achieve the assumed research goal, a stratified-random sample selection was used, while maintaining the value of representativeness due to 4 size categories of enterprises. The sample also includes the division into provinces. Such an approach in constructing the research sample allowed us to objectify our observations by generalizing them to the entire group of entrepreneurs. Based on the above criteria, 600 interviews were conducted.
In the next steps, we intend to apply (with appropriate modifications) the above solutions to other social groups and thus test and possibly verify the indicators of the impact of open data. Therefore, we treat the survey conducted among entrepreneurs as a pilot of the process of creating a methodology for measuring the impact of open data.

Union of Polish Metropolises commissioned a unique study to estimate how many people from Ukraine are in our country, where they live, how many of them are children under 14. This information is an essential starting point for both the government and local governments to design systemic solutions, such as integration activities or the financial policy of the state.
The study assesses with great accuracy firstly, how many Ukrainians remained in Poland or came to it after the outbreak of warfare and, secondly, where exactly they are (including such unique insight as where these people are at night, and where during the day - for example, it is now known that they mostly sleep in the metropolitan communes surrounding big cities, where most of their daily affairs are carried out). The data can therefore help to better understand how Ukrainians use the. All this translates into more effective city management. Due to this data cities that received the majority of Ukrainian refugees can better adjust their daily operating, services and effectively manage resources to avoid increase in social tensions related to the situation on i.a. labour market, deepening housing crisis or the deterioration of the standard of some services.
The uniqueness of the study lies in the methodology that analysis geo-localisation data from smartphones. The results are then combined with other data, including open data on the number of Ukrainians applying for refugee status, to verify them.

Improving air quality is an important environmental and social issue that arouses great interest among residents, because it has a major impact on the quality of their life. Local authorities take various actions aiming at improving the air quality. A radical example was the decision of the city of Krakow to completely ban the burning of solid fuels in small heating installations. The solution adopted in Krakow is being closely watched by many local governments in Poland. The assessment of its effectiveness was of key importance to them. If its effectiveness is confirmed, there is a chance that this radical solution will be replicated by other cities.
The task of verifying its effectiveness was undertaken by scientists from AGH University, commissioned by the Krakow Smog Alert. They analysed many years of data from measurement stations to compare the level of pollution before and after the introduction of the anti-smog resolution. The analysis was carried out to collect the widest available open database of measurement results from the Chief Inspectorate for Environmental Protection and the Provincial Inspectorate for Environmental Protection. Impact: The results are clear - air quality has improved significantly. Over 10 years, the average concentration of PM10 dust in Krakow decreased by 45.4% and PM2.5 dust by 43.8%

According to the Access to Public Information Act, which transposes the EU Open Data Directive, (Article 10.b) – the open Data policy – obligations of the public sector bodies are as follows:
Article 10.b – Slovenian Access to Public Information Act
(1) The public sector bodies should allow re-use of public sector information by publication on the World Wide Web by publishing in open formats and in machine-readable form, together with metadata, except where this would involve disproportionate effort, going beyond a simple operation.
(2) The authorities should publish at the national open data portal a list of all databases within its competence with the relevant metadata and databases as such in the form of open data or links to websites where these are published as open data.
(3) Anyone may re-use the data published on the national open data portal, free of charge, under the conditions that:
-         Re-use of data is carried out in accordance with the law governing the protection of personal data and
-         At each re-use the user provides the source of data.

Regarding the field of Open Science - st the end of March 2022, the National Assembly of the Republic of Slovenia adopted the Resolution on the Slovenian Scientific Research and Innovation Strategy 2030 which was published in the Official Gazette of the Republic of Slovenia in April 2022. This is a key Slovenian strategic document for research and innovation until 2030 and is based on the Article 10 of the new Scientific Research and Innovation Activities Act, which introduces Open Science as an important integral part of the scientific research. In the context of the horizontal objectives under Item 6.2., the Strategy defines six key measures in the field of Open Science, as follows:
1. Effective management and financing of the development of the national Open Science ecosystem and related national structures and infrastructures, ensuring their international alignment as well as integration into international associations and infrastructures.
2. Introduction of modern approaches to the evaluation of scientific research activity in accordance with Open Science principles to increase the quality and impact of research (e.g., DORA - San Francisco Declaration on Research Assessment, Leiden Manifesto for Research Metrics, ERAC - European Research Area and Innovation Committee Guidelines).
3. Ensuring that the results of scientific research comply with the FAIR principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable), and that full and immediate open access is provided (subject to legitimate exceptions).
4. Establishment of a National Open Science Community for the introduction and monitoring of Open Science in Slovenia, as well as its integration into ERA and beyond.
5. Promoting the development of citizen science and public involvement in scientific research.
6. Promoting the development of a national scientific publishing system to operate according to the principles of Open Science.
These measures, which are recognised as essential for the development of Open Science in Slovenia, will be the  basis for the Action Plan on Open Science, which is in the process of preparation.

column13: In Slovenia, we do not have regions, but due to the large number of municipalities (212) and small population in municipalities (https://sl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seznam_ob%C4%8Din_v_Sloveniji ), this type of policy is prepared at the national level and coordinated with the local level. All state policies are coordinated with all stakeholders, including the local communities, during the process. Due to the specificity of the organization of local self-government and the lack of an intermediate management level in the form of regions (no regions), all policies for the area of open data are prepared at the national level. Legal obligations under the law in relation to Open Data (including the publication of open data at the national open data portal) as well as the commitment to implement the open data policy are equal for institutions at the national level as well as for municipalities. Thus, municipalities are equally bound as other public institutions.

column6:
Is there a governance structure in place that enables the participation and/or inclusion of various open data stakeholders? 

For Explanation:
*  If yes, please briefly describe the governance structure and its operating model
column13:
The OPSI portal has a well-developed editorial policy. The portal's administrators and editors-in-chief are employees of the Ministry of Digital Transformation and the Ministry of Public Administration.
Other civil servants from ministries, other government bodies, municipalities and others who regularly publish information on the portal act as content editors. They publish, amend and update records and collections on the portal. Their role is to publish, modify and update their collections and some other activities on the portal.
Before a collection is published on the portal, it is reviewed by the editors-in-chief and, if the metadata is entered correctly, they approve the publication of the collection. If they consider that there are errors, they contact the authorities (refuse publication on the portal) to update the data accordingly. Once this has been done, the Chief Content Editor will publish the collection on the portal. The only exception is when the authorities only publish a new file with up-to-date data. In this case, the file is automatically published on the portal. No review and approval by the Editor-in-Chief is required. 
All portal managers, editors-in-chief and content editors cooperate with each other. They meet in meetings, training sessions (content and technical) and other events (conferences, web presentations, training sessions) organised by the Ministry of Public Administration and the Ministry of Digital Transformation.

Are there any processes in place to assess if public sector bodies are charging for data above marginal cost? (please see directive (EU) 2019/1024 on open data and the reuse of public sector information).

For Explanation:
* If yes, please specify the process(es).
column13:
The article 34a of Public Information Access Act says:
(1) The authority may charge marginal costs for the re-use of data, but may not charge a price.
(2) Notwithstanding the preceding paragraph, it may charge a price for re-use:
-         a body which, in accordance with a plan or program of work or financing, must generate revenue in addition to the budget to cover at least 30% of its costs related to the performance of its public tasks, and
-         library, museum and archive.
(3) In the cases referred to in the preceding paragraph, a price shall be charged for the re-use of information, which may not exceed the costs of collecting, preparing, reproducing and disseminating information and the normal return on investment. The price must be cost-oriented and determined in the normal accounting period and in accordance with the prescribed accounting rules for the authority. The calculation basis for the price is information of a public nature.
(6) The Ministry shall decide that the body may charge a price on the basis of the first indent of the second paragraph of this Article for a period of two years, on the basis of a proposal which must be substantiated by figures from the adopted annual substantive and financial program and report. The body's appeal against the ministry's decision is not allowed, but an administrative dispute is allowed.

column13:
The approach is actually well defined in the Governmental decision on Editorial Policy which obliges all ministries and public bodies (sectoral editors) to publish and maintain data. The data or datasets to be published must first be approved by the Sectoral Editor and after that also by the Chief Editor. The task of the editors is also to maintain data, that is make sure that they are up to date
Gov. decision n.b.38200-17/2013/3  (http://vrs-3.vlada.si/MANDAT13/vladnagradiva.nsf/71d4985ffda5de89c12572c3003716c4/384a4d9329d25d8fc1257c4400332ab0?OpenDocument)

The purpose of CRP ITzaSKP was to encourage the opening of public administrative (micro) data in agriculture in Slovenia for as many purposes as possible, including or above all those that were not defined when the data was created. The project took place in the context of new social expectations and needs in the field of agriculture and in related fields and in the context of the possibility of using information technology. 

It was based on data science – the disciplines of social science and information science. In this way, it complemented other related projects, mostly in the field of agrarian economics, which pursued the goal of using data for a specific objective and/or in a specific area of agriculture. The project was financed by the Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Food (MKGP) and the Public Research Agency of the Republic of Slovenia.
Link to study OPENING DATA IN SLOVENE AGRICULTURE FOR FACT-BASED DECISION-MAKING: https://www.fdv.uni-lj.si/docs/default-source/zalozba/acmo-22-21-12-2021.pdf?sfvrsn=2

The Slovenian case  of ERAR (a web site of the Slovenian Commission for Prevention of corruption providing for the transparency of public spending via publishing open data) has been recognised as a best practice by the EC in their 2023 Handbook of good practices in the fight against corruption. 

https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/news/handbook-good-practices-fight-against-corruption-2023-02-15_en  

See page 46: 

2.2.4 Slovenia: Combining Open Data sources for public reuse - ERAR online application


Additional clarification:
In terms of data demand, there is a comparison with the FLINT project indicators which was focused on the FADN base, showed that it is possible in Slovenia with help of public administrative resources to provide (at least partial) microdata for as much as a third from around 30 economic ones (investments and insurance - based on measures, duration of farms, quality schemes, exposure to risks - non-agricultural activities), environmental (permanent grasslands, areas with ecological importance, potential calculations TGP with the help of standard factors) and social indicators (involvement in Education and Training).

On the basis of expressed needs and assessed possibilities for data analytics, we within the  framework of the experiment, obtained data from AKTRP for farms included in the system of agricultural subsidies (approximately 57,000 farms) for the period 2015-2019 (the current CAP cycle), which include up to about 400 variables on an annual basis. From MKGP (RKG) also obtained data on land (using) surfaces. We are data combined at the KMG unit level and performed some test tasks in the freely available and open source software environment (Orange). It was not the purpose of the experiment identifying individual cause-and-effect relationships and predicting, but also showing the potential of data for various analytical tasks in a more time-efficient way and generally accessible way and evaluating data systems from the point of view of data analytics based on practical IT problems that arose during the experiment appeared.

The experiment confirmed that the data has tremendous potential, but the obstacles are the knowledge of the structure of the resources and the necessary different knowledge and competences for meaningful use and interpretation. Obtaining, combining and editing data for individual purposes is due to its complex structure, fragmentation into areas and in time, lack of documentation, also in relation to quality and methods of use, various single-purpose systems, the absence of standard interfaces and others demanding in terms of time and human resources.
Several suggestions emerge from the conducted research, which are presented in bold in more detail in the conclusions of the chapters of the monograph, and we summarize them in the following Table 1 on page 277.

In the end, we can conclude that the conducted research complements existing research, which pointed out the non-targeting of measures in Slovenian agriculture and the problems access to individual data in a manner indicative of general public benefits and specific options for opening administrative data for various purposes use both in the social and technical-information sense.

Yes, there is an open data law at federal level. In July 2017, Section 12a of the E-Government Act (EGovG) entered into force (First Open Data Act), which for the first time created a legal basis for the mandatory provision of open administrative data by federal authorities. The Second Open Data Act, which entered into force in July 2021, further adapted the content of the existing obligations under Section 12a of the EGovG and extended them to the entire federal administration.

The Data Use Act (DNG) which also entered into force on 23 July 2021 aims to modernise and replace the Information Re-Use Act (IWG). In order to improve the usability of data, open data will need to be used in machine-readable formats. In addition, the DNG stimulates open data initiatives beyond the boundaries of the federal administration and establishes the principle of ‘open by default’ also for the use of data by the Länder, municipalities and public undertakings in the areas of water, transport and energy supply. The Federal Government’s Open Data Strategy, adopted on 6 July 2021, provides a framework for action to improve the Federal Open Data Ecosystem. The Federal Government’s data strategy forms the overarching data policy framework for the Open Data Strategy. Over a period of five years, the Open Data Strategy covers three areas of action, with a total of 68 implementation measures taken by different federal ministries and authorities. The three strands of action include improving the provision of data and developing data infrastructures, increasing innovative, public-interest and responsible use of data, and promoting data literacy and a data culture to increase the quality and usability of data provided. The implementation of the Open Data Strategy is accompanied by continuous monitoring.

column13:
The legally required Open Data Progress Report, submitted to the German Bundestag every two years, contains proposals for possible further development of the legal and strategic framework. Section 12a, Paragraph 11, Sentence 2 of the E-Government Act explicitly requires a separate evaluation for a specific expansion of the legal framework (independent administrative areas such as the Deutsche Rentenversicherung Bund (the Federal Pension Insurance), legal entitlement to open data).

The proposals outlined in the progress report are not yet part of a concrete political agenda (which is also due to the change of government since May 2025). The required evaluation of the legal entitlement and self-governing bodies as the Federal Pension Insurance has not yet begun (as of July 2025). But the evaluation is, at least from a financial perspective, included in the current federal budget preparation.The evaluation itself is expected to begin in autumn 2025. Furthermore, the Open Data Strategy 2025 will be evaluated in the next months.

column13:
2025:
GovData: On average, the metadata is updated after 2 days. If metadata is changed manually directly in the GovData portal, the changes are visible immediately. If a dataset is changed in the geoportal of a city, the city harvests its geoportal, the city may be harvested by the portal of the district, which in turn is harvested by the federal state, which is harvested by GovData. This chain can result in a delay of several days when updating the data.

We are transferred the high-value datasets award to the European data portal correctly. DCAT-AP.de is only complement to DCAT-AP, so it is completely conforming to DCAT-AP. The complement to DCAT-AP are necessary to depict German peculiarities.
https://www.dcat-ap.de/ // R2: For an exact explanation, we would have to answer the question separately.

In short, there are two legally different approaches between the CC BY 4.0 licence and the German data licence. CC BY focuses on material property law, while the German variant classifies the licensing of (official) datasets as a dedication/administrative act. This results in a different legal assessment. In addition, there are aspects from the regulations in Germany regarding general terms and conditions (GTC) in the context of civil law.

So there is a subtle legal distinction behind the data licence - a "German peculiarity". :-)

Nevertheless, the necessity of a national licence is currently being discussed and possibly reassessed in future.

"The retrieval of data pursuant to the first sentence of (1) [(= § 12a (1) contains the obligation for publishing open data by federal authorities)] shall be made possible free of charge and for the unrestricted re-use of the data by any person. Retrieval of data pursuant to the first sentence of (1) should be possible at any time, without mandatory registration and without justification."

"When is open government data for the purposes of this [open data]strategy?
- Authorities have collected the data themselves or have them collected by third parties;
- freely accessible on public networks,
- machine-readable,
- non-personal
- freely usable,

The open provision of weather and climate data has recently had a positive impact on the achievement of political goals with broad public acceptance, for example, in climate protection.
Open geodata is used in various political decision-making processes as basic information for visualizing local, regional, or national contexts, but also for statistical analyses. Data is provided via:
- https://www.geoportal.nrw/
- https://open.nrw/
Berlin (federal state): We use open data from the field of renewable energies to demonstrate how we can achieve the goals of the Berlin Energy and Climate Protection Concept, for example, how we can improve the use of solar energy systems on the roofs of public and private buildings. Link: https://energieatlas.berlin.de/ (with the data and visualization of which renewable energies are used and how much energy is consumed).
Further examples can be found here:
1) "Wegweiser Kommune" (https://www.wegweiser-kommune.de/) is a platform that uses open data (statistics) from the Federal Statistical Office to visualize demographic information (forecasts, demographic data, and migration data). The goal is to provide cities with more than 5,000 inhabitants with an information system that enables them to (i) visualize their development and (ii) actively shape their respective futures.
2) Pegel-Online (http://pegelonline.wsv.de/gast/start) is a highly successful open data app and online platform of the Waterways and Shipping Authority (WSB), which provides information on the water levels of more than 7,300 km of rivers and canals in Germany. It is used as a basis for decision-making not only by private users (citizens) who use these rivers/canals or live nearby, but also by public bodies and officials dealing with water issues in Germany (e.g., construction work, flood protection, etc.).
3) Integreat (https://integreat-app.de/ueber-uns/) is a local, multilingual open data platform whose goal is to prevent "information poverty" and facilitate the inclusion and integration of immigrants. It is aimed at immigrants themselves as well as integration officers and city administrations, and offers an overview of language courses, administrative procedures, job openings, and everyday topics.

In Latvia, we conduct several structured activities to better understand user behaviour and improve our portal:
1. Web Analytics: We use tools such as Google Analytics to monitor website traffic, user behaviour, and engagement metrics. This helps us identify which sections of the portal are most used, where users drop off, and what content drives the most interaction.
2. Social Media Monitoring: We also monitor social media channels and online forums for user comments and feedback about the portal. This helps us stay informed about public perception and emerging issues.
The data and insights gathered from these activities are regularly reviewed and used to guide updates to the portal’s design, content, and functionality—ensuring that it remains user-centric and responsive to evolving needs.

The shift from "all" to "the majority" of public sector data providers contributing to the portal reflects a refinement in the reporting methodology and a more precise assessment of actual data contributions. In 2024, the response was based on a broader interpretation that included all institutions with the potential to contribute, regardless of the volume or frequency of their data uploads.
For the 2025 reporting cycle, a more detailed evaluation was conducted, focusing on the regularity, completeness, and practical use of data contributions. As a result, some institutions were reclassified as non-contributors due to technical delays, internal restructuring, or limited capacity to meet current data publication standards.
There are no significant legal barriers, but some minor technical and organizational challenges persist, particularly among smaller or regional institutions. Efforts are ongoing to support these institutions and improve overall participation.

We are MSARD, the institution that invites both the public and the private sector to share re-use cases.

In Latvia, public bodies do not systematically classify reuse cases once they are submitted. There is currently no formalized or centralized mechanism in place at the national level—either by MSARD or another institution—for categorizing reuse requests according to predefined criteria.
However, certain reuse cases may be reviewed on a case-by-case basis, particularly when they involve sensitive data, public interest, or require legal or technical evaluation. In such instances, responsible authorities may apply internal procedures or refer to relevant legislation to determine how the request should be handled. These practices, however, are not part of a consistent or mandatory classification framework.
Efforts are ongoing in the broader context of digital government and open data to improve the handling and transparency of reuse cases, but systematic classification remains an area for potential development.

In Latvia, several hackathons supported by government institutions and NGOs have resulted in solutions with tangible policy or service impacts. Below are examples where hackathon-generated ideas or open data applications have been adopted or used by public administrations:
1. Anti-Corruption Open Data Hackathon 
Organized by Transparency International Latvia (Delna) in cooperation with TI Estonia and TI Finland on 25–26 January 2024, this hackathon focused on using open datasets to reveal corruption risks and inform governance strategies Delna.
• Tools Developed:
o A corruption index of state institutions,
o A tracker of companies that continued trade with Russia/Belarus and simultaneously participated in public procurement.

• Policy Potential:
o These prototypes highlight risks in public procurement and can support reform proposals to restrict procurement by companies with certain foreign ties.
o They leverage open data from the Company Register, Beneficial Ownership Registry, and public procurement system (EIS) via [data.gov.lv] and other registers Delna.

• Open data sources:
o Company register and beneficial ownership data published by government,
o Public procurement data (EIS).

You can review the published outcomes and tools via Delna’s summary article on the hackathon outcomes, including links to the developed prototypes.

2. Digital Tool Prototype Presentation 
On 26 April 2024, Delna presented a digital prototype based on hackathon results that identifies companies importing goods from Russia or Belarus while winning public contracts in Latvia in 2022–2023 Delna:
• Findings:
o 33 companies met both criteria.
o Estimated procurement value: ~€400 million in 2022–2023.
o The number decreased in 2023.
• Policy relevance:
o Enables public administration to assess and potentially restrict procurement from companies posing security or conflict of interest risks.
• Datasets used:
o Imports (customs trade data),
o Public procurement contracts (EIS),
o Beneficial ownership and enterprise registry data.

3. Open Government Action Plan & Data Governance 
While not a hackathon, Latvia’s Fifth National Open Government Action Plan (2022–2025) supports taking these tools further.
• Since September 2023, the MSARD functions as the Single Information Point to mediate reuse requests, coordinating data access across agencies.
• Mid 2024 review confirmed the government added milestones related to improving open data availability, local government transparency, and data-driven oversight Open Government Partnership (https://www.opengovpartnership.org/documents/latvia-midterm-review-2021-2025/).
These structural improvements increase the chances that hackathon prototype tools can inform actual policy or administrative decision-making.

A strong illustrative example from Latvia is the CareQueue project, developed during the Open Data Hackathon 2018 in Riga. This open-source web application was built using public‐sector open data—specifically municipal and national datasets on preschool locations, waiting-list lengths, and available places. It visualized this data on an interactive map to help parents find preschools with available spots, thereby improving decision-making and informational literacy among citizens. This service enhanced digital skills by enabling developers and users to work with open data, geo visualization, and civic tech tools in an educationally relevant context. The project explicitly built on data from Latvia’s national open data portal, and the prototype is designed for reuse across cities or countries (joinup.ec.europa.eu).
This qualifies as a reuse case where open data was actively employed to improve societal skills—both for developers (data and mapping) and end users navigating public services and digital civic tools.

DabasDati.lv for biodiversity & environmental observation:
The nature-observation portal and citizen science platform DabasDati.lv (run by Latvian Fund for Nature and Latvian Ornithological Society) allows people to upload wild plant and animal observations across Latvia Interreg Europe+1Interreg Europe+1ResearchGate.
The platform aggregates and provides open access to these observational data, under CC0 / open licences—though specific dataset links are available through their website (e.g. DabasDati.lv catalog and exported observation files) as described in the publication ResearchGate.
• Citizens and professional naturalists upload geotagged sightings (e.g. of birds, plants, insects). Researchers and conservation authorities use these records to track species occurrence, abundance, phenological shifts, and range expansions.
• Impact on biodiversity and environmental protection:
o Species monitoring & early detection: Enables early flagging of declining or invasive species, prompting timely conservation action.
o Public awareness & stewardship: Engages broad public participation, raising environmental awareness and community ownership of biodiversity protection.
o Data informed decisions: Helps government bodies and NGOs plan protected areas, set priorities, and evaluate habitat changes.
• The initiative supports maintenance of air- and water-related biodiversity, by identifying species indicative of quality habitats (e.g. wetlands, forests, rivers) and enabling response when ecological conditions worsen.

LAKES GO DIGITAL — real time lake water quality monitoring
The “LAKES GO DIGITAL” programme (Latvia Lithuania cross border) implements smart buoys to gather continuous water quality readings from urban lakes, sharing them via an online dashboard and geoportal in real time LatLit.
While formal portal data endpoints are being built (e.g. ArcGIS StoryMap, municipal geoportals), the project documentation outlines that real time measurements and ecological models will be publicly available open data via QR-linked dashboards and an integrated online platform ccre-cemr.org+2LatLit+2reddit.com+2.
Real time sensors measure parameters like turbidity, temperature, microplastic indicators, etc. Data is openly accessible to municipalities, researchers, educators, and the public.
Improved & timely water-quality management. Continuous data lets authorities detect pollutants or ecological stress quickly—faster than infrequent lab testing.
Enhanced biodiversity protection. By detecting early signs of eutrophication or contamination, remedial measures (e.g. runoff mitigation, aquatic management) can be applied before harm to habitat-dependent species.
Public engagement & accountability. Educational dashboards raise awareness and support data driven local stewardship.

Balticmaps Solution by SIA Jāņa sēta:
SIA Jāņa sēta is a private company specializing in cartography and GIS services. It integrates open geospatial data into its web map platform Balticmaps.eu and its mobile app, offering features for both professionals and the public—such as parcel delivery optimization, route planning, address search, cadastral data access, tourism info, and customizable map layers.

Beyond its popular map platforms, SIA Jāņa sēta also offers a range of API services that allow developers and businesses to easily access and integrate geospatial data into their own products. By making this data available in a developer-friendly way, Jāņa sēta helps lower the barriers for creating new digital solutions. The obligation to publish a data inventory was determined by the Information Commissioner of the Republic of Croatia through instructions on the reuse of information. Namely, there is an obligation for bodies to publish on their websites a list of databases they maintain, with accompanying metadata, methods of access and reuse ("Asset lists").
https://pristupinfo.hr/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/Ponovna-uporaba-informacija-upute.docx?x45242
2024:
Such obligation is not explicitly stated in the Open Data Policy, but there is legal obligation stipulated by the Right to Access to Information Act – according to Art 10. Para 1. Pt. 5. all the public authority bodies (including local and regional self-government units) are obliged to publicise registers and databases from their domain, or the information on the registers and databases they possess, as well as publicising the conditions to access and re-use of the data. In addition, Art 28. Para 1. of the RAIA imposes the obligation of all the public bodies to publish the data for re-use, which should be easily searchable, described by metadata, available in machine-readable and open format, aligned to open standards.

In addition, publication of the metadata is necessary also within the open licence that we have protected some register (open licence is necessary). It is regulated by the Rulebook on the types and contents of permits that determines the conditions of reuse of information, Art 4. Para.5: Metadata is always published with an open license, regardless of what permission the publisher publishes a set of data to which the metadata relates.

The Coordination for the Implementation of the Open Data Policy is the body responsible for monitoring, coordinating and improving the implementation of the Open Data Policy. The main purpose of the Coordination is to ensure that data collected and processed by public authorities is made available to the public in an open and reusable manner. This Coordination works to encourage compliance with legislative and strategic documents, enable better accessibility of data and provide technical and organizational support to public authorities in this process.
The main tasks of the Coordination are:
• drafting a proposal for an Action Plan for the implementation of the Open Data Policy, 
• monitoring the implementation of measures from the Action Plan,
• updating and revising the Open Data Policy,
• ensuring the achievement of the goals and effects of the Open Data Policy,
• determining and updating a list of high-value datasets,
• issuing recommendations and guidelines for opening public sector data,
• encouraging cooperation and exchange of experiences between public sector bodies in publishing open data,
• promoting and encouraging the reuse of data in the private sector, civil society and citizens,
• submitting an annual report on the status of the implementation of the Action Plan and progress related to the use of open data in the Republic of Croatia as part of the annual report on the work and development of the state information structure.

Working Group (experts from the relevant public authorities) has drafted the text of the new Open Data Policy and the Action Plan for the Policy implementation (for year 2024 and 2025). The process of adoption and entry into force is under way. Expected adoption time: September 2024.     The revision of the policy was made now because it will ensure better cooperation and communication between the relevant institutions, especially in the context of high-value data sets. An action plan has been drawn up to achieve better results. The open data policy applies to a period of five years from the moment of its adoption.
After this period, a new Open Data Policy will be revised and adopted, harmonized in regulatory, technological and other necessary aspects. Coordination for the implementation of the Open Data Policy may, if necessary, propose an update or revision of the Open Data Policy even before the expiration of the specified period. With the adoption of this Open Data Policy, the Open Data Policy adopted on July 19, 2018 ceases to be valid.

-	encourage state administration bodies to open and publish high-value datasets from their jurisdiction
-	organize and implement training for public authorities related to the publication of data via the Open Data Portal API
-	online training (webinars) on open data
-	create promotional materials with information on open data, the possibilities and benefits of the open data system
-	Inform the public about the management of open data through the Open Data Portal
-	Production of promotional video materials for citizens
-	Annual monitoring of the reuse of open data by public authorities
-	Annual monitoring of the needs for open data by various stakeholders: private sector, scientific community, civil society organizations
-	Annual monitoring of the needs of visitors to the Open Data Portal and the reuse of open data via the Open Data Portal
-	Monitoring the reuse of high-value datasets published on the websites of the authorities

column6:
Do you have a methodology in place to measure the impact of open data in your country?
 
For Explanation:
* If yes, please briefly describe the key points of this methodology.
column13:
The ex-post index of the influence of the set of open data is a measure of the realized influence of the set of open data in solving the problem area. Due to its complexity and all the variables involved, the construction of the impact index of the open data set is built according to four categories:
- Economic impact,
- Social impact,
- Political influence,
- Environmental impact.
At the same time, it is important to emphasize that the construction of the ex-post index of influence of the set of open data additionally includes a fifth category - the index of use. Usage index - which is constructed based on the download rate, referencing rate, rating of the usefulness of the data set by the user and the up-to-dateness of the data set.

1) Total impact index value of open data set (A)
2) Economic Impact Index (B)
3) Social Impact Index (C)
4) Political Influence Index (D)
5) Environmental Impact Index (E)
6) Usage Index (F) - Ex-post
Where A = B + C + D + E + F

B) The economic impact index is constructed based on scores on questions divided into three categories:
1. Macroeconomic impact,
2. Microeconomic and sectoral impact, and
3. Impact on the public sector.
C) The social impact index is constructed based on three categories:
1. housing,
2. inclusion of marginalized social groups, i
3. reduction of social inequalities.
D) The political influence index of the open data set is constructed based on the following categories:
1. transparency and responsibility,
2. effectiveness,
3. efficiency, i
4. decision making.
E) The environmental impact index is constructed based on the four selected most important environmental impact categories
1. Water and/or air quality,
2. Management/management of waste,
3. Environmentally friendly transport, and
4. Noise level
F) The usage index is used exclusively in the construction of the ex-post index of the influence of the set of open data after a minimum of one year has passed since the publication of the data set.
The usage index consists of:
1. download rates,
2. referencing rates,
3. evaluations of the usefulness of the data set by users i
4. assessments of the up-to-dateness of the data set based on the up-to-date report,

column13:
One of the goals of Estonia’s Digital Agenda 2030 (https://www.mkm.ee/media/6970/download) is achieving human-centric digital government. To achive that we plan to raise the awareness of people and the general public of human-centric digital government and the reliability of technology. Our Open Data Action plan includes activities on creating and keeping up-to-date e-courses including topics of open data, which describe open data concept, publication process, and reuse both for public oficials and citizens. Moreover, we constanly working on raising user-friendliness of our open data national portal and making data publishing as easy as possible.
====
To help boost publication to data generated by citizens we have created online courses at our government digital academy on open data and its publication (https://digiriigiakadeemia.ee/), we also carry out trainings on specific fields. We have carried out trainings on data literacy, which we plan to roll-out across the nation to raise competences and awareness. Today, this is covered in our digital-centric data governance vision and agenda. From technical means, we have created consent service, which enables citizens to share their government held data with external stakeholders. Today, over 300 000 consents have been generated to enable access to citizen data. 

There are also domain specific activities to incentivse publication and access to data generated by citizens. For instance, eBiodiversity (https://elurikkus.ee/en), which operates much on citizen generated data to understand biodiversity in Estonia, nation-wide campaigns are ran to incentivse. We carried out Donate your Speech campaign to incentivise people to make their speech data available as open data (https://oecd-opsi.org/blog/estonians-donate-a-speech-preserving-language-and-driving-digital-service-delivery/). Similarly, there are other initiatives related to weather, trash, energy consumption, infrastructure which incentivise publication/access to citizen generated data.

column13:
2025:
Our community has grown and now we have around 700 people. 
2024:
We have large network of data-related experts from the public, private sector and academia, which includes around 600 people. 
The Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications (MoEAC) is responsible for leading open data policy in Estonia.
The have established public sector inter-departmental open data working group, which involves members from different interested ministries and other public sector organizations (e.g. National Audit Office, City of Tallinn). The working group meets on a regular basis (at least once a month) and participation is also open to non-members (e.g. civil society, private companies, academia). The working group aim is to share news, upcoming changes, share experiences. 
Other stakeholders can participate in the governance process through stakeholder discussion events, such as the annual Open Data Forum or smaller workshops throughout the year devoted to specific open data issues. 
Almost two years ago the MoEAC together with other public authorities established Data Stewards Steering Group. Data Stewards Steering Group brings together data stewards from different public authorities to ensure the sustainable and balanced development of the data field. Steering group focuses on such topics as data retrieval, data quality improvement, data re-use, data life cycle management, and data protection requirements.
Moreover, we have our own network on place connecting more than 600+ public sector officials, which we use for information sharing, conducting surveys, promotion of events, etc.

column13:
All mentioned problems and others are constantly addressed. The greatest potential we see in open dialogue and being open for support requests.
1) "Making publishing and (re)use of data a priority for the authorities" - we underline the importance of the open data through various events and showing the real impact of open data using different reuse cases. We've created the support mechanisms like help with dataset description, meetings where we talk about open data 101, educational videos and courses about our portal and open data in general for the begginers, etc.  
2) "Increasing open data quality and availability" - together with other authorities we work on creating the guidlines and instructions for data managment in general. Also, we have a regular steeward group meetings, where all data related questions are addressed and best data managment experiences get shared. From the side of the technical infrastracture, we are working daily on making national open data portal more useful, comfortable and having range of functionalities. 
3) "Tackling human resource problem" - educating public sector officials is one of lines we are puting a lot of effort. We create our own e-courses, hire professionals for conducting physycal and online courses, as well as working with universities to involve more data and open data topics into all universities' programms and creating a new once.

* Please describe (1) the workflows you have to automate the harvesting of metadata and (2) for which types of data these apply to
column13:
We use metashare and geosync. As for mirroring jobs API endpoint the client sends data to the data portal. 
Metashare and geosync have IDs that link the datasets in our portal to the source. Every morning our CRON checks if the id's match with the source, if the id matches and new information is given, then the dataset is overwritten. Geo-sync:https://koodivaramu.eesti.ee/andmete-teabevarav/geonetwork-sync (access restricted). Mirroring job datasets are only updated when the client has sent a new request to overwrite data or create new datasets. Majority of such workflows cover statistical, geospatial, linguistic and administrative data.

column13: The implementation of the HVD profile, incl applicable legislation element, is in progress along with the implenentation of DGA harvesting and the overall re-development of the Estonian National Data Portal. The technical implementation of the HVD profile is relatively simple, we note that the use of the profile might be inconsistent, especially in the way on how different agencies and countries define HVD data services and distributions. Clear guidelines with rich examples would be much needed in this regard.

column6:

For Explanation:
* If yes, please specify how and highlight challenges if any.
* If you are an EFTA or a candidate country to the EU, please select 'not applicable'.
column13:
2025:
We have supported HVD holders to ensure their data is in the required formats and properly described.
2024:
We have updated the national metadata standard, the latest version fully supports the DCAT-AP HVD profile, therefore also ensuring interoperability with all other countries that have implemented the HVD profile. We have established core vocabularies which are required to be used. The main challenge we foresee is the lack of clear guidance on defining HVD data services and distributions, which might lead to inconsistent practices throughout member states. We hope that the EC will extend its current guidance as a matter of urgency.

Do you have a definition of open data reuse in your country?
 
For Explanation:
* If yes, please specify it.
column13:
According to Public Information Act (https://www.riigiteataja.ee/en/eli/ee/510122021005/consolide/current) § 3.  Re-use of public information
 (1) The re-use of information is the use of such public information, the public use of which is not restricted by law or pursuant to the procedure established by law (hereinafter open data), by natural persons or legal persons for commercial or non-commercial purposes other than the initial purpose within the public duties for which the information was obtained or produced. The exchange of information between holders of information for the performance of their public duties does not constitute re-use of information.

column6:
Is any data on the impact created by open data on governmental challenges (e.g. efficiency, effectiveness, transparency, decision-making capacity) available in your country such as from research studies, impact assessments, or other systematic investigations that quantify the results or broader effects of open data being reused?

For Explanation:
* If yes, please (1) specify what kind of data source proves this impact and (2) provide the URLs to this data.
column13:
Main impact includes government being more efficient and transparent. Also, we see an increasing trend on data-driven decision/making on governmental level. We notice that enteties tend to have more willingness to develope technologies and find the ways of solving problems using data. 
The impact can be monitored mostly by the reuse. Open data reuse is very popular internally within the organization: many institutions have created interesting usage stories based on their open data, the most common of which are data visualizations. There are institutions that have found that they help non-thematic parties to better interpret very specific data and thus alleviate the institution's workload of clarifying the data logic.  Reuse cases can be found on our national portal in the use cases section https://avaandmed.eesti.ee/usage-stories. The number of use cases is constantly growing.  
Every year we carry out an impact assessment of open data and data managment in the public sector, results are published on our open data portal (on estonian language). Year 2022  - https://avaandmed.eesti.ee/instructions/avaandmete-mojuhinnang-avalikus-sektoris-2022

The yearly impact assessments are a systematic study, not anecdotal. Which are in addition assisted with additional studies and impact assessment requirements for public bodies. There are examples in all ministries and areas, where impact has been created and measured. For instance, Estonian Agricultural Registry is using satellite data (open data available through esthub) to verify whether the grasslands have been mowed to automate and support decision-making capacity, transportation authority is using open data to understand the likelihood of traffic accidents happening and plan investments to improve traffic management, Tallinn is using open data gathered through crowdsourcing to plan public investments in road maintenance and planning (https://gis.tallinn.ee/andmekorje/?fbclid=IwAR14eN87q_KGScM_E8jJVHHPdbOUdKnUKsss3rD-a24dFMZYMosQZ-JH_aU), and so forth. 

For instance, in the traffic accident likelihood project, we understood what are the key factors that contribute to the traffic accidents and how likely it is that traffic accidents take place, the F1 score was for specific classes (road which are less likely to have any major accidents and thus need intervention) was 0.98794618 and so forth. In the agriculture use-cases, the precision is roughly 85%, which means in most cases the public official doesn’t need to do on-site inspections, thus contributing to efficiency.

column13:
2025:
The "Andmetorm 2024" hackathon, organized by the Estonian Environment Agency in collaboration with the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications and Garage48, served as a platform to explore innovative applications of open climate data. Beyond its primary goal of identifying use cases for climate data, the event significantly contributed to enhancing public sector efficiency through the strategic utilization of open data.
One notable outcome was the development of AI models capable of detecting and predicting urban flooding using open datasets such as radar information, traffic camera footage, and elevation models. These tools provide real-time insights and forecasts, offering critical support to emergency services, police, and rescue centers. https://keskkonnaagentuur.ee/node/2053
2024:
Yes, open data in our country is enhancing the efficiency and effectiveness of government services. An example is SATIKAS, an automated satellite-based information system that detects mowing using satellite data. This system automates the EU’s agricultural subsidy checks, reducing the need for inspectors' field visits, saving time and money, and reminding farmers who haven't met mowing requirements. Developed by the UT Tartu Observatory, the Estonian Agricultural Registers and Information Board (ARIB), and CGI, SATIKAS demonstrates significant impact. More information can be found here (https://www.pria.ee/uudised/niitmise-tuvastamise-susteemi-arengud), and the related dataset is available here (https://avaandmed.eesti.ee/datasets/niitmise-tuvastamine-satelliitseirega).

column13: Yes, open data is impacting housing issues in urban areas in our country. The Ministry of Climate's open data is used for planning energy-efficient building renovations, promoting environmentally friendly mobility, and implementing nature-based solutions in urban areas. One key resource is the Building Register (https://avaandmed.eesti.ee/datasets/ehitisregister). column13:
Draft Law for the change of the Law on eGovernment includes articles which incentivise institutions to publish access to real-time and dynamic data. URL: https://mduls.gov.rs/wp-content/uploads/Nacrt-izmena-i-dopuna-Zakona-o-eUpravi.docx                                           
According to Article 27 of the Law on Open Data, public sector bodies are obliged to publish open data on the Open Data Portal, including:
Dynamic datasets,
Datasets of particular social importance, and
All datasets previously created in response to reuse requests,
in a machine-readable format and in a way that facilitates easy access and reuse.
Specific Measures Related to Dynamic Data (Draft Law Highlights):
Dynamic data are explicitly defined (Article 25a) as datasets that frequently change and are updated in real time due to their fast obsolescence.
The law obliges public authorities to make these datasets available, especially when they are of high public value (e.g., transport data, environmental monitoring, emergency services).
The access to such data is provided free of charge, removing financial barriers for reuse.
The law encourages reuse by requiring that any dataset previously prepared in response to a reuse request must also be published – thus expanding the scope of available dynamic data over time.
These provisions, especially the obligation to publish dynamic and high-value datasets, create a strong legal incentive for institutions to actively share real-time data for public and commercial reuse.
 As part of the annual training programs conducted within the curriculum of the National Academy for Public Administration, institutions are recommended to publish real-time (dynamic) data whenever possible.
This recommendation is part of building institutional capacity for open data management and promoting proactive data sharing.
A concrete proof of implementation of this strategic guidance is the existence of several published APIs in the APR (Business Registers Agency) and HVD (High-Value Datasets) categories, which are already available on the National Open Data Portal. These include real-time data services, demonstrating both the technical feasibility and institutional commitment to making dynamic data publicly available.

column13:
2025:
In partnership with the Ministry for Public Administration and Local-Self Governance, Office for IT and eGovernment has tackled main challenges when it comes to open data initiatieve. HVDs are introduced in the draft Law on changes of the Law on eGovernment, standards for HVDs are developed with almost all HVD holders, delegating data officer will be mandatory, etc.  
2024:
The new project focused on open data has started, and it will be implemented by Office for IT and eGovernment, in partnership with UNDP, with support by the United Kingdom. Most of the challenges will be addressed through it. Additionaly, measure for change of the legislative framework has became part of the Programme for development of eGovernment. The new project started in April 2024, and activities which have been implemented up to date are: establishment of the working group for change of the Law on eGovernemnt and Open Data Portal Regulation. Previous to the establishment of the working group, SIGMA has supported consultancy work on Regulatory impact analysis and harmonization with EU PSI Directive and HVD Implementation Act. This has been used as a basis for work of the Working Group. Also, in parallel, we have started cooperation with the Serbian Agency for Environmental Protection to harmonize their open data sets standards with HVD Implementation Act, making them a first institution (pilot), even before it becomes mandatory for all HVD holders.

column6:
Do you have a methodology in place to measure the impact of open data in your country?
 
For Explanation:
* If yes, please briefly describe the key points of this methodology.
column13:
Methodology is developed in partnership with UNDP, in 2019. URL (linked also on the National Open Data Portal) https://www.undp.org/sr/serbia/publications/potencijalni-uticaj-otvaranja-podataka-u-srbiji  Framework for open data impact indicators  which is proposed in this methodology  is
based on several dimensions.
First the dimension of balancing lead and lag indicators. Lead indicators show whether the right
things to enable open data impact are happening (as no impact would be possible otherwise),
and lag indicators to assess what impact is visible.
Second, establishing indicators along the entire value chain that leads to socio-economic impact
of open data, as apparent from the reviewed research. This value chain runs from data provision,
government efficiency gains, demand and adoption, time and resource investment by external
stakeholders, re-use examples, policy implementation, ecosystem formation, to higher order
usage and network effects.
For the different steps in that chain, both lead and lag indicators can be put forward, along with
the methods to measure them where such experience exists in the research taken into account.
Third, indicators as much as possible should be of the ‘vector’ type (measuring direction and
speed), which more likely leads to more objective measurements. The exact list of indicators is available starting from page 53 of the publication.

The Office for IT and eGovernment, as the body responsible for managing the National Open Data Portal, has established an automated monitoring system using a custom Power BI solution. This system enables continuous tracking of user interactions with the portal and the datasets published on it.

The number of visits and downloads for each dataset,
Trends in user interest over time,
The most accessed datasets.

The centralized dashboards and data visualizations have reduced duplication of efforts, accelerated the timing of operational decisions related to environmental monitoring, and fostered a more integrated working culture within SEPA.

Enabled weekly rather than monthly planning meetings, as key insights are now immediately accessible;
Fostered a more proactive approach to field operations, with data trends triggering internal alerts when thresholds are breached or coverage gaps appear.
Moreover, easier access to visualized data has increased staff engagement—environmental inspectors and analysts regularly use the dashboards not only for formal planning but also to support on-the-ground decisions, such as determining optimal times and locations for inspections or community engagement.

2024:
Czech National Open Data Policy is defined by the Free Access to Information Act No. 106/1999 Coll. that enables public bodies to publish their data in open and machine readable formats. It introduces the term “open data” and underlines the role of National Open Data Catalog as its main information platform for open data in the Czech Republic. It is obliged by the Free Access of Information Act that all public bodies that publish open data, have to catalog it into the National Open Data Catalog. Moreover, section 5a of the Free Access to Information Act No. 106/1999 Coll. defines that data that are public by law must be mandatorily published as open data (Open Data by Default). The Open Data Directive transposition was the part of the amendment of the Act No. 106/1999 Coll. that came into force in September 2022. See: https://www.e-sbirka.cz/sb/1999/106/2024-01-01?zalozka=text.

It is obliged by the Free Access of Information Act that all public bodies that publish open data, have to catalog it into the National Open Data Portal. Moreover, Free Access to Information Act No. 106/1999 Coll. defines data which must be mandatorily published as open data. The previous government regulation No. 425/2016 Coll. with a list of datasets was replaced by the new obligation defined in section 5a of the Free Access to Information Act No. 106/1999 Coll. The Open Data Directive transposition was the part  the amendment of the Act No. 106/1999 Coll. came into force in September 2022.

2024:
The National Open Data Strategy is defined by two documents. The first one is the national digitisation strategy Digital Czechia adopted in 2018 and its main part that sets out the basic framework called Information Conception. Open Data Strategy is fragmented into several principles and main goals of the Conception since it is not seen as a self-sustaining policy, but one of the building blocks of the digitization process. OD Strategy is supported primarily by the Principles P4 called Openness and Transparency and P13 called Open Data by Default of the Conception and the main objective 1.5 Development of the National Open Data Catalog and 5.10 Public Data Fund that strengthen the position of the open data both practically by supporting its position in data sharing process and legislatively by introducing the Open Data by Default principle. See https://digitalnicesko.gov.cz/vize/#ctyri-pilire-digitalniho-ceska and https://archi.gov.cz/en:ikcr.
The second one, adopted by the Government in 2024, is called the Strategy for Data Management in Public Administration of the Czech Republic 2024-2030, where Objective 4.1 Publication of Open Data aims to fulfill legal obligations related to the publication of open data and to ensure their traceability, quality and reuse. See: https://data.gov.cz/přílohy/články/projekt-DIA-pomůže-úřadům-zlepšit-správu-dat/Strategie%20pro%20správu%20dat%20ve%20VS.pdf. 
2023:
The National Open Data Strategy is defined by the national digitisation strategy Digital Czechia adopted in 2018 and the main document that sets out the basic framework for this strategy called Information Conception. Open Data Strategy is fragmented into several principles and main goals of the Conception since it is not seen as a self-sustaining policy, but one of the building blocks of the digitization process. OD Strategy is supported primarily by the Principles P4 called Openness and Transparency and P13 called Open Data by Default of the Conception and the main objective 1.5 Development of the National Open Data Catalog and 5.10 Public Data Fund that strengthen the position of the open data both practically by supporting its position in data sharing process and legislatively by introducing the Open Data by Default principle. The Public Data Fund should provide guaranteed open data that users can rely on. In the first phase, these should be the code lists. 
See https://www.digitalnicesko.cz/informacni-koncepce-cr/ and https://archi.gov.cz/en:ikcr.

2024:
The National Open Data Portal created in accordance with Information Conception of the Czech Republic and legislatively enforced by the Act No. 106/1999 Coll., directly and automatically sends all metadata to the European Data Portal, aforementioned types of data included. For the process see: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1PtaZCXN3VBlAgXdeE6y4-qjPP3aPGJHs3Re6wI84jFc/edit#slide=id.ge280a34ec0_0_6 (slide 20). Regarding dynamic data, in accordance with the new standards (from May 2024), which are mandatory, providers should mark the data with a link to the relevant legislation (dynamic data are part of the specific paragraph of the Act 106/1999 Coll.). In the past, they have used keywords and descriptions, which have made their way into the European Data Portal. In the case of citizen generated data, currently, according to the findings in the National Open Data Team, they are published in the National Catalog (and therefore in the European Data Portal) through public authorities and their affiliation to the aforementioned group is usually part of the description (e.g. https://data.gov.cz/datov%C3%A1-sada?iri=https%3A%2F%2Fdata.gov.cz%2Fzdroj%2Fdatov%C3%A9-sady%2F65993390%2F1087749998, https://data.gov.cz/datov%C3%A1-sada?iri=https%3A%2F%2Fdata.gov.cz%2Fzdroj%2Fdatov%C3%A9-sady%2F44992785%2Faee8d88c79b4e167a10b57c0ce827ec5).

For Explanation:
* If yes, please briefly describe the measures.
column13:
2024:
The Act No. 106/1999 introduces the so-called standard conditions of use, which must be respected by obliged entities when providing information (in open data format included). These are defined in § 4a as conditions that are "objective, reasonable, non-discriminatory, non-exclusive and do not limit the method or purpose of subsequent use of the information provided". Therefore, obliged entities cannot limit further use of data and information to non-commercial use only and should support the reuse by the private sector in any possible way.  

The Act further states that information about products and services that use open data and other information should be registered in the national catalog, which, according to the explanatory report to the act, should support reuse by the public and business. Finally, support for re-use is also part of the measures in the Strategy of Data Management for Public Sector - 4.1.3: Provide practical support for the reuse of open data.
2023:
The Information Conception of the Czech Republic fosters the existence of the Public Data Fund. The Public Data Fund should provide guaranteed open data (in the first phase the code lists). Due to new obligations related to fulfillment the base register of rights and duties, the data users will have an overview which public data are collected following the agendas and gain the link to the dataset in the National Open Data Catalog. See Goal  5.10 of the Conception at https://archi.gov.cz/en:ikcr#sub-objective_510develop_open_data_and_public_data_and_public_services or https://archi.gov.cz/en:nap:verejny_datovy_fond

from which source systems the data comes and how and to whom it is shared. Local inventories are harvested by national inventory.
2023:
In the Czech Republic there is an inventory called The Register of Rights and Duties - a register that provides a basic overview of the agendas carried out by public authorities and the related data. According to the Act No. 111/2009 Coll., public authorities are obliged to identify what data in agenda is classified and to distinguish public and non-public data. A new methodology for defining data in the agenda has been developed in 2022/2023, according to which organisations should proceed. The objective 3.04 of the Information Conception is aimed at improving, updating and validating the content of the Register.

column13:

According to the Act No. 111/2009 Coll., public authorities are obliged to identify what data in agenda is classified, it means public as well as non-public data. Only public data are supposed to be open by default and published in the National Open Data Portal (Catalog). The Inventory List created in connection with the DGA is connected to the Register of Rights and Duties, where public and non-public data are distinguished and those data that meet the requirements of the DGA are harvested.
2023:

In addition, the Data Management Act (transposition of Chapter 2 of the DGA) is currently being drafted and includes an obligation to establish an inventory list of all available public sector data sources. It is assumed that this list will be directly linked to the inventory called the Register of Rights and Duties (see 9a).

column13: Implementing regulation on HVD was directly transposed into Act. 106/1999 Coll. and is directly binding on public entities. column13: At the beginning of the process of data opening, a bottom-up approach worked in the Czech Republic - a few providers decided to open data in a good quality as a result of small local iniciatives. Subsequently, a public body (the National Open Data Team) was created within the hybrid governance model to assist these providers, but still without support of legislation. Currently, the data opening takes place within the top-down model, where the obligation to open data is anchored by the principle of open data by default, and all affected entities must participate in the process, cooperate with the National Open Data Team and publish open data in the National Open Data Catalog.

Following previous monitoring and financing options, the Government Council for Information Society's priority plan, which also includes open data, is updated annually. column6:
Is there a pre-defined approach to ensure that metadata is kept up-to-date?

For Explanation:
* If yes, please briefly describe your approach.
column13:
2025:
There is no mandatory part of the metadata record that would have to be updated when the data is updated. However, the quality of all metadata records can be monitored directly on the Open Data Portal, through which the Open Data Team informs providers of discrepancies. The information on the status of the metadata is then further compiled in the Annual Open Data Status Report (https://data.gov.cz/výroční-zprávy/), which is reported directly to government, putting pressure on providers to ensure that the quality of the data and metadata is a high as possible and regularly updated. In addition, the most important providers are part of the OD Working Group under the Government's Information Society Council “RVIS”. At all meetings of the group, which are led by the National Open Data Team, they are informed of the need to regularly update metadata and data itself (meeting are held 4 times a year, see RVIS Annual Report where the emphasis on data quality is specifically mentioned, see https://vlada.gov.cz/cz/ppov/rvis/vyrocni_zpravy/zprava-o-cinnosti-rady-vlady-pro-informacni-spolecnost-od-1--ledna-do-31--prosince-2023-215356/).

column13: The second option for metadata registration for larger or more advanced providers is to use a local catalog. It can be implemented as any software, but the condition for its use with the national portal is compliance with DCAT-AP-CZ, which is also used by the national portal. Such a local catalog is registered only once using one data message, and then all metadata changes take place only in the local catalog. The national catalog then harvests the local catalog at regular intervals (approx. once every 24 hours) - it reads the metadata records and forms their image in the national catalog.

column13: The National Open Data Team has prepared guidelines for ensuring high-quality metadata. It also regularly monitors and evaluates the quality of metadata at the working group, which motivates providers to improve the quality of metadata. At the same time, it conditions the registration of metadata itself by meeting qualitative requirements in accordance with the DCAT-AP-CZ standard, which is also mandatory by law.
